->SENDS MANY GREETINGS<- <note>original Latin: "S. P. D.", an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*, a formal greeting.</note>

For a long time now, the world of scholars has desired that the men of that religion—which even to this day is known by the name of <term>heresy<gloss>a belief or opinion contrary to orthodox religious (especially Christian) doctrine.</gloss></term>—be presented as if on a stage <note>The author uses the metaphor of a "theater" or "stage" to describe the public, organized presentation of these historical figures and their ideas.</note>. I will not dwell on praises of the author; for the sublime gifts of his mind, in

WOLFGANG FABRICIUS CAPITO, minister of the church at Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentinensis"; Latin name for Strasbourg</note>; born in the year 1481. Died in 1541. Concerning him, the Ministers and elders of Transylvania, in their book *On the Divinity of the Mediator, the Man Jesus Christ* <note>original: "de Mediatoris hominis Jesu Christi divinitate"</note>, write the following: *Fabricius Capito, a man distinguished for his piety and learning, after praising the excellent spiritual gifts of his companion Cellarius and the utility of his booklet [specifically, "On the Works of God"], lists several articles of religion about which he had privately discussed with Cellarius; namely, concerning the knowledge of the one God and of Christ, concerning the Holy Spirit, etc.* His works are these:

A preliminary letter, or brief preface, written in Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentinæ"</note> on July 12, 1527, and prefixed to Master Martin Cellarius’s writing *On the Works of God* <note>original: "de Operibus Dei"</note>, published by the aforementioned Ministers of Transylvania at Alba Julia <note>A city in modern-day Romania, then a center of the Transylvanian Reformation</note> in 1568, in quarto format.

Hebrew Institutions <note>original: "Institutiones Hebraicæ"; a textbook on Hebrew grammar</note>.

Commentaries on several prophets.

The author himself, in the preface just mentioned, has this to say regarding his own works: *Indeed, this work of Cellarius on the works of God (however excellent) and Bucer’s <note>Referring to Martin Bucer, the primary Reformer of Strasbourg</note> Matthew, which soberly teaches many things beyond common judgment; likewise Hosea, Malachi, and our Jonah, in which we pursued what belongs to God and truth according to our modest ability, in a style not too different from Cellarius’s phraseology—I say, our works together with their authors, which is to say with us, as is the human condition, will all fall and [perish...]* <note>The text cuts off here due to the page break; the catchword "interi-" suggests the Latin "interibunt," meaning "will perish."</note>

# JUAN DE VALDÉS
## (Johannes Valdesius)
**A Spanish Noble, legal consultant, and Secretary to the King of Naples.** It is said that he brought the writings of Luther, Bucer, and the Anabaptists with him from Germany to Naples. From him, Bernardino Ochino is said to have absorbed his views against the accepted opinion on the Trinity. He flourished in the year 1542. Concerning him, the Ministers of the churches in agreement in Sarmatia <note>A historical name for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note> and Transylvania, in Book 1, Chapter 3 of *On the False and True Knowledge of the One God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit* <note>original: "de falsa & vera unius Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti cognitione"</note>, write the following: *What should be said of Juan de Valdés, most distinguished in lineage and piety? Leaving us specimens of his erudition in public writings, he writes that he knows nothing else of God and his Son than that there is one most high God, the Father of Christ: and our only Lord Jesus Christ his son, who was conceived of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin: one and the same Spirit of them both.*

*   *Dialogues between Charon and Mercury*, printed in Italian.
*   *Pious and Learned Considerations*.
*   *On several Psalms*.
*   *On the Gospel of Matthew*.
*   *On the Gospel of John*.
*   *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*, 1556.
*   *A brief commentary, or a concise and familiar explanation, on the first epistle of Saint Paul to the Corinthians, very useful for all lovers of Christian piety.* <note>original: "Comentario breve, ò declaracion compendiosa, y familiar, sobre la primera epistola de san Pablo à los Corinthios, muy util para todos los amadores de la piedad Christiana"</note> This book is prohibited in the Spanish *Index Expurgatorius* <note>The list of books banned or censored by the Catholic Church</note>, both with and without the author's name.

He left the monastery in the year 1542. Bzovius, in the place cited, says he left Italy because he had been summoned to Rome,

### ANTI-TRINITARIANS

->A 2<-

...to God because of things he had uttered differently in a certain sermon. Specifically (as others have recorded in writing), on Palm Sunday, he sharply criticized the pomp of the Roman Pope in his very presence from the pulpit—making a comparison with the Lord Jesus entering Jerusalem in a state of poverty—and the life of the Roman Pontiffs. When the sermon ended, one of the Cardinals indicated to him that the Pope was offended and persuaded him to escape the immediate danger by flight at once. Thus, he soon set out on a journey and withdrew to Venice. The Duchess of Ferrara aided his flight by supplying him with clothing and other necessities, as Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzovius (1567–1637), a Polish Dominican historian and hagiographer</note> testifies in the aforementioned place. For at that time in those regions, his authority—gained through his teaching, eloquence, and above all, the integrity of his character—was great. This is clear even from a single eulogy by Bzovius himself, which he did not hesitate to offer him; for he says of Ochino in that same place: *He was held in such high esteem then that he was considered the one best preacher in all of Italy, as one who, by his admirable delivery as well as the eloquence of his tongue, could carry the minds of his listeners wherever he wished, and all the more so because his life resonated with his teaching.*

To this also belongs the testimony given to him by Fulvia Morata <note>Olympia Fulvia Morata (1526–1555), an Italian Protestant scholar of great renown</note> in Book II of her letters to her sister Victoria Morata, in a letter written on the 7th of the Ides of August in the year 1555 (as I gather from the immediately preceding letters), where she relates these things: *I hear that Bernardino Ocellus* <gloss>that is what Ochinus sounds like in the Italian language</gloss> *of Siena, a sincerely Christian man, has fled from England to Geneva. So everywhere must the cross be borne by him who wishes to be a Christian.*

In the year 1563, at the age of 76 (according to the testimony of Petrus Perna <note>A famous printer in Basel who specialized in Italian Reformers</note> in a letter to Czechowic), he was expelled by the Zurichers. In the bitterest winter, with all roads blocked by snow and ice—as Bzovius relates from a letter of Dudith to Beza <note>Andreas Dudith, a humanist diplomat, and Theodore Beza, Calvin’s successor</note> in the aforementioned place, section 28—he went from there to Poland.

Regarding his death, various authors write in different ways. Budzinius testifies in his manuscript *History of the Polish Churches of His Time*, chapter 26, that due to mandates issued in 1564 against foreigners who harbored opinions on the Trinity differing from the common one, he was driven out of Poland. Having lost two sons and his eldest daughter to the spreading plague, he withdrew to Moravia, and died there in Slavkov <note>original: "Slavcoviæ"</note> after three weeks had passed. Some (such as Hoornbeek), having misunderstood a passage by Zarnovecius in his book against Fausto Sozzini <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), a founding figure of Socinianism</note>, thought that he [died in the company of] Lælius Socinus...

# HISTORY OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS

->A 3<-

**A Book on Polygamy**, written in Poland and dedicated to Sigismund II, King of Poland: according to the testimony of Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzowski (1567–1637), a Dominican historian and continuator of the *Annales Ecclesiastici*</note> under the year 1542, section 30.

**Thirty Dialogues**, divided into two books, the first of which is concerning the Messiah and contains eighteen dialogues. The second book concerns various matters, but most especially the Trinity. Originally in Italian. The first book is dedicated to the Earl of Bedford <note>Francis Russell, 2nd Earl of Bedford, a prominent English supporter of the Reformation</note>; the second, however, is dedicated to Prince Nicolaus Radziwiłł <note>Mikołaj "the Black" Radziwiłł (1515–1565), a powerful Lithuanian noble and patron of the Reformation</note>, Duke in Olyka and Nyasvizh, Palatine of Vilnius, Grand Chancellor of the Duchy of Lithuania, Supreme Marshal, and Commander of the military.

The same works were published in Latin at Basel by Petrus Perna in the year 1563, with Sebastian Castellio <note>A French theologian and humanist known for translating the Bible and advocating for religious tolerance</note> as the translator. However, Heinrich Bullinger <note>The successor of Zwingli in Zurich and a leader of the Reformed Church</note> wrote in August of 1568 that Ochino, helped in secret by the efforts of certain Italians—just as he himself was Italian—wrote those *Dialogues* of his in the Italian language; and that he saw to it that they were printed in Basel by an Italian who was quite familiar and friendly with him, having been translated into the Latin language (as they say) by the work of certain Italians, without the knowledge of the ministers of the Church of Zurich <note>original: "Tigurinæ ecclefiæ"</note>.

Nevertheless, the persistent report concerning Castellio’s translation is confirmed not only by Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian</note> in Book 35 and Bzovius under the year 1542, section 30, but also by Andreas Dudith <note>Andreas Dudith (1533–1589), a humanist and diplomat who eventually joined the anti-Trinitarian movement</note> in his manuscript notes on these *Dialogues* of Ochino (which I happened to see). Regarding these words of Dialogue 18 on page 13, *The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you: and so that holy offspring shall be called, that is, shall be, the Son of God* <note>original: "Te Spiritus Sanctus invadet, & fupremi vis inumbrabit: itaque fanctus ifte partus dicetur, hoc eft, erit Dei filius"; a variation of Luke 1:35</note>, Dudith notes the following in the margin: *Even from this it is apparent that the translation belongs to Castellio*. This is evidently because the mentioned words were cited from Castellio's own translation of the Bible. 

Indeed, this is most clearly demonstrated by the confession of Castellio himself, which is read in his letter to the Consul and Senate of Basel, the beginning of which is as follows: *It has been shown to me, my most merciful Lords, by the Magnificent Lord Rector and the other Doctors and Pastors of the Church, that a letter was written to you in which I was most gravely accused. There are two parts to this accusation: one taken from the book of Theodore Beza <note>Calvin's successor in Geneva and a fierce opponent of both Ochino and Castellio</note>, and the other regarding my translation of the dialogues of Bernardino Ochino.* To this latter accusation, he responds at the end of the letter in this manner: *As for what pertains to the second part of the accusation, namely that I translated the Dialogues of Bernardino Ochino, I do not think...*

<meta>catchword: puto (think)</meta>

# LIBRARY

...I do not think this should be held against me. For I translated them (*just as I had translated his other works*) not as a judge, but as a translator, and from such work I am accustomed to making a living to support my family: and the printer said he had offered the book, and that according to the Basel regulations, it had been approved by the censorship. It also happens that in the same year these *Dialogues* were published in Basel, Castellio lived in that same place: where he also died on the 29th of December in that year, at the age of forty-eight. Bullinger <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a leading figure of the Swiss Reformation</note> reports in the cited place that copies of these *Dialogues* were burned in a very famous location.

**The same works in Dutch.** <note>The original Latin *Belgicè* refers to the language of the Low Countries, generally Dutch or Flemish in this period.</note>

Furthermore, those *Dialogues* were converted into various other languages, as Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzowski, a Dominican historian</note> asserts in the place mentioned. Where, after he says that Ochino was forced to flee from Krakow into Transylvania, he adds; *there he wrote certain dialogues, which were afterwards translated into various languages, and by Castellio indeed into Latin.* Hornbeeck <note>Johannes Hornbeeck (1617–1666), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note> testifies to the same in the first volume of his *Socinianism Confuted* <note>original: "Socinianismi confutati"</note>.

**A Catechism**, which Bzovius mentions was reprinted in the year 1591, originally in the year 1542, section 31.

**A Dialogue of Reason and Man:** which someone excerpted from his sermons and published in German.

# MICHAEL SERVETUS
otherwise known as Reves, or Renes, or Rennes: (*"Reves" was printed in the first edition of his books on the Trinity and the Dialogues [which by anagram would be "Serve"]; "de Renes" is read in the second edition; "Rennes" however is used in Alfonso Lincurius <note>A pseudonym for Matteo Gribaldi, a jurist who defended Servetus's memory</note>*) from Aragon, also known by the name Villanovanus <note>Referring to his family home in Villanueva de Sigena</note>, a Spaniard of Tarragona, a physician by profession. His opinion on the Trinity became known around the year 1523, since Beza <note>Theodore Beza, Calvin's successor in Geneva</note> writes in the preface to the *Acts of Gentilis* that he perished after thirty years of blasphemies: and in the *Life of Calvin*; *after he had infected heaven and earth for thirty whole years, both by voice and by writing.* Calvin himself, however, says that he had spread his dogmas for twenty years before his death, in letter number 156, written to Sulzer in the year 1553: where he says; *Since Michael Servetus, already twenty years ago, infected the Christian world with his virulent and pestiferous dogmas: no-*

...I think his name <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix of a word, likely "nomen" (name), referring to Michael Servetus.</note> is not unknown to you. Even if you have not read his book, it is hardly possible that you have not heard something about the nature of his doctrine itself. This is the man about whom that faithful minister of Christ, Master Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a prominent German Reformer known for his efforts to find common ground between different Protestant groups.</note> of holy memory—though otherwise of a gentle disposition—pronounced from the pulpit that he was worthy of having his entrails torn out and being ripped apart. Just as he has not ceased to spread his poison since that time, he recently and secretly arranged for a larger volume, stitched together from those same errors, to be printed in Vienna. But when the matter was brought to light, he was thrown into prison. Having escaped from there by some means, he wandered through Italy for nearly four months. Finally, having arrived here under ill omens, one of the syndics <note>A high-ranking municipal magistrate in Geneva.</note>, on my advice, ordered him to be taken to prison. For I do not hide the fact that I considered it my duty to restrain a man who was more than stubborn and untameable, as far as was in my power, so that the contagion would not spread any further. We see how licentiously impiety rages everywhere, so that new errors are constantly springing up; and how great is the laziness of those whom God has armed with the sword to avenge the glory of His name, etc. 

Perhaps in such a way Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), the successor to John Calvin in Geneva.</note> can be reconciled with Calvin, so that he might trace the beginning of these years back to the time when Servetus published his views in print; for in the year 1531, the first edition of his books *On the Errors of the Trinity* <note>original: "de Trinitatis erroribus"</note> was brought to light. He stayed mostly in Lyon <note>referred to in the Latin as "Lugdunum Gallorum"</note>, as Peter Hyperphrogenus of Ghent reports in his manuscript *History of Servetus and His Death*. There he lived quietly enough among the Papists <note>A common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics.</note>; a fact which Daniel Chamier of Dauphiné also testifies in the second volume of his *Catholic Panstratia*, book 1, chapter 5, section 4, where he writes: *God did not want this truth of doctrine [namely, regarding the Trinity] to be smothered in Popery along with many other articles. This same truth Calvin not only confessed, but also most constantly defended against the new heretics, even while the Papists were snoring—among whom Servetus lived safely as long as he lived. It was only then, when he came to Geneva, that he experienced both the force of truth in Calvin and the holy severity of a pious Magistrate, etc.* There in Geneva, while in transit seeking to reach Italy, he was intercepted and thrown into prison, and after several weeks, he was condemned to the stake. While being led to it, he is said to have cried out repeatedly:

->O God, save my soul! O Jesus, Son of the eternal God, have mercy on me!<- <note>original: "O Deus serva animam meam: O Iesu Fili Dei æterni miserere mei!"</note>

The wood-pile was made of bundles of green oak, still leafy, mixed with logs of wood. A crown of straw was placed on his head, and it was sprinkled with sulfur. His body was bound to a stake with an iron chain, and his neck with a thick rope wound four or five times loosely; his book was also tied to his thigh. The aforementioned Peter Hyperphrogenus <note>Likely a Latinized name for an eyewitness recorder or pseudonym for a contemporary chronicler.</note> recorded these things, among others, concerning his death:

*And so at last Servetus was led out and dragged away, and being scorched by a slow fire, he was burned entirely. In this fire, since for nearly two or three hours he was writhing about—and because a strong wind arose which blew the flame away—he was unable to die. Finally, as the wood failed, he began to wail and cry out: "Alas, wretched me, who cannot end my life on this pyre! Were not the two hundred gold crowns taken from me when I was captured—and not burned, despite the law's protest—and the gold necklace hanging from my neck, enough to buy plenty of wood and pile it up here for the consuming of miserable me?" William Farel <note>A prominent French Reformer and close associate of Calvin.</note>, the Senior Minister of the Church of Geneva and Calvin’s deputy, was present, and he did not cease shouting to Servetus in his final moments: "Believe in the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ!" To which Servetus replied constantly: "I believe Christ is the true Son of God, but not eternal" <note>This distinction was the heart of the heresy charge: Servetus believed Jesus was the "Son of the eternal God" but not the "eternal Son of God," denying his pre-existence before the Incarnation.</note>. And thus, finally, scorched and dying, he perished, commending his spirit into the hands of God the Father, etc.*

Servetus was burned at Geneva in the year 1553, on the 27th of October: as is clearly evident from Calvin's letter, Number 161, written to Farel at Geneva on the 26th of October of the year mentioned, where among other things he reports this:

*The "Comic Caesar" <note>Calvin’s derogatory nickname for Ami Perrin, the leader of the Libertine political faction in Geneva who opposed Calvin and sought leniency for Servetus.</note>, having faked illness for three days, finally entered the court to exempt that criminal [namely Servetus] from punishment. For he did not blush to ask that the investigation be brought before the Council of Two Hundred; nevertheless, he was condemned without controversy. Tomorrow he will be led to execution.*

->### HISTORY OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS.<-

It happened in the year 1553. To this also pertains the fact that in the year 1554, a book was published by Calvin <note>John Calvin, the influential French reformer in Geneva.</note> in which an account of the death of Servetus is contained, under this title: *A Faithful Exposition of the Errors of Michael Servetus, and a Brief Refutation of the Same: Wherein it is Taught that Heretics are to be Restrained by the Right of the Sword.* <note>original: "Fidelis expositio errorum Michaëlis Serveti, & brevis eorundem refutatio: ubi docetur jure gladii coërcendos esse hæreticos." The "right of the sword" refers to the state's authority to use capital punishment.</note> How old Servetus was when he met his death, I have not yet been able to ascertain. Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus, a later Italian theologian who founded the Socinian movement, which also denied the Trinity but differed from Servetus.</note> in the aforementioned place says: *It is most certain that Servetus, when he was executed, was an old man, and much older than Calvin,* etc.

Servetus held nearly the same opinion that Paul of Samosata <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who taught that Jesus was a mere man who became divine.</note>, Photinus <note>A 4th-century bishop who denied the pre-existence of Christ.</note>, and their followers and like-minded thinkers once fostered (to pass over some of the Church Fathers who taught the same); specifically, that he made a distinction between Jesus Christ the Son of God, and that "Word" of which St. John treats at the beginning of his Gospel. And in this matter, he differed most greatly from the doctrine of the other Unitarians, who now mostly go by the name of Socinians. Faustus Socinus himself hints at this in his book against Wujek <note>Jakub Wujek, a Polish Jesuit scholar.</note>, chapter 1. I thought it would not be out of place, therefore, if I produced here some excerpts from his books in which he sets forth his opinion on this matter. In the first book of *On the Errors of the Trinity*, pages 6 and 7, he speaks thus:

*Luke does not say that that "power" is called the Son; rather, that which was begotten by that power shall be called the Son of God, because that power of God takes the place of a man's seed. Nor do they notice how great and how wide are the mysteries of this Word and seed, in whose likeness it is said that "the seed of the sower is the Word of God" [Luke 8:11]: because just as Christ was begotten and born by the Word, so we are reborn by the Word of God. Reborn, says Peter, through the living Word of God [1 Peter 1:23], and he calls this an "immortal seed," and [James says] He brought us forth by the Word of truth [James 1:18]. Therefore, they have philosophized poorly who deny that the man [Jesus] is the Son, so that they might make a "Son" out of the Word. However, the truth of the matter is otherwise, and John thought it more fitting to say "the Word" than "the Son"—indeed, it is by reason of the Word that the flesh is called the Son. I will speak of the Word later; for now, let us preserve the proper honor and glory for Jesus Christ,* etc. In the same book, pages 20 and 21, he says this: *the sum of sums—so that you may know where my mind tends—except for that unique "Word" of John, I say that the entire scriptures, from the first even to the last, speak of the man himself [Jesus].*

->### BIBLIOTHECA<-

Christ. And <note>Servetus is being quoted here.</note> *that Word mentioned by John does not speak of him who is, but of him who was; the error lies in not understanding what that Word was, and how it was made flesh.* Do not let your own imaginations seduce you: rather, store this in the very depths of your heart, that in all the scriptures the Man Christ himself speaks: and let your thoughts always be directed toward him. I pray to God that he may give you a cheerful mind for hearing; I shall provide for you (setting aside all malice, hair-splitting, and ambiguity) the clearest scriptures, and I shall set God himself before your eyes, provided you always look into the face of Christ.

Furthermore, in his second book on page 48, while dealing with the beginning of the Gospel of John, he says: *In the beginning, that is, before all things. And Wisdom is said to have been created before all things: because before a man speaks, the meditation of the heart is required. And because God's Word <term>Sermo</term> <note>original: "Sermo." While "Verbum" is the standard Latin for "Word" in John 1:1, Servetus often used "Sermo" (Speech or Discourse) to emphasize the active nature of God's communication.</note> is Wisdom itself: for God cannot speak foolishly.* And thus the book of *Ecclesiasticus* <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach, a book of the biblical Apocrypha.</note> declares itself in chapter 1. For after it said; *Wisdom was created first of all*, it immediately added; *The fountain of Wisdom is the Word of God.* And in chapter 24: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, the first-born before every creature.* Now, that which comes out of the mouth is Speech. etc. And in the same place shortly after: *The Word, therefore, in God as He brings it forth, is God Himself speaking. After it is brought forth, it is the flesh itself, or the Word of God. Before that speech became flesh, it was understood as the very oracle of God, hidden within the darkness of the cloud and not yet manifested, because that Word was God.* 

And after the Word was made man, by "Word" we understand Christ himself, who is the Word of God and the voice of God. For just as a voice, he is brought forth from the mouth of God. And that he now is the Word is clear from the text of *Revelation 19:11. For he is the one whom John saw sitting upon a white horse, whose name is the Word of God.* Therefore, the transition having been made from Word into flesh, the flesh is called the Word. For of what use would it be to us that the Word was made flesh, if the flesh is not now called the Word? For John *saw the Word of life and touched it with his hands.* <note>A reference to 1 John 1:1.</note> In the same work on the following leaf, page 49: *The most powerful Word of God was able, without that mass of material things <note>original: "coagulo," referring to the physical "clotting" or coagulation of matter.</note>, to pass into the matter of flesh, and therefore Christ himself is now called the Word-Man, the Word-flesh.* The phrase *the Word was made flesh* can also be understood according to what is said of Christ: *I will put my Words in his mouth, and he shall speak in my name.* <note>A reference to the prophecy in Deuteronomy 18:18.</note>

*The Method of Syrups* <note>original: "Ratio syruporum"</note>, [published in] Paris 1537 and Venice 1545. <note>This was a medical treatise by Servetus, who was also a physician.</note>

**The Restoration of Christianity** <note>original: "Christianismi Restitutio"</note>, that is, the calling of the entire Apostolic Church back to its origins, with the knowledge of God, the faith of Christ, our justification, regeneration, baptism, and the eating of the Lord’s Supper fully restored; and finally, with the heavenly kingdom restored to us, the captivity of ungodly Babylon dissolved, and the Antichrist with his followers utterly destroyed. This volume is divided into six parts or sections, in the following manner:

**On the Divine Trinity**, showing that it is not an illusion of three indivisible things, but a true manifestation of God’s substance in the Word and its communication in the Spirit. In 7 books.

*Book One deals* with the man Jesus Christ and false idols: *or* it contains three axioms concerning Christ, and three arguments and refutations of the Pharisees, and as many from the Sophists <note>A derogatory term used by Reformers for Scholastic theologians who used complex logic</note>, along with the most absurd inferences regarding invisible things.

*The Second* explains twenty passages of Scripture.

*The Third* concerns the prefiguration of Christ’s person in the Word, the vision of God, and the substance <term>hypostasis; the fundamental reality or "being" that underlies a thing</term> of the Word.

*The Fourth* reveals the names of God and His all-encompassing essence, as well as the principles of all things.

*The Fifth* is about the Holy Spirit. Then follow two Dialogues, which constitute the sixth and seventh books:

*The First deals* with the shadows of the Law and the fulfillment in Christ, and the substance of angels, souls, and hell.

*The Second* teaches the manner of Christ’s generation, that he is not a creature nor of finite power, but truly to be adored and true God.

**II. On the faith and justice of the Kingdom of Christ**, surpassing the justice of the Law, and on charity. In 3 books.

Book I. Chapter 1. On Faith. Chapter 2. On the essence of faith. Chapter 3. On Justification. Chapter 4. On the Kingdom of Christ.

## The Restoration of Christianity
<note>original: "Christianismi Restitutio"</note>
That is, the calling of the entire Apostolic Church back to its origins <note>literally "to its thresholds"</note>, with the knowledge of God, the faith of Christ, our justification, regeneration, baptism, and the eating of the Lord’s Supper fully restored; with the heavenly kingdom finally returned to us, the captivity of impious Babylon <note>A common Reformation-era metaphor for the Roman Catholic Church</note> dissolved, and the Antichrist with his followers utterly destroyed. This volume is divided into six tomes or parts in the following manner:

### On the Divine Trinity
Demonstrating that within it there is no illusion of three indivisible things, but a true manifestation of the substance of God in the Word and a communication in the Spirit. In 7 books.

*Book One treats:* On the man Jesus Christ and false images <note>original: "simulacris falsis"</note>: or, it contains three axioms concerning Christ, three arguments and refutations of the Pharisees and as many of the Sophists <note>A derogatory term for Scholastic theologians who used complex logic</note>, with most absurd inferences about invisible things.

*Second [Book]* explains twenty passages of scripture.

*Third [Book]* on the prefiguration of the person of Christ in the Word, on the vision of God and the hypostasis <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or individual substance of a person</term> of the Word.

*Fourth [Book]* reveals the Names of God and His all-forming essence, and the principles of all things.

*Fifth [Book]* on the Holy Spirit. Then follow two Dialogues, which constitute the sixth and seventh books:

*The First [Dialogue] treats* the shadows of the law and the fulfillment in Christ, and the substance of angels, souls, and hell.

*The Second [Dialogue]* teaches the mode of Christ’s generation, that He is not a creature, nor of finite power, but truly to be adored and true God.

## II. On the faith and justice of the Kingdom of Christ surpassing the justice of the law, and on charity. In 3 books.

Book I. Chapter 1. On Faith. Chapter 2. On the essence of faith. Chapter 3. On Justification. Chapter 4. On the Kingdom of Christ.

Book II. On the Law and the Gospel, and the Jew and the Christian

...distinctions. **Chapter 1.** That the Christian excels the Jew. **Chapter 2.** That in the Law there was the justice of the flesh, while in the Gospel there is the justice of the spirit. **Chapter 3.** That in the Law there was the justice of works, while in the Gospel there is the justice of faith.

**Book III. On Charity compared with faith, and on good works.**
**Chapter 1.** On the difference between reward and glory. **Chapter 2.** On the illustrious titles of Charity. **Chapter 3.** What faith effects, and what Charity and works effect. **Chapter 4.** On the origin and efficacy of deeds. **Chapter 5.** On the comparison of Charity and faith, and the excellence of charity itself.

**III. On regeneration and the heavenly eating** <note>original: "manducatione superna." This refers to the spiritual consumption of Christ in the Eucharist or Lord's Supper.</note>, **and on the kingdom of the Antichrist, presented in 4 books.**

**Book I.** On the destruction of the world and the restoration of Christ. *The second part of the book* concerns the celestial, terrestrial, and infernal power of Satan and the Antichrist, and our victory.

**Book II.** On true circumcision, with the remaining mysteries of Christ and the Antichrist, all now completed: *divided into two parts.*

**Book III.** On the ministries of the Church of Christ and their efficacy: *in which are contained*; On the efficacy of the preaching of the Gospel, on the efficacy of Baptism, and on the Lord’s Supper.

**Book IV.** On the order of the mysteries of regeneration.

**IV. Thirty letters to John Calvin, preacher of the Genevans.** <note>Calvin and Servetus famously corresponded, a relationship that eventually led to Calvin's role in Servetus's arrest and execution.</note>

**V. Sixty signs of the Kingdom of the Antichrist and his revelation which is even now present.**

**VI. An apology on the mystery of the Trinity according to the teaching of the ancients, addressed to Philip Melanchthon and his colleagues.** <note>Philip Melanchthon was a key German Reformer and collaborator of Martin Luther.</note>

All these were printed in the year 1553 at Vienne <note>original: "Viennæ Allobrogum." This is Vienne in the Isère department of France, not Vienna, Austria.</note> in octavo, consisting of 734 pages. One copy of it is preserved in the Library of the Most Illustrious Prince of Hesse, which is in Kassel. This book is called by some the second edition of the books *On the Errors of the Trinity*: but the author changed, expanded, and corrected many things in it; as was evident to me when I compared both volumes with each other. At the front of this second edition of his books, Servetus placed this sentence from Revelation <note>original: "Apocalypsis"</note> chapter 12, verse 7: *There was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his Angels fighting with the Dragon.*

# OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS
## CHAPTER 3

->B 2<-

...[Gen]tile, Giulio Trevisan, Francesco de Ruego, Giacomo de Chiari, Francesco Negro, Dario Sozzini, Paolo Alciato, and others. Once this matter <note>Referring to their secret meetings in Vicenza where they questioned the Trinity</note> was made public, they were overwhelmed by a heavy persecution; some were punished with the death penalty, while the others were dispersed. To escape the most immediate danger to their lives, they left their fatherland and took refuge in various regions. Among these was the aforementioned Lelio Sozzini <note>original: "Lælius Socinus"</note>, who, having left his homeland, traveled through Switzerland, France, Britain, the Netherlands, Germany, and Poland, gradually instilling doctrines contrary to accepted dogmas in no small number of people in these regions. Concerning this, Girolamo Zanchi <note>original: "Zanchius," a prominent Italian Protestant reformer who remained Trinitarian</note> provides the following testimony in the preface to his book *On the Three Elohim*:

*When I was refuting,* he says, *Lelio Sozzini's impious interpretation of the first chapter of the Gospel according to John, I suppressed his name and called him only a "scoundrel" <note>original: "nebulonem"</note>. This was because I did not know for certain that he was the author of that little commentary, nor had I then read his name expressed in the books of our adversaries. Now, because the matter is all too manifest, and the followers of Servetus <note>Michael Servetus was a Spanish physician and theologian executed in Geneva for denying the Trinity</note> have recorded him in the number of their (so-called) "holy and pious doctors," I also make this known to you, Reader. This Lelio was born of a noble and honorable family; he was well-learned in Greek and Hebrew, and even his external life was blameless. For these reasons, a friendship of no ordinary kind had existed between me and him. But the man was full of diverse heresies, which he never proposed to me except for the sake of disputing, and always questioning as if he desired to be taught. Indeed, he fostered this <term>Samosatenian</term> <note>The heresy of Paul of Samosata, a 3rd-century bishop who taught that Jesus was a mere man who became divine, rather than the eternal Word of God</note> error especially for many years, and drew as many others as he could into the same error. And he drew away not a few. Me also, as I said, he tempted with various reasons to see if he could involve me in the same error and eternal destruction along with himself, just as he had done previously with Matteo Gribaldi and others.*

Thus says Zanchi in the place cited. Some things brought forward here do not differ from the eulogy that the Ministers of Poland <note>original: "Sarmatia"</note> and Transylvania tribute to him in this manner: *What shall we say of Lelio Sozzini of Siena, a man most skilled in the Hebrew tongue, whose writings now fly through the hands of the pious? A man irreproachable, who stayed for a long time at Wittenberg, Geneva, and Zurich, to the admiration of all.* This is from Book 1 of *On the False and True Knowledge of the One God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*.

The same in German: *On the resurrection of the bodies.* <note>original German: "Von der aufferstehung der Leiber."</note>

On heretics not being punished by the death penalty, under the name of Mino Celsi of Siena <note>Mino Celsi was an Italian exile; scholars long debated if this name was a pseudonym for Lelio Sozzini or Sebastiano Castellio, though Celsi is now recognized as an author in his own right.</note>: a work which some attribute to Fausto Sozzini; but it is much more likely to be Lelio’s. The second edition of this book appeared in the year 1584 in octavo, by the efforts of Valens Titus Ligius, with his dedicatory letter to Christoph Kniep of Saxony. Attached to this book on the same subject are two opposing letters by Theodore Beza and Andreas Dudith <note>Beza was Calvin’s successor in Geneva and supported the execution of heretics; Dudith was a diplomat and humanist who moved toward religious tolerance and anti-Trinitarianism.</note>: the first of which was written in Geneva on June 18, 1570, and the latter on August 1, 1570.

Rhapsody on the prophet Isaiah. This writing is cited by the collector of the compilation of passages concerning the Trinity.

Paraphrase on the beginning of the Gospel of St. John, written in the year 1561, as Fausto Sozzini <note>Lelio’s nephew and the primary systematizer of Socinianism.</note> testifies in his book *Against Eutropius*, chapter 4, where these words are read: *“Therefore, when either our people or those considered to be ours make John himself the speaker and use a paraphrase, they remain silent about his own voice. Just as was done in that paraphrase which was written in the year 1561 by that very man [a marginal note adds: Lelio Sozzini] who, of everyone in this our age (as far as we know), first taught from the sacred scriptures the opinion which we have embraced concerning the person of Jesus Christ. For in that paraphrase it is read thus: In the beginning of the Gospel was the Word of God <note>original Latin: "In Evangelii principio erat Dei sermo." The Socinians famously interpreted "In the beginning" as the start of Jesus's ministry rather than the start of the universe.</note>, etc. and in that writing, where the adversary reads that interpretation of the words, 'and the Word was God,' which he so strongly criticizes as being our own, shortly before these words there appear: 'John says therefore, In the beginning of the Gospel was the Word,' etc.”* So writes Fausto Sozzini in the mentioned place. Whether, besides this paraphrase (which until now I have not yet happened to see), Lelio Sozzini wrote an explanation on the first chapter of the Gospel of St. John, is not clear to me; just as it is also unclear who the author of that writing is from which Fausto Sozzini produced the last-quoted words. For in these explanations of the beginning of the Gospel of St. John which now exist, I do not find those words.

### LIBRARY

Moreover, around the mentioned time, two explanations of the beginning of the Gospel of St. John appeared. The beginning of one of them is as follows: *Since many abuse this chapter of John to establish the inventions of men, concerning a Son of God, Christ, whom they imagine to be eternal, twice-born, of two natures, and incarnate; and they do this against all truth, whereby not only the whole of Scripture concerning Christ the Son of God is obscured, corrupted, and perverted; but even that Christ the Son of God foretold by Moses, the Prophets, and in the whole Old Testament, and always looked for before by all the pious, who was afterwards conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of Mary, suffered and died for us, is utterly rooted out. Nay, and a second God is introduced, to the abolishing of the only, true, and highest God, the Father of Christ. Therefore, lest the pious suffer themselves to be led away from that one and only God the Father, and also from Christ, His only Son, whom the Father commended to us from heaven; I shall briefly touch upon only the main points of the matters in controversy in this chapter, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Cum plerique abutantur hoc Ioannis capite..." This passage outlines a radical Unitarian view, arguing that the traditional doctrine of the Trinity and the dual nature of Christ actually obscures the biblical Jesus.</note> Furthermore, the other explanation begins thus: *Since (as we warned in the letter to the reader) the things that must be said, being for the most part new and unheard of in our age, will perhaps appear suspicious at first glance, it seemed best to preface a few small things which might both remove suspicion and at the same time contribute not a little to understanding them, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Quoniam (ut in epistola ad lectorem monuimus)..."</note> The first of these explanations is found in the book of the Ministers of Poland <term>Sarmatia; a historical name for the region of Poland and Lithuania</term> and Transylvania <note>A region in modern-day Romania that was a major center for religious tolerance and Anti-Trinitarianism in the 16th century.</note> concerning the false and true knowledge of God, <insert>printed in the year 1567 at Alba Iulia</insert> <note>Alba Iulia (Latin: Alba Julia) was the capital of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom and a site of important religious debates.</note>, where it constitutes the eleventh chapter of the second book. The latter, however, has been printed elsewhere, especially in the *Library of the Polish Brethren Unitarians*, among the works of Faustus Socinus. Francis Junius <note>François du Jon (1545–1602), a prominent Reformed theologian who wrote against the Anti-Trinitarians.</note> inserted both of them into his third defense of the Trinity. However, they did not come into his hands as augmented and corrected as they are read in the aforementioned volumes. He obtained the first in printed form, but the second only as a manuscript (which he nevertheless says was more accurately drafted). This latter one was translated into the Polish language, as is evident from the words of Faustus Socinus, which are read in the book against Eutropius, chapter 4, in this manner: *Moreover, these things which we have said here concerning the beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Adversary could have read in the writings of our people published many years ago, if he was so well-versed in them as to seem* <meta>catchword: to seem (videri)</meta>

...he wishes to be seen. And that is in that very place, where perhaps he reads the word **his** added to the word "Gospel." Namely, in that explanation of the first part of the first chapter of John which was written in Latin about twenty-two years ago, and afterwards published, and soon was also paraphrastically <note>original Greek: παραφραστικῶς (paraphrastikōs); meaning a free translation rather than a literal one</note> translated into Polish and published.

For so it is written there: "In the beginning was the Word"; That is, Christ the Son of God in the beginning of **his** Gospel, namely at that time when John the Baptist began to recall the Israelite people to fruitfulness, etc. All these things are found word-for-word in that explanation whose beginning is, *Since the things which must be said*, etc.; except that the little word **his** is not read in the latest edition; and that indeed for the reason that some things in it were changed by the author.

The translator of the Polish version is said to have been Gregory Pauli <note>Grzegorz Paweł z Brzezin (c. 1525–1591), a leading radical theologian of the Polish Brethren</note>; at that time the Poles considered Lelius Socinus <note>Lelio Sozzini (1525–1562), an Italian humanist whose private papers provided the foundation for later Unitarian thought</note> to be the author of this explanation. This is also clear from Budzinius, who in chapter 31 of his *Historico-Chronological* work writes that there was brought into Poland around the year 1565 an interpretation of the first chapter of the Gospel of St. John, about which he says he does not doubt but that it was by Lelius Socinus; he indeed cites some things from it which fit perfectly with the recently mentioned writing.

Furthermore, Faustus Socinus <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), nephew of Lelio and namesake of the "Socinian" movement</note> asserts that he is the author of this explanation, which was translated into Polish and attributed to his uncle Lelius by the Poles—as also by Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note> in the preface to the *Acts of Valentino Gentile* in 1567, and by Zanchi <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), an Italian Reformed theologian</note> in the preface to his book *On the Three Elohim* in 1572. For Fausto himself writes thus to Morstinius in his second letter: *My works published so far are these, etc. The explanation of the beginning of John's Gospel which was also published in Polish, long before I arrived here.* And to Andreas Dudith in the year 1580 he said: *I do not know whether there has ever been presented to your eyes a certain brief explanation of the beginning of the first chapter of John, ascribed to Lelius by Zanchi and Beza, and in part by those Poles: but it came forth from our workshop eighteen years ago.*

Johannes Cloppenburg, however, says that the one which the ministers of Sarmatia <note>An archaic term used here for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note> and <term>Transylvania</term> <note>A principality where Unitarianism was legally recognized and flourished in the 16th century</note> published, according to Zanchi's testimony, is by Lelius Socinus; but the other (namely this one which we have just discussed), joined to the former by Franciscus Junius, is by Faustus. Similarly, Hornbeeck also thinks it is the same one that Zanchi refutes, along with that which...

# BIBLIOTHECA

...the said Ministers published in the *Summary of Controversies*. But they are deluded and distinguish things that should not be distinguished: for it is the same one that Zanchius <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), a prominent Reformed theologian and critic of the Socinians</note> refutes in book 6 of *On the Three Elohim* <note>original Latin: *De tribus Elohim*; a defense of the Trinity</note> chapter 2, as that which Junius <note>Franciscus Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot scholar and professor at Leiden</note> placed in the second position: namely, that one which begins, "Since the things which must be said," <note>original Latin: *Quoniam quæ dicenda sunt*</note> etc., which, not without cause (as we have seen), Cloppenburg <note>Johannes Cloppenburg (1592–1652), a Dutch theologian known for his anti-Socinian polemics</note> attributes to Faustus. Furthermore, Péter Méliusz <note>Péter Méliusz Juhász (1532–1572), a leader of the Hungarian Reformed Church</note> in the second disputation at Alba <note>Alba Iulia, a center of the Unitarian movement in Transylvania</note> in the year 1568, attributes the following explanations to Lelio Sozzini (whom he says he knew when he was at Wittenberg):

1. **Beginning**, understood as the start of the Gospel preaching <note>a typical Socinian interpretation, arguing that John 1:1 refers to the start of Christ's ministry rather than the beginning of creation</note>.
2. **To have glory with God before the world was made**, understood as being hidden in the world.
3. **The Word was God**, i.e., in foreknowledge or imagination, just as creatures are.
4. **The Word was made flesh**, can be said in the same way as that phrase: "Who, though he was rich, was made poor" <note>referring to 2 Corinthians 8:9</note>.
5. **Only-begotten**, i.e., by the overshadowing of the power of the Most High, conceived through the Holy Spirit.

The first fits both of the mentioned explanations. Furthermore, the second, third, and fifth—according to the literal text <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν (kata to rhēton)</note>—fit neither. The fourth fits only that one which begins, "Since most people abuse," <note>original Latin: *Cùm plerique abutantur*</note> etc. From these, as well as from those things we alleged above from Faustus Sozzini, it is clear that today we lack the work of Lelio Sozzini on the beginning of the Gospel of St. John. How it might have been lost, or where it may yet lie hidden, we have not yet been able to discover. Just as we cannot yet determine who the author is of this explanation which was inserted into the book by the Ministers of Poland <note>original Latin: *Sarmatiæ*</note> and Transylvania, *On the False and True Knowledge of the One God*, etc. For that it is not the offspring of Lelio Sozzini is proved both by the diversity of style from his other writings, and also by the fact that such opinions and explanations of certain passages of Holy Scripture are proposed in it which disagree with Lelio's views, and with the interpretations which Faustus Sozzini testifies were peculiar to him—nay, even invented by him. 

König <note>Georg Matthias König (1616–1699), author of the *Bibliotheca vetus et nova*, a major biographical dictionary</note> in his *Old and New Library*, attributes a Commentary on the first chapter of John to Biandrata <note>Giorgio Biandrata (1515–1588), an influential Italian antitrinitarian physician who worked in Poland and Transylvania</note>: whether this is the same as the one we are now discussing, I would not dare to affirm with certainty; although it is certain that Biandrata was the primary author of the aforementioned book *On the False and True Knowledge of the One God*. ### Articles of Faith.

**Theses on the triune and one God**, or *On the Trinity*; these came to light around the year 1562, unless by chance they are the same Theses attributed to **Niccolò Paruta**, who was also one of the members of the aforementioned group. **Ambiguous words in Holy Scripture**; the principal ones are said to have been: *Beginning, create, make, world, God, all,* etc., according to the testimony of **Budziński** <note>Stanisław Budziński (c. 1530–1595), an early historian of the Polish Reformation and secretary to several prominent Unitarians</note>. Regarding this matter, Budzinski <note>Stanisław Budziński (c. 1530–1595) was a Polish historian and secretary to several prominent reformers; his history of the Polish Reformation is a primary source for this period</note> records that the opinion of Paruta <note>Niccolò Paruta, an Italian nobleman and religious refugee</note> was this: namely, that those joining the church ought to be baptized to avoid dangers regarding the ceremony, without inquiring whether this rebaptism is necessary for the attainment of salvation.

**GIOVANNI VALENTINO GENTILE** of Cosenza-Campania, from the Kingdom of Naples. Budzinski, in chapter 27, reports that he was already an old man when he was persecuted by the people of Geneva. Captured through their efforts, he was cast into prison in the town named Gex <note>original Latin: *Gajum*; Gex is a town near Geneva</note>. Since he was unable to escape because he was poor, he was ransomed by his companion **Paolo Alciato**. Because Alciato was wealthy, born of noble lineage, and even a soldier, they did not dare to move against him in a similar manner. Both of these men came to Poland around the year 1562. From there, Gentile later returned to Savoy; there he was captured again and examined as to whether he still persisted in his opinion. Upon his confession, he was beheaded at Bern in the year 1566. His opinion, which he had proposed in Poland at the Synod of Pińczów <note>original: *Pinczovia*; a major center of the Polish Reformation</note> celebrated on November 4, 1562, was this: *That God created, in the breadth of eternity, a certain most excellent Spirit, who later, in the fullness of time, was incarnated.* As the same Budzinski testifies in the aforementioned place.

**Confession offered to the most illustrious Lords of Geneva**, 1558.

**Likewise another confession**, drafted by order of the illustrious Lords, etc., 1558. These are extant, printed in the *Acts of Gentile*, pages 3–13, 1567, in quarto.

**Antidotes**, Manuscript.

**Confession on the Trinity**, to which is prefixed a preface under the name of the printer "Theophilus" to the sons of the church. To this were added "Protheses" <note>Theses or propositions</note> (the title of which in the *Acts of Gentile* is: *The Protheses of Valentino Gentile.* — However, because the author of these—whether it was Gribaldi <note>Matteo Gribaldi, an Italian legal scholar and radical reformer</note> or someone else similar—seemed to himself rather clever, etc.) and accusations against Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius, the 4th-century defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism</note>. Budzinski, in the place cited, mentions that he dedicated a short Confession with annotations on the Athanasian Creed, published at Lyon, to the Governor of the aforementioned town of Gex, by whom, through the efforts of Alciato, he had been released from prison.

A book written in his own hand, and dedicated to Sigismund, the King of Poland, together with a long preface to the same. In this book his entire doctrine is contained, although he used to say that a fuller version had been written down by Blandrata <note>Giorgio Biandrata (1515–1588), an influential Italian physician and reformer in Poland and Transylvania</note>. Then he refutes chapter 13 of the first book of Calvin’s *Institutes*, where he thoroughly condemns the doctrine of the Trinity as it has been handed down in all churches until now. To these, he added theses <note>original: *protheses*</note> from Augustine, especially from the fifteen books *On the Trinity*, which he rejects along with their excellent author and translates slanderously. He added new collections from Scripture, the Church Fathers, and the Quran <note>original: *Alcorano*; early modern radicals sometimes cited Islamic monotheism to critique the Trinity</note>, to establish his own opinion. Poems written in his own hand concerning the Trinity.

An Italian booklet also, and a similar one composed in Latin concerning the incarnation of Christ, were found among the writings which he had in his possession; but whether they recognize him as the author, I have not discovered.

### GEORGIUS BLANDRATA
**GEORGE BIANDRATA**, an Italian from Saluzzo, escaped from Pavia <note>original: *Ticino*</note> and came to Geneva. Fleeing the anger of Calvin in the year 1558 due to differences in religion, he betook himself to Poland. There he was made an elder of the churches in the district of Krakow. However, as he could not live here in peace either—Calvin pursuing him with his writings—he was summoned by Prince John Sigismund around the year 1563 and departed for Transylvania. There he served as the personal physician <term>archiatrum|A chief physician to a monarch</term> and intimate counselor to the Prince himself, and later to Stephen and Christopher Báthory, Princes of Transylvania; indeed, he even served Stephen after he had been elevated to the throne of Poland. He is called an old man at the time of the dispute he had with Francis David <note>Ferenc Dávid, the first Unitarian bishop in Transylvania, who eventually clashed with Biandrata over the worship of Christ</note> in 1579. He was still surviving when Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Catholic Counter-Reformation cardinal</note> was writing about Christ, that is, around the year 1585. He had died by 1592, when Socinus was refuting Wujek; and perhaps as early as the year 1586.

**Commentary on the First Chapter of the Gospel of St. John.** König attributes this to him: but perhaps he means the one inserted in the book *On the False and True Knowledge of God*; of which book (as we shall soon say) Biandrata was the primary author.

**Questions**, to which Calvin responded, found in the *Acts of Valentino Gentile*, pages 50–56.

# BIBLIOGRAPHY
<meta>catchword: Chapter</meta>

We have decided that the writings which were published in Transylvania should be placed here under Biandrata; for he seems to have been the first to bring the doctrine of one God and His only Son to those regions. He spread it widely there under the patronage of Prince John Sigismund, who had embraced the same view (having rejected the belief in the Trinity). He was also the primary speaker, along with Ferenc Dávid, the Superintendent of the Transylvanian Churches, in the disputations that were held there. These, then, are the books which were published from Transylvania at that time:

**The first Disputation of Alba Iulia** <note>original: "Albana seu Albensis", the capital of the Principality of Transylvania</note>, held on February 24, 1566, and printed at Kolozsvár <note>original: "Claudiopolis", modern-day Cluj-Napoca, Romania</note> in the same year.

**A Demonstration of the falsehood of the doctrine of Péter Melius** <note>a prominent Hungarian Reformed/Calvinist bishop and a fierce opponent of the Unitarians</note> **and the rest of the sophists**, through Oppositions <note>original: "Antitheses"</note>, together with a refutation of the *Oppositions of the true and Turkish Christ*, now printed for the first time at Debrecen. Published at Alba Iulia, in quarto. In the second Opposition, the following is read: *But these things will be treated more extensively in the disputation, and in the book which follows immediately, regarding the true and false knowledge of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.*

**Two books on the false and true knowledge of the one God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit**; by the Authors and Ministers of the churches in agreement in Poland <note>original: "Sarmatia"</note> and Transylvania. Published at Alba Iulia, in quarto. To the most Serene and most Distinguished in Piety Prince, Lord John II, elected King of Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, etc., the Ministers of the consenting Churches pray for grace and peace. *These various fragments of distinguished men, so greatly desired by everyone, now finally gathered into two small books concerning the false and true knowledge of the one God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—like the Sileni of Alcibiades* <note>original: "Silenorum Alcibiadis". A reference to Plato's "Symposium," describing something that appears humble or ugly on the outside but contains something divine and precious within</note>, *we humbly consecrate to your Most Serene Majesty, without any seductive ornaments of words, etc.* This dedication was written at Alba Iulia on August 7, 1567. To which is added the following poem to the reader:

> *Painted things do not help; whatever exists under a false image,*
> *the learned times drag into the light.*
> *The kindled fire will consume the empty stalks,*
> *no force can restrain the course of God.*
> *He who is wise waits, searching the mysteries of the Word;*
> *he who is headlong in judgment undergoes many dangers.*

In the first book of this volume, these things are contained:

# OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS.
<meta>catchword: Chapter</meta>

Ch. I. Forewarnings of Christ and the Apostles regarding the abolition of the true Christ by the Antichrist.

Ch. II. In what manner the Antichrist gradually corrupted the church of God and the simplicity of the divine word.

Ch. III. On the origin and progress of the Trinity <note>original: "Triadis"</note>; on the beginning of sophistry; and on various dissenters.

Ch. IV. Regarding the horrific images depicting the triune and one God. <note>This likely refers to controversial medieval artistic representations of the Trinity, such as the "three-faced" head, which Unitarians found idolatrous.</note>

Ch. V. What the Sophists <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to the Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages whom the reformers accused of using convoluted logic to obscure biblical truth.</note> teach in summary, and which articles of faith they propose.

Ch. VI. A compendium of Augustine’s books on the Trinity. We believe Valentino Gentile <note>An Italian anti-Trinitarian who was executed in Bern in 1566; his works were highly influential in the Polish and Transylvanian movements.</note> to be the author of this short work, as we suggested above.

Ch. VII. How varied and inconsistent the interpreters have been, twisting the scriptures for the sake of victory, based on the annotations of Erasmus of Rotterdam. <note>Erasmus, though remaining Catholic, provided much of the philological ammunition used by anti-Trinitarians through his critical notes on the New Testament.</note>

Ch. VIII. Concerning the monstrous words and phrases which the Tritheists <note>original: "Tritoitæ"; a derogatory term used for those who hold to the Trinity, implying they worship three separate gods.</note> are forced to use. At the end of this chapter is an exhortation "To the lovers of divine truth" which begins thus:

> Pious brothers in mind, hearts most faithful to Christ the Lord,
> and beloved souls, whom the Son of God himself
> redeemed from cursed death by his shed blood:
> Recognize the true, exalted Father of Christ
> as that one God who created all things by his word.
> And recognize the Christ of the one true God, etc.

This poem is by Grzegorz Paweł <note>original: "Gregorii Pauli", a leader of the Polish Brethren known for his radical social and theological views.</note>, as I infer from its harmony with his other poems of a similar kind.

Ch. IX. On the ridiculous doctrine of the Sophists regarding the Trinity of God.

The title of the second book is as follows: *On the true knowledge of the one God the Father, of our one Lord Jesus Christ his Son whom he sent, and of the Spirit of them both.* In which the following are contained:

Ch. I. How Christ restores his church.

Ch. II. On the distinction between the Law and the Gospel.

Ch. III. On the Word <note>original: "Logo", referring to the Greek "Logos" in the Gospel of John.</note>.

Ch. IV. On the one God the Father with all his powers, and a brief confession of faith.

Ch. V. The first explanation of the confession, concerning those words, "Now this is eternal life," from John 17.

...received him with his [favor] in Poland), he laid aside the monk's cowl <note>Francesco Lismanino was a Franciscan provincial who famously left the order to join the Reformation movement.</note>. Felix Cruciger <note>A leader of the Reformed Church in Lesser Poland.</note>, Superintendent of the churches in Lesser Poland, and about thirty other Elders and Ministers subscribed to it along with him, among whom was Grzegorz Paweł, Elder in the district of Kraków. *On Reforming the Commonwealth* <note>original: "De Republica emendanda"</note> in five books, of which the 1st is on morals, the 2nd on laws, the 3rd on war (addressed to the King), the 4th on the church, and the 5th on the school. Kraków, 1551. Basel, octavo and folio editions, 1554.

*Four Miscellanies* <note>original: "Sylvæ," literally "Woods," a common title for a collection of various poems or prose works.</note>.

I. *On the three persons and one essence of God*: addressed to Sigismund Augustus, King of Poland. Written in the year 1565, in the month of December, at Wolbórz.

II. *On the necessity of holding a convention to settle religious controversies*: addressed to the same King, written in the same place, year, and month.

III. *On Jesus Christ, Son of God and man, and the same our God and Lord*: addressed to Pope Pius V. Written in the year 1568, in the month of June, at Trzebnica.

IV. *On Consubstantiality* <term>Homousio: From the Greek "Homoousios," the core Nicene doctrine that Jesus is of the "same substance" as God the Father.</term>, and those things which pertain to this: addressed to Jakub Uchański <note>Jakub Uchański (1502–1581) was the Archbishop of Gniezno and Primate of Poland, noted for his conciliatory approach to the Reformation.</note>, Archbishop of Gniezno, Legate by birth, and Primate of the Kingdom of Poland. Written in the year 1569, in the month of June, at the "sharp meadow" of the Poticanii. Printed from the author's own manuscript. To this is added,

*A Theological Question* of a similar argument examined by the same author: In which it is asked, *how the union of the divine and human nature of Christ was made in the person, not in the nature; even though nature and person are precisely the same things in our Lord God?* All these things were published in the year 1590, in the month of July, in quarto.

in the preface to the King prefixed to the first *Miscellany* <note>original: "Sylva," literally "wood," used here to mean a collection of various writings.</note>. However, while he complies with the King's custom, he incurs the indignation of others, especially that of the Supreme Pontiff himself, Pius V, whom he addresses in the preface of the third *Miscellany* as follows: *I thought it was not without purpose if I myself brought these controversies to you, and dedicated this book to you, to provide an opportunity for you to judge them; and at the same time to commend my slender studies to you. Concerning which you seem to have conceived a sinister opinion: and therefore to have commanded those in whose hands power rests, that they should cast me out of my modest possessions: overturn my fortunes: and make me an exile from my home, the forum, my hearth, and the company of men. Is this the reward for those who have served well? Is this a humane act, Most Holy Father?*

From the same preface, it is clear that his book was translated into the German, French, and Spanish languages; for these things are further contained there: *Therefore there is one who, by praising my book, says that no more distinguished work has come to light in over a thousand years. Another contends that since the founding of the world, no other similar to it, at least in this genre, has been published until now, whether by the ancients or the moderns. A certain man, even citing some things from my books, says I am almost the most acute and learned of all the Evangelicals* <note>In this context, "Evangelicals" refers generally to Protestants or those seeking church reform based on the Gospels.</note>. *There is one who, writing to me, says: "I value you and your writings so highly, Frycz* <note>original: "Frici," the Latinized vocative form of his name.</note>, *that I would not wish even a single syllable to perish." Another even puts it this way: "I have valued all your works so highly until now, and I still do, that I will not allow them to become worthless to me because of anyone’s prejudice." These are their words; whether they are true or otherwise, let them see to it. But what need is there for words, when the book is in everyone's hands. For it is read not only in Latin, as it was written by me, but also in German, French, and Spanish.*

It also comes to be remembered here that the author attempted the printing of these *Miscellanies* quite often; but ill-wishers delayed it and almost suppressed this work. He himself indicates this in the preface to the fourth *Miscellany*, where he writes these things: *And so it had been settled between me and Johannes Oporinus* <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was a famous humanist printer in Basel known for publishing controversial and scholarly works.</note> *that, when he had printed our Miscellanies with his types, he should send them from the Frankfurt Fair (where many people from almost the entire Christian world are accustomed to gather), both to every most learned man and to the Universities, whichever acknowledge Christ, whether they be Roman, Lutheran, or Sacramentarian* <note>original: "Sacramentariis." This term was used for reformers—particularly followers of Zwingli—who held a symbolic view of the Eucharist rather than believing in the physical presence of Christ.</note> (*u-*

The architect of the plots laid against this book was Trecius <note>Jan Trzecieski (d. 1576), a Polish Protestant scholar.</note>, as Erazm Otwinowski <note>A Polish Socinian poet and historian.</note> relates in his *Life of Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski*, which he inserted among his other lives of Christian Heroes written in Polish verse. There he mentions that when this deed became known, the following couplet was composed:

> King Augustus ordered it, Frycz wrote it, but Trecius by craft,
> Twice-black, hindered these writings while under the press.
<note>original Latin: "Rex Augustus jussit, Fricz scripsit, Trecius astu, / Sub praelo scripta haec, bis niger impediit." Augustus refers to King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland.</note>

Budziński <note>Stanisław Budziński, a pioneer of Polish Reformation history.</note>, recounting the same story in chapter 36 of his manuscript *History*, says that after this act by Trecius, Frycz reassembled his *Miscellanies* from his notebooks and nearly discarded papers, and expanded them with the help of Transylvanian books (which had come to light in the meantime).

The edition of this work, as we have mentioned, came to light in the year 1590; it was produced at Raków <note>original: "Racoviae," the center of the Polish Brethren (Socinians).</note>, as I have learned from the accounts of my elders. The *Gesnerian Library* <note>The "Bibliotheca Universalis" originally by Conrad Gessner.</note> published in the year 1583 mentions three *Miscellanies* and says they had not yet been printed at that time: *The first*, it says, *is on the three persons and one essence of God; the second on the necessity of holding a council to settle religious controversies; the third on infant baptism.* But it is mistaken, for there is nothing in the third *Miscellany*—nor indeed in the others—concerning infant baptism. There are also ascribed to Frycz:

...around the year 1546, he <note>Referring to Adam Pastor, whose biography began on the previous page.</note> held a dispute with Theodore Philippi (commonly known as **Dirk Philips**) in the town of Goch, concerning the supreme divinity of Christ, which he opposed. For this reason, Menno Simons <note>The influential Anabaptist leader from whom the Mennonites take their name.</note> and his followers fiercely pursued him. Nevertheless, he persisted in his opinion, which he primarily supported with the testimonies of Christ himself in John 17:3 <note>“Now this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent.”</note> and John 14:28 <note>“...for the Father is greater than I.” These verses were frequently cited by those questioning the traditional Trinity.</note>. Eventually, because of this, he was excommunicated by Menno and the rest of the Anabaptists. He cared little for this, however, and had no few followers. There was almost no other difference between his followers and the rest of the Anabaptists, except that some of them considered it permissible to occasionally take an oath before a Magistrate. Bullinger <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a Swiss Reformer and historian of the period.</note> reports these and similar matters in the place cited. Furthermore, his opinion regarding the person of Christ and the Word <note>original: "Verbo," referring to the *Logos* of the prologue of John's Gospel.</note>, which St. John discusses at the beginning of his Gospel (as I have been able to gather from his books, the titles of which we have appended below), was almost the same as that which we showed above that Michael Servetus <note>A famous Spanish physician and theologian burned at the stake in Geneva for his anti-trinitarian views.</note> had urged.

# OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS.
C 5
<meta>catchword: these</meta>

...to the readings of David, mixing evangelical dogmas, especially against the invocation of saints, Peter Gonesius <note>Piotr z Goniądza (c. 1525–1573), a pioneer of the Polish Reformation and a founding figure of the Polish Brethren</note> set himself in opposition among a crowd of others. The Bishop of Vilnius, along with his clergy, had sent him to Wittenberg for the sake of his studies; but while traveling through Germany, Switzerland, Savoy, and Moravia, he drank in opinions contrary to those commonly received and brought them back with him to his homeland. He was the first who openly attacked the dogma of the Trinity in Poland. He first did this on January 21, 1556, at the Synod of Secemin, in which he is said to have proposed the following: that he indeed approved of the Apostles’ Creed, but rejected the others, such as the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds, etc. Likewise, he held that the Trinity was not God, and that the Son of God was indeed God, but less than the Father. Furthermore, he affirmed that the Son of God always showed honor to the Father, and he proved that Christ received all things from the Father, frequently repeating that sentence, *the Father gave to me* <note>original Latin: "dedit mihi Pater"</note>. Likewise, *Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son* <note>John 5:26</note>, etc. He also asserted that God the Father alone is the only true God, based on John 17:3. The *Word* <note>original Greek: "Λόγον" (Logos)</note>, that is, the invisible, immortal Word, was in time turned into flesh in the womb of the virgin; and that invisible Word is the seed of the incarnate Son. Furthermore, denying the communication of properties <term>communicatio idiomatum: a theological concept where the attributes of both the divine and human natures are ascribed to the person of Jesus</term>, he asserted that there was only one substance or nature in Christ. Specifically, however, he attacked the consubstantiality <term>consubstantialitas: the doctrine that the Son is of the same essence or "substance" as the Father</term> of the Son with the Father. To these points, he said that Christ the man was turned into God, and God or the Word into man, etc. These things are read in the Manuscript Acts of the Polish Synods, from which we have transcribed them. He also inveighed against the doctrine of infant baptism <term>pædobaptismus</term>. Likewise, he taught that it was not permitted for a Christian man to hold public office or to use the sword; Budzinius <note>Stanisław Budziński, a historian of the Polish Reformation</note> says that he drew this opinion from the Moravian Brethren <note>Also known as the Hutterites or Anabaptists in Moravia, known for their communal living and pacifism</note>. He records that Gonesius returned to his homeland from his travels girded only with a wooden sword. See chapter 20 of his Manuscript History. Many people later embraced these opinions of his and urged them forward sharply.

**Books against Infant Baptism:** which were publicly read and examined at the Synod of Brest on December 15, 1558.

**A Writing to Laurentius Oriscovius**, against infant baptism, composed in the year 1562, on the day after the feast of John the Baptist.

Gonesius also wrote not a few things against the Rakowians <note>The Polish Brethren or Socinians who established a major center at Raków</note>, or
