...who denied that the Son of God existed before his mother: as Budzinius <note>Stanisław Budziński (c. 1530–1595), a historian of the Polish Reformation and secretary to Jan Łaski</note> testifies in chapter 31.

**STANISLAUS LUTOMIRSCIUS** <note>Stanisław Lutomirski (c. 1510–1575), a Polish nobleman and influential Protestant leader</note>, a Polish Knight, Secretary to King Sigismund Augustus, and Superintendent (following Felix Cruciger) of the churches of Lesser Poland. He was formerly a Papal Priest, the Parish Priest of Konin and Tuszyn, etc. Indeed, he was even the designated Archbishop of Gniezno. He was one of the principal figures who raised the standard against the dogmas of the Roman Church in Poland. When, therefore, he was accused of the crime of heresy in the year 1555 by the Archbishop of Gniezno, the Primate of the Kingdom, he was summoned to Łowicz. When he appeared there, equipped with the Holy Bible and accompanied by a great crowd of relatives and noblemen, he was not admitted to judgment by the Archbishop: as Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzowski (1567–1637), a Dominican historian and continuationist of Baronius's *Annales Ecclesiastici*</note> reports in the year 1555, section 48, and Wengerscius <note>Andrzej Węgierski (1600–1649), a historian of the Protestant Reformation in Slavonic lands</note> in book III, chapter 15. When he had returned home, the following works were recorded by him in writing:

**A Confession of his Religion:** which he presented to the King, the Archbishop, and other magnates of the Kingdom, and afterwards published in print.

**A Letter to certain magnates and brothers,** in which he tries to deter them from the schism that Stanisław Sarnicki <note>Stanisław Sarnicki (1532–1597), a Polish Calvinist writer and historian who eventually broke with the more radical Arians</note> was plotting with his followers; at the same time, he clears Gregory Pauli <note>Grzegorz Paweł z Brzezin (c. 1525–1591), a leading radical theologian of the Polish Brethren</note> of the charges with which he was being attacked. Written in Kraków at the Synod held on May 17, 1563; and besides Lutomirski himself, it was signed by twenty-two elders and ministers.

**Another letter,** written to the ministers and brothers of Lithuania and Podlachia on the same subject, likewise in the name of the Synod, at Kraków in the year 1563, May 17. Budzinius inserted a copy of both these letters into his work: the former (which was composed in the Polish language) in chapter 24; the latter, however (which was written in the Latin language), in chapter 25.

**The Conclusion of the Synod of Węgrów** regarding the article of true Baptism <term>Baptismus</term>, already decreed, confirmed, and concluded on the penultimate day of December in the year 1555. It was composed by the same Lutomirski as Superintendent, with the consent of the Synod. A Polish manuscript. Budzinius displays it in chapter 42 of his History.

...then residing with Jan Niemojewski <note>Jan Niemojewski (c. 1526–1598), a Polish nobleman and judge who became a prominent leader of the Polish Brethren</note>, the Judge of Inowrocław <note>original: "Judicem Vladislaviensem"</note>, he invites others to the Synod of Brzeziny (which was later delayed for certain reasons). In this synod, a discussion was to be held concerning the Son of God with some brothers who denied that there was any man before Christ, nor did they acknowledge two natures in him. After many hesitations, Lutomirski eventually embraced and professed their opinion.

**A writing on the questions raised in the church at that time,** namely whether it is lawful for a Christian man to hold political office and bear arms: written in the year 1574.

**A Letter to Nicolaus Paruta** <note>Niccolò Paruta (d. 1581), an Italian religious refugee and influential figure in the Radical Reformation in Poland</note> written in the year 1574, on the question of Baptism, in which he responds to Paruta in this manner: *Piety-loving and sensible people do not deny that Baptism, just like the Lord's Supper, ought to be administered in the assembly of the elders; yet we know they are not bound to specific places and times. Let superstition be gone; let all things serve the edification, peace, and tranquility of the church.*

**GREGORIUS PAULI of Brzeziny,** a Pole, in the year 1555. He was already a Master and a Minister of the church in Wola near Kraków, and later the Pastor and Elder of the church in Kraków. While he was preaching in Kraków in 1562 against the common dogma of the Trinity, on the very day of the Holy Trinity around noon, a lightning bolt struck the church called "Holy Trinity" and knocked down the globe <note>likely a decorative orb or cross-mount</note> situated at its peak. Driven from Kraków because of his religion, he moved to Raków <note>the intellectual center of the Polish Socinian movement</note> where he died at a great age around 1591—one month after Georg Schomann, his companion and contemporary.

**A Table of the Trinity,** which the author himself cites in the letter soon to be mentioned to the Zurich Ministers and Calvin. There he says: *My Table which I published, drawn from the pure fountains of God's word, is accused of Arianism; but you shall see how deservedly, etc.* <note>original: "Tabula mea quam edidi..."</note> Calvin mentions the same in his *Brief Admonition to the Polish Brethren* in these words: *I have inspected, not without the most bitter sorrow, the Table recently published in Poland, which makes Christ and the Holy Spirit other gods distinct from the Father, etc.*

**The Tower of Babel.** Octavo. Published at Frankfurt by Sciurus <note>likely referring to the printer's mark of a squirrel</note>.

**Antidote,** against the new articles of faith presented by Sarnicki <note>Stanisław Sarnicki (1532–1597), a Polish Calvinist polemicist</note> at Warsaw, as if by a new Pope; or, an Antidote against the canons of Sarnicki's decrees. Octavo. Published at Nieśwież by Daniel Łanczycki.

-># B I B L I O T H E C A<-

**A warning letter to the ministers of Zurich** <note>original: "Tigurinos"</note> **and to Calvin:** in which he also publishes his confession regarding God, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit, against his detractors. In octavo. To this are appended: **Testimonies of pious men** who lived with the Apostles or immediately after them, concerning this simple and Apostolic faith with which they were content. These testimonies are brought forward from Ignatius, Irenaeus, Justin, and Tertullian. <note>These are Early Church Fathers used by Pauli to argue that the earliest Christians did not hold to later Trinitarian dogmas.</note>

**A poem to John Calvin and the pious brothers.** Octavo. Which begins thus:

> *Of all the errors that exist, or ever were before,*
> *Or ever shall be, Calvin, your own error is now caught:* <note>original: "Maximus errorum quot sunt, quotque ante fuerunt, / Quot vel erunt, Calvine tuus deprenditur error"</note>
> *You who with such a headlong pen describe how in one*
> *God reside three: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "Paracletum"</note>
> &c.

**A brief demonstration concerning the personified "essence-God" of the Antichrist, defeating itself.** Octavo. <note>Pauli frequently argued that the philosophical concept of "essence" used in Trinitarian theology was an invention of the Antichrist.</note>

**Explanation of difficult places in Holy Scripture.** Published at Pińczów. <note>original: "Pinczoviæ"; Pińczów was a major center for the Polish Reformation and the "Sarmatian Athens."</note>

**A letter to Bullinger,** <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), the successor to Zwingli in Zurich.</note> in which he sets forth his opinion on the prerogative of God the Father against Stancaro: <note>Francesco Stancaro (1501–1574), an Italian theologian whose views on Christ as mediator caused great controversy in Poland.</note> written in the year 1562. Manuscript.

**An explanation of the beginning of the Gospel of John,** written by Socinus (by Laelius, as was then thought; but in truth, as we have shown and will show, by Faustus); <note>Lelio Sozzini (1525–1562) and his nephew Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604) were the namesakes of Socinianism. This refers to the radical re-interpretation of the "Logos" in John 1.</note> it was rendered into the Polish language by him.

**The first Racovian Catechism,** <note>The defining statement of faith for the Polish Brethren, though this refers to an early version prior to the famous 1605 edition.</note> which I have no doubt was primarily composed by the author himself (who was then the leader <note>original: "antesignanus," a military term for a standard-bearer</note> of the Racovians). The care of reforming this work was entrusted to Faustus Socinus and Petrus Statorius, as we shall see below. Furthermore, I believe this volume is the same one mentioned by Wisnovius in his book published in 1575, on leaf 21; there he charges the Racovians with the crime of having translated that passage in Philippians 2:6 as: *He did not wish for this robbery.* <note>original: "Noluit hanc rapinam." This refers to a controversial translation of the Greek "harpagmos," arguing that Jesus did not strive to be equal to God.</note>

**Letters to Stanislaus Budziński** <note>Stanisław Budziński (c. 1530–1595), a Polish historian and secretary to several Reformation leaders.</note> on the question of the Magistrate and the use of arms. Year 1574. Manuscript.

**Against those who defended the pre-existence of the Son of God.** A writing published around the year 1574.

-># BIBLIOGRAPHY OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS<-

**A judgment on the invocation of Jesus Christ.** Composed around the year 1579. <note>This work likely addresses the "Non-Adorantist" controversy—a debate within the Polish Brethren over whether Jesus, as a created being, should be prayed to.</note>

**Against the writing of Jacobus Palaeologus,** in which he taught that Christ did not abolish political office, etc. Written in the name of the Racovians, <note>The "Racovians" were the community at Raków, the center of the Polish Socinian movement.</note> among whom, besides Gregorius Pauli himself, the following were prominent: Siekirinius, Czechovicius, Kalinovius, Schomanus, Niemojovius, etc. All of these men urged that it was not permitted for a Christian man to hold a political office. <note>The early Polish Brethren often practiced a form of Christian anarchism or radical pacifism, believing that true followers of Christ could not serve as judges, soldiers, or magistrates.</note> This book was written in the year 1573.

**Treatise on the thousand-year Reign of Christ:** composed around the year 1590. Manuscript. <note>Pauli was a known proponent of Millenarianism, the belief that Christ would return to establish a literal 1,000-year kingdom on Earth.</note>

**Interpretation of the words of Paul in 1 Corinthians 8:** *There is one God the Father from whom are all things*, etc. Written in the Polish language by the people of Pińczów: <note>original: "Pinczoviis"; referring to the reformed community in the town of Pińczów.</note> as Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski <note>A famous Polish Renaissance scholar and reformer.</note> testifies in chapter 1, treatise 1 of his *Sylvae*, which was composed in 1565. We have decided that this book should be placed here under Gregorius Pauli, because he was a major part of the Pińczów circle; furthermore, because it contains teachings that clearly agree with the opinion he cherished at that time.

### MARTIN CROVICIUS

A Polish Knight and Pastor of the church at Pińczów, and later at Piaski near Lublin, where he also finished his life in the month of December, 1573. In the year 1555, he was captured through the trickery of Andrzej Zebrzydowski, the Bishop of Kraków, but was freed by the skill of his patron, the illustrious Mikołaj Oleśnicki, the Lord <term>Toparcha</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for a local governor or lord of a place.</note> of Pińczów. When he was attacked with bitter writings by the aforementioned Bishop (who could no longer harm him by other means), he composed a substantial volume in his mother tongue under this title:

**Defense of the ancient true Christian doctrine, against the false new Roman doctrine, which Bishop Andrzej of Kraków defends by force and not by scripture.** <note>original Polish title: "Obrona starozytney prawdziwey nauki Chrześcianskiey, na przeciwko falszywy nowy nauce Rzymskiey, ktorey gwałtem nie pismem broni Andrzej Biskup Krakowski."</note>

**A Letter to Stanisław Budziński** (who inserted it into his *History*) written in Piaski in the year 1573. Manuscript. In this letter, he accuses the Racovians of excluding the Magistracy <note>political authority or government office</note> from the church; he teaches further that the magistracy is necessary and that one can obtain salvation while holding office; he likewise permits the use of arms, etc. <note>Crovicius represents the more moderate or "socially conservative" wing of the Polish Reformation, which disagreed with the radical pacifism of Gregorius Pauli and the Racovians.</note>

-># BIBLIOGRAPHY<-

**The testament of his last will,** in which he narrates what he did and what was done with him. Manuscript. The original of this, in the time of our parents, was in the possession of Jacobus Milius, Pastor of the Reformed church of Bełżyce in Poland: Andrzej Wiszowaty <note>Andrzej Wiszowaty (1608–1678) was a leading Socinian theologian and the grandson of Fausto Sozzini.</note> reported to me that he had seen and read the aforementioned Testament there.

That he wrote, in addition to the things mentioned, against the common opinion regarding the Trinity and the person of Christ, is indicated quite clearly by Andreas Dudith <note>Andreas Dudith (1533–1589) was a Hungarian nobleman and diplomat who became a prominent supporter of the Anti-Trinitarians.</note> in a letter to Theodore Beza of Vézelay, <note>Theodore Beza was John Calvin's successor in Geneva.</note> when he says: *“However, I am so far from ever denying this that I even freely profess that this entire heavenly doctrine, after God, is primarily owed to those most illustrious men endowed with great learning, talent, judgment, and piety; in the sharing of whose glory, by their own right, come Alciati, Gregorius Schomanus, Krowicki, Socinus, and other most excellent men, who put much effort into illuminating this doctrine both by writing and teaching.”* <note>original: "Hoc tamen tantum abeſt... poſuerunt." Dudith is acknowledging the collective effort of radical reformers in challenging traditional Trinitarian dogma.</note>

**ALEXANDER VITRELINUS,** <note>Also known as Aleksander Witrelin.</note> in the beginnings of the Reformation in Poland, specifically in the year 1555, was the Pastor of Pińczów under the protection of the aforementioned Mikołaj Oleśnicki; later he was at Węgrów in Podlachia, under the patronage of Jan Kiszka, the General Governor of Samogitia, etc.

**The Judgment of the Polish Churches, regarding the case of Ferenc Dávid,** <note>Ferenc Dávid was the founder of the Unitarian Church in Transylvania; his "case" refers to the controversy over whether Christ should be addressed in prayer (Adorantism vs. Non-Adorantism).</note> concerning the true invocation of the man Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God: a writing transmitted to Giorgio Biandrata and the other brothers in Transylvania, written in the synod celebrated in Bełżyce on August 24, 1579, and signed by Alexander Vitrelinus in the name of all the Ministers. Printed at Cluj <note>original: "Claudiopoli"</note> in the workshop of the widow of Gáspár Heltai, 1579. It has the passage from Matthew 10:32–33 <note>"Whoever acknowledges me before others, I will also acknowledge before my Father in heaven..."</note> inscribed on the first page, and a preface by the Ministers of Cluj prefixed to it; at the end of which these words are read: *“Regarding the things which the Polish brothers touched upon in passing in this writing concerning Baptism and some others which do not pertain to the main scope of the intended inquiry, we have deliberately omitted them, so as not to mix things that should not be mixed, nor to cause a longer delay to the printing.”* <note>original: "Quæ verò Poloni fratres... prætermiſimus." This suggests a theological rift or a desire for focus among the Transylvanian Unitarians compared to their Polish counterparts.</note>

The same work, with a refutation made by Jacobus Palaeologus, <note>Jacobus Palaeologus was a Greek friar turned radical reformer who frequently clashed with the main Socinian movement.</note> printed in the book whose title is: *A Defense of Ferenc Dávid in the matter...*

-># OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS #<-

...[Johan]nes Cazanovius, Stanislaus Farnovius <note>Stanisław Farnowski (d. 1615), leader of the "Farnovian" branch of the Polish Brethren who maintained a belief in the pre-existence of Christ.</note>, Johannes Niemojewski (Judge of Inowrocław), Nicolaus Żytno, Johannes Falconius, Martin Czechowic <note>A significant radical theologian and leader of the Polish Brethren.</note>, Daniel Bieliński; and the scribes, Laurentius Kryszkowski and Thomas Święchowski.

## **JOHANNES CAZANOVIUS**
A Polish Knight. He held nearly the same views <note>original: *homodoxus*</note> as Gonesius <note>Piotr z Goniądza (c. 1530–1573), a pioneer of anti-Trinitarianism in Poland.</note>, and served as a minister for the community of that opinion; later, however, he served as the sub-judge of Łuków.

*Against the letters of Calvin to the Polish brothers.*

There is also attributed to him, by Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski <note>A preeminent Polish Renaissance scholar and social reformer.</note>, a book written against the Trinitarians, as he states in *Silvae* <note>Modrzewski's work *Silvae quatuor* (Four Woods).</note> book 1, chapter 6: *"These and many other testimonies from the scriptures are collected by those who strive to demonstrate the unity of the essence of the Father and the Son. These testimonies indeed, the Italian Bernardino Ochino and our own Johannes Cazanovius, have refuted individually and accurately, in my opinion, in their books. At another time, he also clarified the colloquy <note>A formal theological discussion or debate.</note> held at Piotrków in the year of Christ 1565. We shall be briefer, etc."*

## **NICOLAUS SIENICKI**
A Polish Knight, commonly called the "Polish Demosthenes" <note>An homage to the famous Greek orator, reflecting Sienicki's reputation as the greatest speaker in the Polish Sejm.</note>, High Chamberlain of Chełm. In the Sejm <note>The parliament of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.</note> of Piotrków in the year 1565, he was the Marshal <note>The speaker or presiding officer.</note> or Director of the delegates of the equestrian order <note>The *szlachta* or nobility.</note>; there, in the colloquy held with the Trinitarians, he was a speaker on behalf of the Unitarians. He held nearly the same opinion regarding the person of Christ as Gonesius and Cazanovius.

He diligently collected all the acts of both the Kingdom and the Church into one volume; this manuscript codex was brought to Zamość after his death and preserved there.

## **JOHANNES NIEMOJEWSKI**
A Polish Knight, Judge of the district of Inowrocław; an office which he voluntarily resigned after embracing the Unitarian faith. He debated as one of the principal participants against the Trinitarians in the aforementioned colloquy of Piotrków in the year 1565. He died in Lublin on May 5, 1598.

At first, he insisted on the pre-existence of Christ before his birth, but later he conceded to the opinion of the Rakowians or of Socinus <note>Fausto Sozzini and his followers, who argued that Christ did not exist as a person prior to his human conception.</note>.

*A Demonstration that the Papal Church is not Apostolic, nor holy, nor one, nor Catholic; together with a response to the slanders of Doctor Wilkowski <note>Kasper Wilkowski, a physician and polemicist who converted back to Catholicism and attacked the Polish Brethren.</note>.* Written in Polish.

## **MARCIN CZECHOWIC**
<note>Marcin Czechowic (1532–1613) was a primary theologian of the Polish Brethren and an early advocate of believer's baptism and Christian pacifism.</note>
A Pole or Lithuanian. A teacher and minister of the church in Vilnius, later a pastor in Kuyavia, and finally in Lublin. He was still living in the year 1608, in which he seems to have died. Having rejected the doctrine of the Trinity, he initially defended the pre-existence of Christ according to the views of Gonesius <note>Piotr z Goniądza (c. 1530–1573), a pioneer of the anti-Trinitarian movement in Poland.</note>, alongside Niemojewski; but later, around the year 1570, he embraced the opinions of the Raków group and Sozzini, along with many others.

*On the origin of those who practice infant baptism <term>Paedobaptists; from the Greek 'pais' (child) and 'baptismos' (washing)</term>, and on the opinion that believes infants must be baptized at the very beginning of their birth. Printed by Theophilus Adamis. In quarto format. Dedicated to the illustrious and magnificent Lord Jan Kiszka <note>Jan Kiszka (1552–1592) was one of the wealthiest magnates in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and a major protector of the Polish Brethren.</note> of Ciechanowiec, General Governor of Samogitia, and Cup-bearer to his Sacred Royal Majesty in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, etc. Lublin, April 7, 1575.*

*A Three Days' Conversation <note>original Polish title: "Trzech dni Rozmowà"</note>, etc. That is, a colloquy of three days [in which a Christian, a Protestant <note>original: "Evangelicus"</note>, and a Catholic <note>original: "Pontificius," literally one loyal to the Pontiff or Pope.</note> are introduced speaking] regarding certain articles of faith,*

Objections to Faustus Socinus’s <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was an Italian theologian whose ideas led to the development of Socinianism, which denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ.</note> explanation of the beginning of the Gospel of John: which he brought forward because he was offended by the brothers' explanation of those words; *The Word <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos)</note> who was with God was the man Christ, that is, known to God alone.* <note>original: "Erat apud Deum ille λόγος homo Christus, id est, Soli Deo notus." This refers to a specific Unitarian interpretation that "the Word" refers to the human Jesus in God's plan, rather than a pre-existing divine being.</note> This writing was recorded by Jan Wojdowski as Czechowic recited it; it is found at the end of the aforementioned *Explanation* by Socinus.

**STANISŁAW FARNOWSKI** <note>Also known as Stanislaus Farnovius.</note> or **FARNESIUS**, a Pole. Around the year 1568, he created a schism <note>A formal split or division within a religious group.</note> from the other Unitarians (who were first named Pinczovians, and later Racovians, after the primary locations of their residence). He betook himself to Nowy Sącz <note>original: "Sandeciam"</note> to Mr. Stanisław Mężyk, the Starosta <note>original: "Satrapam"; a high-ranking regional official or district governor in Poland.</note> of Nowy Sącz, under whose protection he maintained a church and a famous school there. He was of the same opinion as Gonesius <note>Piotr z Goniądza, an early radical reformer.</note> regarding the doctrine of the person of the Son of God, whose pre-existence <note>The belief that Christ existed in some form before his human birth.</note> he sharply defended, almost according to the decree of Arius <note>Arius (c. 256–336) taught that the Son of God was a created being, subordinate to the Father; Farnowski shared this "Arian" view of Christ's pre-existence.</note>, and because of this, he caused the aforementioned schism. Whether he and his followers considered the Holy Spirit to be a person or not is not entirely certain; the latter, however, is more likely, for they had no dispute on this matter with the followers of Socinus. But it is certain that they believed it was a sin to invoke the Holy Spirit or to pour out prayers to him. Farnowski instituted among his followers the baptism of adults, and that by immersion, just as the other Unitarians did. This community of Farnovians lasted in Poland for some time, and Farnowski himself was still alive in 1614; after his death, most of his followers joined those other Unitarians who shared the opinions of Socinus.

A Polish work in quarto which I once saw, but neglected to transcribe the title. Wiśniowski <note>original: "Wisnovius"</note>, in the codex just mentioned, cites Farnowski’s *Preface to the Poles*; whether it was prefixed to the said work or to his other writings, I cannot assert for certain. Budziński <note>Stanisław Budziński, a 16th-century historian of the Polish Reformation.</note> reports in chapter 52 that Farnowski published several books against those who denied the pre-existence of the Lord Jesus Christ. The same Wiśniowski—

Farnowski <note>Stanisław Farnowski (Farnovius), leader of the "Farnovian" sect of Polish Brethren who held that Christ existed before the world, though was not equal to the Father.</note> frequently cites books under this title:

*Demonstration of falsification and confession of the true doctrine.* <note>original Polish: "Okazanie zfalszowania, y wyznanie prawdziwey nauki."</note> He says these books were published recently (writing this in the year 1575); he cites the first chapter of the book *On God the Father* at leaf 296; the book *On the Son of God*, chapter 17, leaf 447, and chapter 41, leaf 597; and the book *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 14, leaf 704b (or page 1408). I have not discovered for certain who the author of these books was—whether it was Farnowski or Wiśniowski, or perhaps all of them together. The following work, however, is definitely by Farnowski:

**Books against the Luławice Peace:** <note>A reference to the "Pacification of Luławice," an attempt to reconcile different factions of the Polish Brethren.</note> dedicated to Stanisław Szafraniec, the Castellan of Sandomierz. In these, he attacks the opinion of those who denied that the Son of God existed before his mother. <note>This refers to the "Adoptionist" or "Socinian" view that Jesus only began to exist at his conception, a view Farnowski opposed.</note> Martin Czechowic gave a response to this writing in the year 1579.

**A Book of Polish Prayers**, published by the widow Zabawska, a noble matron from Farnowski’s congregation.

**STANISŁAW WIŚNIOWSKI** <note>Stanislaus Wisnovius</note>, a Pole and an associate of Farnowski who shared his doctrines. He served as a pastor in Luławice under the patronage of Stanisław Taszycki, who later abandoned his pastor Wiśniowski and joined those other Unitarians known as the Racovians. <note>The Racovians were the more radical wing of the Polish Brethren based in the town of Raków.</note>

*A Dialogue on the sincere knowledge of God the Father, his Son, and the Holy Spirit*, etc. <note>original Polish: "Rozmowa ö szczerą znajomosci Boga Oyca, syna jego, y Ducha Swietego"</note> that is: *A Dialogue on the sincere knowledge of God the Father, His Son, and the Holy Spirit; especially concerning the Son of God and his adversary; on the true and false church and their certain signs; likewise on the principal doctrines and institutions of the true Church of the Lord,* etc. A "Preface to the Faithful" is attached, written at Luławice on February 26, 1575. The book contains 91 leaves (or 182 pages) in quarto format.

**STANISŁAW PAKLEPKA** <note>Stanislaus Paclesius</note>, a Pole. He was among the first of those who attacked the doctrines of the Trinity and infant baptism <term>Paedobaptism (from Greek 'pais' child and 'baptismos' washing): the practice of baptizing infants, which many radical reformers rejected in favor of adult 'believer's baptism'.</term>. He served as a pastor in Lublin under the patronage of Tenczyński, the Palatine <note>A high-ranking regional governor in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.</note> of Bełz and official of Lublin. He died there in the year 1565, after first having recorded his last will and testament in writing; this is praised in the *Account of the origin of the contentions regarding Baptism* mentioned above under Martin Czechowic.

# BIBLIOTHECA

<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

...superintendent or Bishop of the Unitarians in Transylvania. In the year 1566 <note>The original text reads 1666, which is an evident printing error for 1566, as the subject died in 1579</note> and the following years, together with Giorgio Biandrata <note>Georgius Blandrata (1515–1588), an Italian physician and influential Antitrinitarian diplomat</note>, under the patronage and presidency of Prince John Sigismund <note>John Sigismund Zápolya, the only Unitarian King in history</note>, he disputed sharply against the Trinitarians. Chiefly at the instigation and in partnership with the same Biandrata, he published many books against them (which we have listed above under the entry for Biandrata). Later, having fallen into the dogmas of the semi-judaizers <term>Semi-judaizers: A derogatory term used by contemporaries for reformers like Dávid who, by denying the duty to pray to Christ, were accused of moving too close to Jewish monotheism</term>, while he spread the doctrine that Christ the Lord is not to be invoked in prayer; he was condemned as an innovator by Christopher Báthory, Prince of Transylvania, and thrown into prison at Déva. There, in the year 1579, on the 15th of November, already an old man, he departed from this life.

*Letter to the Polish Churches*, regarding the question of the thousand-year reign of Jesus Christ here on earth. *Alba Iulia, 1570 <note>original: "1670"</note>. Manuscript.*

*Treatise on Duality*, divided into three chapters. To which are added:

*The Second Treatise; That the Father of Christ is the one and only God of Israel, and no other is to be invoked:* containing fifteen theses proposed in the general synod of Thorda <note>Turda</note>. Also:

*The Third Treatise; Observations on the theses of Giorgio Biandrata.*

*Three Theses:* to which Biandrata opposed nearly thirty theses, as witnessed by Palaeologus <note>Jacob Palaeologus (1520–1585), a Greek friar turned Antitrinitarian</note> in his *Confession of the Judgments of the Polish Church*, page 232.

*A small booklet*, written in opposition to the Thirty Theses of Biandrata, in which it is argued that Jesus Christ cannot now be called God, since he is not the true God; that Jesus cannot be invoked in prayers; and that justification and predestination were poorly understood by Luther and Calvin. Concerning the kingdom of his Messiah, whom the prophets divined would be Jesus Christ. Published in the year 1578.

*Sixteen Theses*, attributed to him by Possevino <note>Antonio Possevino (1533–1611), a Jesuit diplomat and counter-reformer</note> in Section III, chapter 7. In the first of these, he is said to assert that *the Lord Jesus was conceived from the seed of Joseph.* Furthermore, in the eleventh: *No worship is to be deferred to Christ, except that which we defer to him by keeping his precepts.* These theses (which I have not had the chance to see) must have been written by him not long before the end of his life; for in the previously mentioned observations on Biandrata's Theses, he explicitly states: *Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit.* Observation on Thesis II, concerning the Son of God.

# OF THE ANTITRINITARIANS

57
<header>OF THE ANTITRINITARIANS.</header>

<meta>catchword: concerning</meta>

Four theses on the non-invocation of Jesus Christ in sacred prayers, proposed to Fausto Socinus. <note>Fausto Socinus (1539–1604) was an Italian theologian whose ideas led to the development of Socinianism; unlike Dávid, he argued that while Christ was not God, he should still be prayed to.</note>

Refutation of Fausto’s response: that is, of those arguments which Fausto Socinus opposed to the said theses. This book, together with the immediately preceding short work, was printed in the *Defense of Ferenc Dávid in the matter of not invoking Jesus Christ in prayers*; published through the efforts of Jacobus Palaeologus, Matthias Glirius, and David, the son of Ferenc Dávid, in the year 1580, in octavo. Several questions: these exist published with Fausto Socinus’s response to them, among his own *Fragments*, attached to the *Disputation against Christian Francken*.

JOHANN SOMMER of Pirna in Meissen <note>A region in Saxony, Germany</note>, Reader at Klausenburg <note>The German name for the city of Cluj-Napoca, or Kolozsvár, a center of the Unitarian movement</note>: to perform which duty he was summoned from Germany by Biandrata and Ferenc Dávid: as Possevino <note>Antonio Possevino (1533–1611) was a Jesuit diplomat and polemicist who wrote against the "heretics" of Eastern Europe</note> testifies in Section III, chapter 7. There, after he says, *Biandrata thereafter and Ferenc Dávid, raising their crests <note>acting with growing confidence</note> in the hope they had conceived that this impiety would soon creep everywhere, chose several young men imbued with that depravity to send to Padua, so that having acquired greater learning, they might do what they could to deceive anyone in that Academy; he soon adds, Likewise they appointed Johann Sommer—a talkative man who seemed to know Greek, summoned from Germany after he had defected from the Lutherans—to preside over the school at Klausenburg. In his place (because he died not much later from the plague along with his wife and mother-in-law), they substituted a certain Matthias the Pole, as one skilled in the Hebrew language, yet in such a way that Jacob, who called himself Palaeologus and was born in Greece, presided over him. To him they commanded, as one skilled in Greek letters—using a Greek for Greek—that he should correct the Bible, etc.* Sommer flourished in the year 1569. He was of the same opinion <note>original: "homodoxus"</note> as Ferenc Dávid regarding the dogma of not invoking the Lord Jesus.

He celebrated the Hungarian Kings in elegiac verse.

Theses on the Papal Triune God, one in essence, threefold in persons, taken from its foundations and published in the year 1571.

Refutation of the writing which Péter Károlyi <note>original: "Petrus Carolius," a Reformed/Calvinist bishop who opposed the Unitarians</note> published in the year 1571 under the title *Explanation of the Orthodox Faith, concerning the one true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*, against the errors of Giorgio Biandrata and Ferenc Dávid. Various treatises on [theological] matters were added.

-># LIBRARY<-

->58<-

...[continuation of the previous entry]... <note>original: "bus", the suffix of a word from the previous page</note>: prefixed to this book is a letter from a certain person who called himself **Theodosius Schimbergius**. <note>Theodosius Schimbergius was a pseudonym used by the Transylvanian Unitarians to publish controversial works.</note> For he saw to it that the aforementioned refutation was published in the year 1582.

*Several Treatises on the Christian Religion*, which the same Schimbergius published with his own preface, ostensibly at Ingolstadt, <note>The use of "Ingolstadt" as a place of publication was likely a false imprint intended to deceive censors, as Ingolstadt was a staunchly Catholic city and unlikely to host such radical works.</note> in the year 1583, in octavo format. In that work are contained:

1. *A Confutation of Objections*, which were mentioned at the end of the letter prefixed to the booklet of **Johann Sommer**.

2. *On the Justification of Man before God*, by **Johann Sommer**. Also, *Propositions on the Same* presented to the Elders of Turda, <note>Thorda/Turda: a town in Transylvania famous for the 1568 Edict of Torda, an early decree of religious tolerance.</note> September 19, 1572, together with the *Response of the Elders* presented at Klausenburg, <note>Claudiopolis: the Latin name for modern-day Cluj-Napoca, Romania.</note> September 29, 1572, and a *Confutation of the Response*, October 5, authored by **Johann Sommer**.

3. *The Aim of the Seventh Chapter to the Romans*, by **Adam Neuser**. <note>Adam Neuser (c. 1530–1576) was a German pastor who fled to Transylvania and eventually to the Ottoman Empire, where he famously converted to Islam.</note>

4. *A Short Declamation against the Predestination of the Moderns*. <note>The "moderns" (neoterics) here refers to the Calvinist theologians of the time.</note>

5. *A Declamation against Adult Baptism*, by **Johann Sommer**.

6. *Theses on the Triune God in Persons and One in Essence, drawn from his own foundations*, by **Johann Sommer**. [I have no doubt these are the same as those mentioned above, published in the year 1571.] The type-faces seem to belong to **Alexius Rodecius**. <note>A prominent printer in Kraków and later in Transylvania who worked extensively for the Unitarian community.</note>

<margin>*</margin>**JACOBUS PALÆOLOGUS**, a Greek born on the island of Chios, descended from the lineage of the Emperors of Constantinople. <note>Palaeologus claimed descent from the last Byzantine dynasty; he was a radical theologian who sought to reconcile Christianity with Judaism and Islam.</note> He served as the primary Rector of the school at Klausenburg after the death of **Johann Sommer**. He held the same views as **Ferenc Dávid** and the aforementioned **Sommer**. As an old man, he was burned at the stake in Rome because of his dogmas, on March 22, 1585.

*On the Ripetan Judgment at Rome, and on the Condemnation of the Best and Most Innocent Men, in the Times of Paul IV.* <note>Pope Paul IV (r. 1555–1559) was known for his rigorous enforcement of the Inquisition.</note>

*On Baptism.* Palaeologus himself cites this book in his *Confutation of the Judgment of the Polish Churches*, page 368, in this manner: *“But regarding the baptism of **Grzegorz Paweł**, and the resurrection which he imagines and comments upon, as well as his regeneration and liberation from sin, which **Vitrelinus** <note>likely referring to a colleague or opponent in the Polish Brethren</note> mentions here—we have taught elsewhere how far this is from the whole Truth of the Gospel.”*

...but also that the baptism of which the Gospels speak does not pertain to us, the children of the testaments and of the covenant of God, as our book on this subject teaches. <note>This refers to the "Adiaphorist" or "non-ritualist" view held by some radical reformers who believed that water baptism was a temporary rite for the apostolic age, not required for children born to Christian parents.</note> Here he makes mention of two of his own works, but we have not had the opportunity to see either, and therefore we cannot provide their titles exactly.

*On the Political Magistrate*: Published at Losk <note>Losk: a town in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, a major center for Simon Budny’s printing press.</note> in Lithuania in the year 1573, through the editorial efforts of **Simon Budny**. <note>Simon Budny (c. 1530–1593) was a Polish-Belarusian reformer who advocated for a more rationalist approach to scripture.</note> This book was refuted by the Racovians <note>Racovians: The "Polish Brethren" based in Raków, who held more pacifist views than Palaeologus.</note> primarily through the work of **Gregory Paul**. To this writing, **Palaeologus** again opposed a book under this title:

*A Defense of the True Opinion on the Political Magistrate*: Likewise printed at Losk through the work of **Budny** in the year 1580. A response to this book was given on behalf of the Racovians by **Fausto Sozzini** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), the Italian theologian whose name gave rise to "Socinianism."</note> in the year 1581.

Through the efforts of the same **Palaeologus**, as well as **Matthias Glirius** and **David** (the son of **Francis David**), a book was released into the light in the year 1580, in octavo format, under this title:

*Defense of Francis David, in the Matter of Not Invoking Jesus Christ in Prayers.* <note>This refers to the "Non-adorantist" controversy: Francis David argued that because Christ was a human being and not God, he should not be addressed in prayer.</note> In which book the following items are contained:

*Four Theses of Francis David* regarding the non-invocation of Jesus Christ in sacred prayers, proposed to **Fausto Sozzini**.

*Response of Fausto Sozzini* to the said theses.

*Francis David’s Refutation of the Response by Faustus.*

*Judgment of the Polish Churches* regarding the case of **Francis David**, on the question of the true invocation of the man Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God.

*A True and Solid Refutation of the Judgment of the Polish Churches* regarding the case of **Dr. Francis David**, on the question of the true invocation of the man Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God. Authored by the most famous philosopher and theologian, **Doctor Jacob Palaeologus**. To which is prefixed a preface to all brothers and ministers of the church of Jesus Christ who profess one God, who is the Father alone. Inserted into this refutation is:

*A Writing of the Transylvanian Brothers to N. N.* <note>N. N. (Nomen Nescio) indicates an anonymous recipient.</note> In which is contained a narrative of the events that took place in Transylvania because of the mentioned controversy. These are contained in the aforementioned *Defense*; which was first printed at Frankfurt am Main, but later reprinted in Krakow by **Alexius Rodecki**, who, because of this and other things of the same kind, was thrown into prison <note>original: "conjectum"</note>

...had been rejected, as reported by Fausto Sozzini <note>original: "F. Socinus"</note> in letter 30 to M. Radecius.

<margin>*</margin>**MATTHIAS GLIRIUS**, <note>Real name Matthias Vehe-Glirius (c. 1545–1590), a German theologian who moved toward a radical unitarianism that incorporated many Jewish elements.</note> a Physician. An associate of **Francis David**, **Sommer**, and **Palaeologus**. **Possevino** <note>Antonio Possevino (1533–1611), a Jesuit scholar and bibliographer.</note> seems to hint at him in those words which we cited under the entry for **Johann Sommer**: when he says that "Matthias the Pole" succeeded Sommer in the administration of the school at Klausenburg <note>original: "Claudiopolis," the Latin name for the Transylvanian city of Kolozsvár (modern Cluj-Napoca), a center of the Unitarian movement.</note>. However, I doubt that he was Polish; for he was an associate of **Johann Sylvanus** and **Adam Neuser** (about whom we will speak shortly), and a participant in their persecution in the Palatinate. <note>The Palatinate was a territory of the Holy Roman Empire where radical theologians were purged in the 1570s.</note>

**Martin Ruar** writes concerning him in a letter to **Abraham Calovius**: *Dietrich Dorsch—who is the same person as Nathanaël Ælianus Matthania, and also Matthias Glirius—clearly judaizes regarding the kingdom of Christ.* <note>To "judaize" was a derogatory term used by mainstream Christians for those who interpreted the Bible through a Jewish lens or denied the divinity of Christ.</note> This work by Nathanaël Ælianus Matthania is said to have been published in the German language in the year 1578, containing semi-Jewish arguments against the Christian religion.

The same work exists in a Latin manuscript.

**JOHANN GLIRIUS.**
*A Treatise on the Old and New Covenant.*

**HERMAN VAN VLECKWYCK**, a Belgian. *A Disputation on the Commonly Received Opinion of the Trinity*, which he held during the time of the Inquisition in the Low Countries with Brother **Cornelius Adrian**, the "Scourger" (commonly called **Broer Cornelis**). Through the efforts of this man <note>the inquisitor</note>, once this disputation was concluded, he [van Vleckwyck] was burned at the stake for his views in Bruges, Flanders, on June 10, 1569. This Disputation, written in the Dutch language, can be read in the very ancient *Martyrology of the Mennonites*, <note>The Mennonites are a group of Anabaptists named after Menno Simons.</note> in which he is listed among the martyrs; however, more recent copies have been censored <note>original: "castrata," meaning passages deemed too radical or controversial were removed.</note>. Nevertheless, it was published again separately. **Gerard Brandt**, a Remonstrant <note>The Remonstrants were a Dutch Protestant group following the teachings of Arminius.</note> minister in Amsterdam, also presents it in Book 10 of his *History of the Reformation* which occurred in the Low Countries.

**JOHANN SYLVANUS**, Inspector of Ladenburg and (as some claim) Superintendent of the Churches of the Rhenish Palatinate. Formerly a teacher of **Frederick**, the Elector. He was executed by beheading <note>original: "capite mulctatus est"</note> on account of his religion in the year 1572.

*Against the Eutychian Error*, in German, octavo volume. <note>Eutychianism was an early Christian heresy regarding the nature of Christ, often used as a polemical label in the 16th century.</note>

*Against the Books of Johann Marpach* (two volumes, if I am not mistaken, as the *Gesnerian Library* <note>The *Bibliotheca Universalis* by Conrad Gessner, a massive 16th-century bibliography.</note> records). Later, when he had defected to the Samosatenians... <note>Followers of Paul of Samosata; a term used by the orthodox to describe those who believed Jesus was a mere human who became divine.</note>

<header>OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS</header>

<meta>catchword: Lives</meta>

He is said to have written in defense of the Samosatenian or Servetan heresy <note>The "Samosatenian" heresy refers to the teachings of Paul of Samosata, a 3rd-century bishop who denied the pre-existence of Christ. the "Servetan" heresy refers to Michael Servetus (c. 1511–1553), who was executed for his denial of the Trinity. Both terms were used as derogatory labels for Unitarians.</note>; these works, however, have not been published.

**ADAM NEUSER** <note>original: "Adamus Neusnerus"</note>, Pastor of the Church of Heidelberg. After he had served in the ministry for ten years, he was thrown into prison in the Lower Palatinate in the year 1571 because of his religious views, along with the aforementioned **Sylvanus**. He escaped from there in a miraculous manner, as **Budzyński** <note>Stanisław Budzyński (c. 1530–1595), a Polish Unitarian historian.</note> relates in chapter 35, and fled to Transylvania. But since he was by no means safe there from persecution and the Emperor's wrath, he found it necessary to withdraw to Constantinople. <note>Neuser's flight to the Ottoman Empire was a scandal of the era; he eventually converted to Islam to avoid extradition and execution.</note>

*A Manuscript Letter to the Illustrious Lord Békés* <note>Gáspár Békés (1520–1579), a Transylvanian nobleman and Anti-Trinitarian.</note>, *Legate of John Sigismund, Prince of Transylvania, to Emperor Maximilian II: written at Heidelberg in the year 1571.* It was by the interception of this letter that the Emperor ensured Neuser was thrown into chains with Sylvanus, as we have mentioned.

*The Aim of the Seventh Chapter to the Romans*, written in the year 1572 and published as if at Ingolstadt, 1583, in octavo.

<margin>*</margin>**ANDREAS DUDITH** <note>original: "Andreas Dudicius," a famous Hungarian humanist and diplomat (1533–1589).</note> of Horecoviza Sbardellatus, a Hungarian. First the Bishop of Knin <note>original: "Tiniensis."</note>, later of Csanád <note>original: "Chonadiensis."</note>, and finally of Pécs <note>original: "Quinqueecclesiensis."</note>. He was a Counselor to His Sacred Imperial Majesty and a legate to the King of Poland. He was formerly a delegate on behalf of the clergy of the Kingdom of Hungary to the Council of Trent. There, having seen the secrets of the Roman Church, and since this religion had displeased him, he joined the Reformers. In Poland, having been naturalized among the native citizens of the Kingdom at the Sejm of Piotrków <note>original: "Comitiis Perticoviensibus," the Polish parliament.</note> in the year 1565, he took a wife from the noble Strausz family. After her death, he joined himself in marriage to the daughter of the Castellan of Krakow, **Zborowski**, who was the widow of **Count Tarnowski**. By her, he fathered a daughter named **Regina**, the wife of **Hieronymus Moscorovius** <note>Jerzy Moskorzowski (c. 1560–1629), a prominent Polish Unitarian and co-author of the Racovian Catechism.</note>. Later, since he judged that even the Reformed followers of **Calvin** still lacked much in the way of reformation—and especially seeing their bitterness toward the "Minor Church" <note>original: "coetum minorem," the official name of the Polish Brethren or Unitarian church in Poland.</note> which professed one God—he separated from them and joined the latter. He embraced their views, and both professed and defended them until his death. Indeed, in his town of Śmigiel <note>original: "Smigel."</note>, he established a church and school for the use of this religion and stood as their patron.

He was born at Buda in Hungary <note>original: "Pannonia."</note> in the year 1533, on February 5. He died at Breslau in Silesia <note>original: "Uratislavia," modern-day Wrocław, Poland.</note> in the year 1589, on February 15, or according to others, February 23, New Style.

<meta>catchword: Ora-</meta>

His life, preserved in writing, still exists.

He admits, in a letter to Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a French Protestant theologian and the successor of John Calvin in Geneva.</note>, that he drew his views on the <term>Unitarians</term> <note>original: "Unitariorum"; a Christian group that believes God is one person, rejecting the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> concerning God and His Son Jesus Christ primarily from the writings of the Transylvanians, published by **Giorgio Blandrata** and **Francis Davidis**. In this letter, he writes among other things:

*But so that I may say something concerning those two most illustrious men, G. Blandrata and Francis Davidis, I profess before God and His Angels that I was not moved by any authority of theirs to depart from the widely accepted opinion of the Trinity. I can also solemnly affirm that I have never seen either of them. Therefore, no friendship so close could have existed between us, nor did any benefit proceed from them that could dazzle my sight. Thus, their favor and authority could not have deceived me, as you falsely guess. Nor could the authority of any man be so great as to lead me away from true piety. Yet, I am so far from ever denying this that I even freely profess that this entire heavenly doctrine is, after God, chiefly owed to those most illustrious men, endowed with great learning, talent, judgment, and piety. Into the fellowship of this glory come, by their own right, **Alciati**, **Grzegorz Paweł** <note>original: "Gregorius Schomanus"</note>, **Krowicki**, **Socinus** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), the namesake of Socinianism.</note>, and other most excellent men, who applied much effort to illustrating this doctrine, both by writing and by teaching. They first, as far as I know—those two most excellent men, Blandrata and Davidis, I say—by publishing books in Latin on this matter, rescued Christ from the tomb for us; into which those Fathers of yours, both the founders and architects of <term>Popery</term> <note>original: "Papismi"; a derogatory term for Roman Catholicism used by reformers.</note>, held him detained, thrust down and crushed, with guards stationed around. Therefore, I will candidly confess that these men showed me the way, pointing as if with a finger, to understanding the doctrine of the Gospel simply as it was written and handed down.*

*A Small Commentary on the Significance of Comets, and new dissertations on Comets.* Basel, 1579. Quarto.

*Medical Letters* in the volume of philosophical, medical, and chemical letters by **Lorenz Scholz**. Frankfurt, 1598, and Hanau, 1610.

*Poems* in volume 2 of the *Delights of German Poetry*. All these are permitted in the *Spanish Index of Prohibited Books* <note>original: "Indice Hispanico expurgatorio"; a list of books that the Catholic Church required to be censored or "purged" of specific passages rather than banned entirely.</note>. The rest are forbidden. As for what he wrote besides these, they are as follows:

The letters were printed in the **Library of the Polish Brethren (Unitarians)** <note>The *Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum* was a massive multi-volume collection of the core theological works of the Socinian movement, published in the 17th century.</note>, attached to the letters of **Fausto Sozzini**.

**Letter to Justus Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was one of the most famous humanists and classicists of the age.</note>, written from Wrocław <note>original: "Breslâ"</note> on March 17, 1584; the first among the letters of famous men addressed to Lipsius.

**Letters to various people**, Manuscript.

I also made use of the *Dialogues* of **Bernardino Ochino** <note>An Italian reformer who fled to Poland; his *Thirty Dialogues* were controversial for discussing polygamy and the Trinity.</note>, which came from the library of the most distinguished man **Johannes Pesserus**, Consul of Rotterdam (who was a lover of such books); in which **Dudith** had written notes in his own hand. Which same thing, before him, **Valentin Gentile** <note>An Italian anti-trinitarian executed in Bern for heresy in 1566.</note> and **Giorgio Biandrata** <note>A court physician and influential reformer in Poland and Transylvania.</note> had done in the same volume: whose handwriting Dudith himself (having written his own name at the beginning of the book as the owner) identified in notes, signing beneath them: *the hand of V. Gentile, beheaded at Bern; likewise, the hand of Biandrata.*

->**FAUSTUS SOCINUS** of Siena, Italy.<-

Born to **Alessandro Sozzini**, a legal expert <note>original: "JC" for "Jurisconsultus"</note> and nobleman of Siena, the brother of Lelio; and to **Agnese**, daughter of **Borghese Petrucci**, Prince of Siena. He was therefore joined by blood to many princes and magnates of Italy, as well as to **Pius II** and **III**, and also **Paul V**, the greatest Roman Pontiffs. After spending twelve years in the Florentine court of the **Grand Duke of Tuscany**, and having disregarded the favor of the Duke and other Italian nobles, he voluntarily left behind his wealth and possessions (which were later entirely stripped from him by a decree of the Pope as a heretic). He went into voluntary exile from his homeland in the year 1574. After traveling through various regions, he came to **Poland** in the year 1579 and established his residence there. He was born in **Siena** in the year 1539, on December 5th, nearly 23 hours before sunrise. He died in the year 1604, on March 3rd, in the village named **Lusławice** <note>original: "Luclawrice"</note>, located in the Palatinate of Kraków, and was buried there. **Samuel Przypkowski** <note>original: "Samuel Przypcovius"</note> recorded his life in writing.

Furthermore, we have demonstrated more extensively above, under the entry for **Lelio Sozzini** <note>Lælio Socino, the uncle of Faustus</note>, that this work was falsely attributed to him. Apart from the *Paraphrase on the first part of the first chapter of the Gospel of Saint John*—which Faustus Socinus mentions in the aforementioned book against Eutropius <note>A reference to Sozzini’s *Refutation of the Libel of Christoffel Eutropius*</note>—it is not clear whether Lelio wrote anything else. I found the mentioned explanation printed in a certain work by the Transylvanians, published by them in the early days of the Reformation; it formed the first part of the second book, with a preface attached. **Franciscus Junius** <note>A prominent Huguenot theologian</note> also published it without the preface and in a less complete form elsewhere, just as the manuscript had reached him. The same work was published by **Hieronim Moskorzowski** <note>Hieronymo Moscorovio, a Polish nobleman and prominent Socinian</note> at Raków <note>Racoviæ</note> in the year 1618, in octavo format, with the addition of explanations for Chapter 9 of Romans and certain other passages of Holy Scripture. Added to this were the responses of Sozzini to the objections raised by **Marcin Czechowic** <note>Martini Czechovicii</note> against this explanation.

The same work was translated into Polish, as Sozzini himself teaches in the aforementioned book against Eutropius and in the noted letter to **Morsztyn**; where, after saying, *“My labors published until now are these,”* etc., he adds: *“The Explanation of the beginning of the Gospel of John, which was also published in Polish long before I arrived here.”* **Grzegorz Paweł of Brzeziny** <note>Gregorius Pauli Bresinensis</note> is said to have been the author of this translation.

The same in Dutch <note>original: "Belgicè"</note>, 1664, in octavo.

The book **On the Authority of Holy Scripture** <note>De Auctoritate Sacræ Scripturæ</note>, written in Italian around the year 1570 for the sake of a certain great man, and published without the author's name at the front.

The same work in Latin, translated by the author; published at Seville <note>Hispali</note> in 1588, in duodecimo, by Lázaro Ferrer with the permission of the superiors, under the name of the Reverend Father **Domenico Lopez** <note>Dominici Lopezii</note> of the Society of Jesus <note>the Jesuits</note>, who seems to have wanted to claim this little work for himself. However, in the preface, something to the contrary is praised compared to what is read in the book itself; thus, he betrays himself. **Cloppenburg** <note>Johannes Cloppenburg, a Dutch theologian</note>, however, thinks the names of the author, the place, and the printer were fabricated; and he says there were those who, based on the evidence of the typefaces, attributed it to a printer in Amsterdam, the once quite famous bookseller **Cornelis Nicolaasz** <note>Cornelio Nicolai</note>. But besides this, he offers no other reason to dismantle what has been said.

The same, at Raków, April 1611, in octavo.

**Disputation between Faustus Socinus and Christian Franken** regarding the honor of Christ: that is, whether Christ—since he is not God by the most perfect definition—is nevertheless to be worshiped with religious adoration, or not? <note>Franken argued that if Christ was not God by nature, he should not be prayed to; Socinus defended the practice of "invocation" even while denying Christ’s divinity</note> This was held on March 14, 1584, in the hall of **Lord Krzysztof Morsztyn of Pawlikowice**; and published in 1618, in octavo. However, this was transcribed by Franken himself as it seemed fit to him, and not as it truly took place. For he himself confessed in Chmielnik before **Lord Georg Schomann**, **Lord Simon Ronemberg**, and others, that in transcribing it, he did not look so much at what Socinus said, but what he ought to have said to be consistent with his own principles. To this are added quite a few notes and responses to what Franken says, as well as certain corrections of those things which he makes Socinus say.

**Fragments of a fuller Response** which Faustus Socinus was preparing to **Francis David’s** <note>Ferenc Dávid (1510–1579), the founder of the Unitarian Church in Transylvania</note> writing on the non-invocation of Christ. Six chapters of this fragment remain; the rest have perished.

**A certain fragment of Observations** by Faustus Socinus on the writing of a certain person concerning the difference between the Old and the New Covenant.

**Some Questions by Francis David**, and Faustus Socinus’s response to them.

**Antitheses**, collected by Socinus himself from the dispute held between Faustus Socinus of Siena and Francis David.

### LIBRARY

**Theses**, by which the opinion of **Ferenc Dávid** <note>original: "Fr. Davidis"; the founder of the Unitarian Church in Transylvania who eventually rejected the practice of praying to Jesus</note> concerning the office of Christ is explained: together with the antitheses of the Church, written by **Faustus Socinus** and presented to the most illustrious Prince of Transylvania, **Christopher Báthory**.

Certain matters to be especially observed in the dispute regarding the **Invocation of Christ** <note>The practice of addressing prayers to Jesus Christ, a central point of contention between Socinus and the "Non-adorantist" faction led by Ferenc Dávid</note>.

Concerning the **book of Revelation**, and the testimonies which are sought from it against those who utterly deny the invocation of Jesus Christ.

**Against the Semi-Judaizers** <note>A polemical label for those who, like Dávid, denied Christ’s right to be worshipped or insisted on the continued validity of Mosaic law</note>.

Three letters from **Martin Seidel** of Ohlau, Silesia, in which his opinion concerning the **Messiah**, or that promised King, and concerning religion is contained: addressed to the former congregation at Kraków, called the **Minor Church** <note>The "Ecclesia Minor," or Polish Brethren, who held Unitarian views</note>, which confesses that the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is that One God of Israel: in whose name Faustus Socinus responded to the same Seidel.

**A Disputation** between **Erasmus Johannis** and **Faustus Socinus** of Siena, concerning the existence of the only-begotten Son of God. In which the former [Johannis], affirming that Christ was the only-begotten Son of God before he was born of the virgin <note>An Arian or "High" Unitarian view that Socinus rejected</note>, takes the role of the challenger; while the latter [Socinus], asserting the contrary opinion, takes the role of the respondent. This dispute was completed on November 30, 1584, but printed in 1595, at Raków, in octavo. Prefixed is Socinus’s preface to **Hieronim Moskorzowski**: added also is a question on the same subject, proposed to Socinus by the same Erasmus Johannis, and Socinus’s response to it.

**The Aristotelian Instrument of Doctrines**, for the use of Christian schools, illustrated with theological examples, by **Gratianus Prosperus** <note>A pseudonym used for this work</note>. Łuck, 1586, octavo.

Also among the works of **Franciscus Junius**, with his refutation. **Wolfgang Frantzius** and **Abraham Calovius** <note>Prominent Lutheran theologians and critics of Socinianism</note> attribute this work to Socinus in *Against Crell*, § 476. However, Socinus himself does not mention it in the stated letter to **Morsztyn**: and it may not without merit be doubted whether it is his own creation <note>original: "an ipsius sit foetus," literally "whether it is his offspring"</note>.

**A Synopsis of our Justification through Jesus Christ**, which first came to light under the name of **Gratianus Turpio of Gerapolis**, Gerapolis, 1591, quarto; and Raków, 1611, octavo, under the true name of **Faustus Socinus**. Moreover, the following are found in this book:

# OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS
<sig>E 5</sig>
<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

1. A first synopsis of our **Justification through Christ**, and a second synopsis of our **justification before God**.

2. **Theses on Justification**.

3. A **Dialogue on Justification**, by N.N. <note>This "N.N." typically stands for *Nomen Nescio*, indicating an anonymous author whose identity the editor chooses not to reveal or does not know</note> with the notes of **Faustus Socinus**.

4. **Fragments on Justification**.

5. **On Faith and Works**, as pertains to our justification: from Italian letters to the most renowned man N. N.

6. **Theses concerning the cause and foundation** within man himself of that faith in God by which men are justified, as the Holy Scriptures testify.

**A Refutation of the booklet** which **Jacob Wujek**, a Jesuit, published in Polish in the year 1590, concerning the **Divinity of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit**: where in the same work is refuted whatever **Robert Bellarmine**, likewise a Jesuit <note>Bellarmine was one of the most important cardinals of the Counter-Reformation; his "Disputations" were the standard defense of Catholic doctrine against Protestantism</note>, wrote in the first volume of his *Disputations*, in the first book of the second general controversy, concerning the same matter. This **Response** was written in the year 1592, and in the following year 1593, it was first published in Polish, translated by **Peter Statorius the Younger**, in octavo <note>term: octavo; a book size created by folding a standard sheet of paper three times to form eight leaves</note>.

Also in Latin, with the author’s preface, written September 6, 1595; printed in the year 1591 <note>original: "1591"; this appears to be a printer's error in the source text, as the preface is dated four years later, in 1595</note> in octavo, with the author’s name suppressed. At the end of this book, Socinus promises that he will bring to light a book containing arguments against the common opinion regarding the **Trinity**, when he says:

*If God ever gives so much leisure and good health, that just as my mind is inclined, we may ourselves eventually take up the role of the proponent <note>original: "actoris partes"; literally "the parts of the actor" or the lead in a legal/academic argument</note> in this question of divinity; I hope that I, with the favor of that same God, shall collect arguments and reasons of that kind sought from the Holy Scriptures for our opinion, and at the same time so fortify them against all attacks, that, perhaps for pious men and those kindled with the love of divine truth, if this present labor of ours be joined with that which we hope for in the future, very little may seem to be desired for a full treatment of this matter.*

I do not see whether these words can be correctly applied to any work of Socinus which he composed and published after this book: perhaps, therefore, that labor was never written by him (as he was always distracted by other things); or if it was written, it perished in the **plundering of his goods**, (which happened in the year 1598) <note>Socinus's house in Kraków was attacked by a mob in 1598; his papers were scattered or burned, and he was physically assaulted for his heretical views</note>.

<term>Justification</term>: The theological doctrine of how humans achieve a right standing with God.
<term>Faith</term>: In the Socinian sense, not just mental belief but an obedient trust in God.
<term>Faustus Socinus</term>: The Italian theologian who became the intellectual leader of the Polish Brethren.
<term>Jacob Wujek</term>: A Polish Jesuit famous for translating the Bible into Polish.
<term>Robert Bellarmine</term>: A preeminent Catholic theologian and defender of the Papacy.
<term>Peter Statorius Junior</term>: A prominent member of the Polish Brethren and translator of Socinus's works.
<term>Trinity</term>: The orthodox Christian doctrine of one God in three persons, which the authors of this catalog rejected.
<term>Anti-Trinitarians</term>: A general term for groups like the Socinians who denied the traditional doctrine of the Trinity.

With grace and*

**JAN KISZKA of CIECHANOWIEC**; A Polish knight, or rather Lithuanian: A disciple of Sebastian Castalio <note>A French theologian and early proponent of religious toleration</note>, to whom he erected a monument in foreign lands even after Castalio's death. -> ### OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS <-
F 3

...[continued from previous page] published a book under this title: *Arian Mists, scattered by Master Raphael Ritter of London: dispersed by the light of divine truth, by Master Johannes Wigand, Bishop of Pomesania. Königsberg in Prussia <note>original: "Regiomonti Borussiæ"</note> published by Bonifacius Daubmann in the year 1575, in octavo.* In this volume, the aforementioned booklet by Ritter is contained in its entirety. Furthermore, it is clear from his own words—which are read on page 51 and following of the mentioned book—that this Ritter was not an follower of **Arius** <note>Arianism taught that Christ was a created being, but existed before the world</note>, but rather of **Socinus** <note>Socinianism, or Unitarianism, taught that Jesus did not exist before his human birth</note>; for at the end of his writing, he says the following:

*But I must not conceal that which provides many with a great occasion for error: that is, while Christ is called the Son of God, many are ignorant of the cause of that name. They think he was begotten from the essence or substance of God, and is therefore called the Son of God. This error is indeed deep-rooted, but it is not to be tolerated on that account. For Jesus, the Son of God, is not, and is not called so, because he was born of the substance of God: these are the trifles of the Sophists <note>The author uses "Sophists" here as a derogatory term for Scholastic theologians who used complex philosophical arguments to define the Trinity</note>. Rather, let the pious reader learn from the Gospel the cause of this matter—namely, why Jesus Christ is called the Son of God. For there, the Angel, instructing the Virgin Mary regarding the manner of the Messiah's wondrous conception, speaks to her in this way: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you, and therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God."*

*Here the cause of such a great Name is most clearly indicated: specifically, that the Messiah is called the Son of God because he was conceived and then born without the embrace of a man. Therefore, Gabriel says, that "Holy Thing" shall be called the Son of God, because the most holy infant was to be conceived by the Holy Spirit coming upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowing her. Let it be observed, moreover, that the Angel did not say of Christ that he was already or had formerly been called the Son of God, but that he would finally be so called once he was born. Consequently, it was not that Spirit which had descended from the heavens, but that man who was born of the Virgin Mary, who was called the Son of God; and this because he was conceived and brought forth by the agency of God, contrary to the order of nature. This is why, although all the Prophets foretold his coming and spoke many things about him, he was nowhere called the "Son of God" by them until he finally appeared and was baptized in the Jordan. For Jesus Christ is a man, just as the Apostles call him, because he is also the Son of Man (as he frequently calls himself), yet he is nonetheless also God. But only in the manner we have stated above...*

<summary>This page discusses a 1575 work by Raphael Ritter, an English physician, arguing that his theology was Socinian rather than Arian. It includes a lengthy translated excerpt where Ritter argues that Jesus is called the "Son of God" solely due to his miraculous conception and birth, rather than a pre-existent divine nature.</summary>

Response to three orations of Warkawicius <note>Stanisław Warszewicki (1530–1591), a Jesuit polemicist</note> the Jesuit, by which he incites King Stephen <note>Stephen Báthory, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania</note> and the Senators to persecute the Protestants; written under the name of **Nicolaus Regius**.

Letter to the Synod of the Polish Brethren celebrated at Wegrowia <note>original: "Wegroviae," modern-day Węgrów, Poland</note>: dealing with the same matter: written in the mentioned year 1584. Manuscript.

Books against the Trinity: at the press of **Alexius Rodecki** <note>A prominent printer for the Polish Brethren in Kraków</note>. On account of these books, Franken suffered persecution, while Rodecki the printer suffered the loss of his printing shop and was thrown into chains.

**ERASMUS JOHANNIS**, Rector of the Antwerp school: Where, since it was not permitted for him to live safely on account of dogmas differing from those received by the common people, he betook himself to Poland, and from there to Transylvania, where the office of pastor at Klausenburg <note>original: "Claudiopoli," modern-day Cluj-Napoca, Romania</note> was committed to him by the Unitarians, with this condition: that he should not teach from the pulpit that Christ, the Son of God, existed in reality before his mother. For he taught, along with the ancient Arians <note>Followers of Arius who believed that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, rather than co-eternal with Him</note>, that the Son of God was created out of nothing before all things by God the Father, and that through him finally, the supreme God produced the rest of the creatures: concerning which matter he disputed with Faustus Socinus in Poland.

While he was still Rector of the Antwerp school, he secretly sent out a certain book of his opinion: but William, Prince of Orange <note>William the Silent, leader of the Dutch Revolt</note>, "nipped his efforts in the bud" <note>original: "in herba stitit," an idiom meaning to stop something before it can grow or flourish</note>: as Henry Antonii says in the Preface to his *System of Theology*.

*Antithesis of the doctrine of Christ and Antichrist concerning the one true God*, year 1585, in octavo <note>8°, a book size where the printed sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves</note>. Printed by Alexius Radecius, as Faustus Socinus testifies in the third letter to Matthew Radecius, from which I learned that Erasmus is the author of this little work, for no name is prefixed to it. The same book appeared with a refutation by Hieronymus Zanchius <note>An Italian Renaissance humanist and Reformed theologian</note>, at Neustadt, in the year 1586, in quarto <note>4°, a book size where the sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note>. It is also found in the works of the same Zanchius which were published together.

A writing to Faustus Socinus, in favor of the pre-eternal preexistence of Jesus Christ, published with the response of Faustus Socinus: this disputation was finished on November 30, 1584. Joined to it is:

A question on the same argument proposed by Erasmus Johannis to Faustus Socinus.

A writing in which [he explains] the causes on account of which eternal life happens...

**EVERARD SPANGENBERG** of Antwerp, a Reformed preacher, called the opinion on the Trinity into doubt at the urging of Erasmus Johannis; for this reason, he found it necessary to leave his homeland: from there he betook himself to Poland and Transylvania. He held a peculiar opinion regarding the approaching restoration of all things <note>A theological concept known as *apocatastasis*, the belief that all things will eventually be restored to a state of perfection in God</note>.

Theses on the two beasts of the Apocalypse: to which Faustus Socinus made notes.

Disputation held among the Frisians <note>People of Friesland, a province in the Netherlands</note>.

Theses on the destruction of the empire of the Roman Church.

Letters to Faustus Socinus, Manuscript. To which Faustus Socinus responded in the year 1593 and following.

A writing containing a narrative about Erasmus Johannis. Manuscript.

1. His own and the Polish Brethren's Confession regarding the humanity and divinity of Christ, and his Priestly and Royal office.

2. His confession regarding the excellence of Christ when he shall have handed over the kingdom to God his Father.

3. The reasons why he was excommunicated by the Polish Brethren, along with his own defense.

4. A disclosure of who his accusers were.

**ANDRZEJ LUBIENIECKI** <note>original: "Andreas Lubieniecius"</note> of Lubieniec, a Polish Knight. Historical Observations on matters worthy of note in the business of religion.

A book containing the Acts and Conclusions of the Synods celebrated in Poland from the beginnings of the Reformation; since his death, these have been continued by his son-in-law Joachim Rupnowski and other scribes of the Synods. Polish Manuscript.

He departed this life in the year 1633, at the age of 74 or 75, being seven years younger than his brother Andrzej.

*Apology, addressed to the decree of the Illustrious and Most Ample...*

**ANDRZEJ WOJDOWSKI** <note>original: "Andreas Voidovius"</note>, a Pole, Pastor of the congregation at Lublin, and later at Raków. Manuscript. <note>This section refers to Piotr Statorius the Younger, whose name concludes the list from the previous page's context</note> Son of Piotr Statorius of Thionville; son-in-law of Grzegorz Paweł of Brzeziny. *A Response to the book of Marcin Śmiglecki, a Jesuit*, in which he attempts to prove the pre-eternity of Christ’s divinity. Polish.

*An Oration or Sermon*, which he delivered at the funeral of Fausto Sozzini in 1604. Polish manuscript.

The same, rendered into Latin. Manuscript.

*Sermons on various passages of Holy Scripture*, especially on a large part of the Gospel of St. John. Polish manuscript.

# B I B L I O T H E C A
<note>Library / Bibliography</note>

Preface to the New Testament of the Racovian version. However, Enyedi died before the Racovian Catechism <note>The *Catechesis Racoviana*, the defining statement of Socinian faith</note> that now exists—prepared primarily through the efforts of Valentin Smalcius and Hieronim Moskorzewski—was published. This is unless, perhaps, one refers to that first Catechism of the Racovians, which we discussed under the entries for Grzegorz Paweł and Fausto Sozzini. Furthermore, it is entirely unknown to me whether any other Racovian version of the New Testament existed besides the Polish one by Smalcius and the German one by Crell and Stegmann, both of which were produced after Enyedi’s death. I strongly doubt, therefore, whether he can rightly be asserted as the author of the aforementioned writings, especially the latter.
