### JAKUB SIENIEŃSKI <note>original: Iacobus Sieninius</note> of Sienno, Polish Knight, son of the Palatine of Podolia, Lord of Raków. 
In the year 1600, he organized a formal debate between the Reformed <note>Calvinists</note> (in whose religion he had been raised) and the Unitarian Christians. Because their arguments seemed more weighty to him, he embraced their faith. For their use, he established at Raków a <term>gymnasium</term> <note>a secondary school or academy</note> for the liberal arts, which later flourished to such an extent that it provoked envy; the number of young people studying there often reached one thousand. He was already seventy years old when the said school, along with the church and the Raków printing house, was abolished in the year 1638 (due to the reckless behavior of certain students of that school) <note>Students had reportedly thrown stones at a crucifix, providing a pretext for the Catholic authorities to shut down the center of Polish Socinianism</note>. He survived this event by only one year. After these misfortunes, Raków declined so much that nothing remains of it but the shadow of a great name. Its lordship is now said to belong to the widow of Krzysztof Wiszowaty, who was born to the son of the aforementioned Palatine of Podolia <note>meaning she was Jakub Sienieński's granddaughter</note>; after her husband’s death, she changed the religion of her ancestors and her father, embraced the rites of the Roman Catholics, and took possession of Raków by hereditary right.
Dedication of the book by Valentin Schmalz <note>original: Valentini Smalcii</note> on the Divinity of Jesus Christ.

### CONRAD VORSTIUS
Of Cologne, Professor at Steinfurt, from where he was called to Leiden <note>Latin: "Lugdunum Batavorum"</note> in the year 1610 to perform the same duties, and was designated as the successor to Jacobus Arminius. Born in Cologne <note>Latin: "Colonia Agrippina"</note> in the year 1569, on July 19th; he died at Tönning in 1622, on September 29th or October 9th. For a long time, I was doubtful whether I should rightly include this author in our catalog. However, this doubt was removed, among other reasons, when I read the confession of faith written by his own hand while he was dying: in which he reveals quite clearly what his opinion was regarding God and Christ the Lord. Also supporting this inclusion is the fact that in the synodal records of the Polish Brethren, it is noted that Vorstius was invited by them, while they were gathered at the Synod of Lublin in the year 1600, to lead the academy at Lucławice. Furthermore, it is well known in what high esteem Vorstius held the writings of the Polish Unitarians <note>original: "Sarmatarum Unitariorum"</note>.

*Disputations on God, or on the nature and attributes of God.* Steinfurt, 1602. 4to.

*The Anti-Pistorian Fourteen.* <note>original: "Tessaradecas Anti-Pistoriana." A work refuting fourteen arguments by the Catholic convert Johannes Pistoris</note> Hanau, 1607. 8vo.

*Counter-demonstration on the first three articles of faith.* Hanau, 1609, 8vo. Also at the same place, 1665, 8vo.

*The Anti-Bellarmin Abridged.* <note>A rebuttal to the works of the famous Catholic Cardinal Robert Bellarmine</note> Hanau, 1610. 4to.

*Treatise on God.* Steinfurt, 1610, 4to. Also Hanau, 1610, 4to. In England, by order of King James, it was publicly burned in 1611. <note>King James I of England was so outraged by Vorstius's views on the nature of God that he intervened to prevent his appointment at Leiden and had his books burned.</note>

*Apologetic Explanation for the Treatise on God.* Hanau, 1610. 4to.

The same work in Dutch.

Preface to the book of Faustus Socinus, *On the Authority of Holy Scripture*: which was published through his care; it is added at the end

### VALENTIN SCHMALZ
<note>Latin: "Valentinus Smalcius"</note>
Of Gotha in Thuringia, born March 12, 1572. First Rector of Śmigiel, then Pastor of Raków, later of Lublin, and finally again of Raków, where he passed from this life on December 4, 1622, as some report; however, Crellius <note>Johannes Crellius, another leading Unitarian scholar</note> assigns the eighth day of December to his death, in a manuscript letter.

The same work was later corrected by several men in Poland: and again, after several years had passed, it was revised by Johannes Crellius <note>Johann Crell (1590–1633), a leading Socinian theologian</note> the Franconian, and finally by Jonas Schlichting of Bukowiec <note>Jonas Schlichting (1592–1661), a Polish Unitarian theologian and biblical critic</note>, and expanded by more than half. A preface was added, written by Andreas Wissowaty <note>Andreas Wissowaty (1608–1678), a prominent Polish Unitarian and grandson of Fausto Sozzini</note> and Joachim Stegmann the younger. The notes of Martin Ruarus on the Catechism were also appended, along with certain responses by Jonas Schlichting. Published in Irenopolis <note>Irenopolis, meaning "City of Peace," was a common pseudonym for Amsterdam in Unitarian publications</note> at the expense of Friedrich Theophilus, after the year of our Lord 1659—that is, around the year 1665, in <term>octavo (8º)</term>.

The same work was revised and corrected by Andreas Wissowaty, and illustrated with the notes of both those mentioned above, as well as those of himself and others. In addition to the aforementioned preface, an address to the reader by another author was prefixed. Published in Stauropolis <note>Stauropolis, meaning "City of the Cross," was another pseudonym often used for Amsterdam or Geneva</note> by Eulogetus Philalethes in the year 1680, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

The same Catechism appeared in German, dedicated to the Academy of Wittenberg. Published at Raków <note>Raków was the intellectual center of the Polish Brethren</note> in the year 1612, in <term>duodecimo (12º)</term>.

The same appeared in Dutch <note>original Latin: "Belgicè"</note>, translated by Johannes Cornelii, commonly called Knoll. He mutilated this book, omitting the chapters on Baptism and the Lord's Supper; therefore, the Unitarians do not acknowledge this edition as their own.

A full edition was therefore issued in the same language, with the notes of Schlichting and Ruarus, in the year 1666, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

Refutation of the disputation of Albert Grauer <note>Albert Grauer (1575–1638) was a prominent Lutheran "defender of orthodoxy" and rector at the University of Weimar</note> concerning the Holy Spirit. Raków, 1613, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

Response to the book by Ravensperger <note>Hermann Ravensperger (1586–1625) was a Reformed/Calvinist theologian from Groningen</note> titled: *A pair of Socinian sophistries, examined according to the standard of truth*. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

Refutation of the theses of Schopper <note>Jacob Schopper (1545–1616) was a German Reformed theologian</note> concerning the Most Holy Unity of the divine essence, and the Trinity of persons within that same Most Holy Unity. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

The same in Dutch. 1664, in <term>octavo (8º)</term>.

Refutation of Grauer’s theses concerning the incarnation of the Son of God. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>. Truly, I do not know for certain whether this book is different from the one I found cited as follows: *Refutation of Grauer’s theses, by which he wished to defend the incarnation of the eternal Son of God from the attackers of our churches*.

Response to the book by Ravensperger, which he titled: *The Most Holy Mysteries of the Unity of the Divine Essence*.

Refutation of the pamphlet by Smiglecki <note>Marcin Śmiglecki (1563–1618) was a famous Polish Jesuit whose work on logic was used as far away as Oxford; he was a fierce opponent of the Polish Brethren</note> titled: *The Word was made flesh: or, on the divine nature of the incarnate Word*. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

Refutation of the theses of Frantzius <note>Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), a Lutheran theologian at Wittenberg</note> concerning the principal headings of the Christian religion. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>; also in <term>octavo (8º)</term>.

Notes on the pamphlet by Smiglecki, which he calls a refutation of the "empty dissolution" of his *Gordian Knot* <note>original: "Nodi sui Gordii." The "Gordian Knot" was a title Smiglecki used for his polemical challenges</note>: under the name A. R., that is, Andreas Reuchlinus <note>A pseudonym used by Valentin Schmalz</note>. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>. Scherzer <note>Johann Adam Scherzer (1628–1683), a later Lutheran theologian</note> calls the author Andreas Radecius, though where he gets this from is unknown to me, for I have heard nothing of any Andreas Radecius.

An exhortation to Isaac Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was one of the most famous classical scholars of the Renaissance</note>, under the name Andreas Reuchlinus. Raków, 1614, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

A brief refutation of the *Treatise on the Church and the Mission of Ministers* by the Reverend Lord Borkowski: in which he attempts to attack Socinus along with Theophilus, and to defend Międzyboż <note>A town in Ukraine where theological debates occurred</note>; written by the same Theophilus Nicolaides <note>Another pseudonym for Valentin Schmalz</note>, in the month of March in the year 1614. Raków, from the Sternacki press <note>The Sternacki family operated the famous press for the Socinian movement in Raków</note>, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

Dedication of Fausto Sozzini’s *Commentary on the First Epistle of Saint John*, to the Councilors of Strasbourg, November 20, 1614.

An examination of one hundred errors which Smiglecki collected from two parts of a book published against his own "monstrosities." Raków, 1615, in <term>quarto (4º)</term>.

**THOMAS PISECIUS** of Martowice, a Silesian Nobleman. His sister, named Rosina, was married to the previously mentioned Simon Pistorius; from her he <note>Simon</note> fathered Rosina, the wife of Johannes Crellius. It is not certain to me when he was born or when he died. However, I have received word from those who knew him that he was still among the living a few years before 1648, being then about seventy years of age.

**On the Origin of the Trinity:** a work written after the refutation of Wujek’s book <note>Jakub Wujek (1541–1597) was a Polish Jesuit famous for his Bible translation and polemics against "heretics"</note>, and after Keckermann <note>Bartholomew Keckermann (1572–1609) was a famous Reformed theologian and philosopher from Danzig</note> had written, as he is mentioned within it. This work perished in a fire.

**Whether the doctrine of the Trinity is a mystery hidden from the ages;** which ought to have been made known to men through the revelation of the divine word: transcribed from the treatise entitled *On the Origin of the Trinity*, 1605, 8vo; 1608, and 1654, 12mo.

**A Response to the ten reasons of Edmund Campion the Jesuit:** by which he <note>Campion</note> attempts to prove that the Catholic Church is to be preferred over others. Printed at Raków <note>original: "Racovia," the intellectual center of the Polish Brethren</note> in 1610, 12mo. Added to this are notes on the *Wilkovian Appendices* <note>Refers to works by Kasper Wilkowski, a physician who converted from Anti-Trinitarianism back to Catholicism</note>.

**On the Antichrist**, in two books, under the name of **Marcus Camillus**. 8vo. That he was the true author of this work was confirmed to me—besides constant rumor—by those who knew him and were related to him by blood; some, however, thought that Jonas Schlichting or Elias Arciszewski the younger wrote this book, but they were mistaken.

**Against Lessius the Jesuit** <note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623) was an influential Flemish Jesuit theologian</note>.

**Commonplaces** <note>A "Commonplace book" was a personal journal where a scholar would compile useful quotes, arguments, and ideas organized by topic.</note> from all the writings of the Unitarians, arranged in alphabetical order. A large volume in manuscript. folio.

**Solutions for various passages of Holy Scripture** and outlines of sermons, produced for the benefit of students of Theology. Prefixed to these is the anagram: *Girded by the perpetual mercy of Jesus* <note>original Latin: "A Ihesu jugeclementia cinctus." This is an anagram for the author’s name, Michael Gittichius.</note>. They began to be written on February 3, 1640, and were finished on March 25, 1641. Manuscript.

**A Letter to Johannes Crellius** <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633) was a major German-Polish Socinian theologian.</note>, included in the fourth volume of his works in the *Library of the Polish Brethren* <note>The "Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum" was the definitive 17th-century collection of Socinian scholarship.</note>: written at Nowogródek on November 16, 1613.

**Letters to Martin Ruar**: included in the first century <note>A "century" refers to a collection of 100 items, in this case, letters.</note> of Ruar's select letters. Amsterdam, 1677. 8vo.

## ÉTIENNE DE COURCELLES [Stephanus Curcellaeus]
A Frenchman, born at Geneva on May 2, 1586. He was first a minister of the Reformed churches in France, and later a Professor of Holy Theology among the Remonstrants <note>The Remonstrants were a Dutch theological movement based on the ideas of Jacobus Arminius, often associated with more liberal or tolerant views than the strict Calvinists.</note> at Amsterdam, in which office he succeeded Master Simon Episcopius. He died at Amsterdam on May 22, 1659. His life is recounted in the funeral oration by Arnold Poelenburg (his successor in the aforementioned office), which is prefixed to his theological works.

**Advice of a Disinterested Person, etc.** <note>original French: "Advis d' un Personnage desinteressé"</note>. This work was published when a controversy regarding Predestination <note>The theological debate over whether God pre-ordains who will be saved.</note> arose between Amyraut and Du Moulin; in this writing, he interposes himself as a mediator. 1638.

**A Defense**, in which the opinion of Lord Arminius regarding the right of God over innocent creatures is defended against Moïse Amyraut, Professor of Holy Theology at Saumur. Amsterdam, 1645. Published by Blaeu.

**Preface to the first volume of the works of Simon Episcopius.** Amsterdam, 1650. folio.

**He translated Comenius's *Gate of Languages*** into Greek <note>John Amos Comenius was a famous educator; his "Janua linguarum reserata" was a standard textbook for learning languages.</note>.

**A Letter to the distinguished Samuel Sorbière** regarding the abuses or errors of the Roman Church. Written in French at Amsterdam, December 24, 1655. Published in octavo; neither the time nor the place of publication were added. Attached to it is a letter from the aforementioned Samuel Sorbière to Pope Alexander VII.

**A Letter to Adriaan Paets**, an advocate of Rotterdam, regarding the superstitions of the Roman Church. Written in French at Amsterdam, 1656, and published together with the preceding letter.

->### THEODORUS RAPHAELIS CAMPHUYSIUS <-
commonly known as **Dirk Raphaelszoon Camphuysen**. Dutch. Born in Gorinchem in 1586, died in Woudrichem in 1627. Having laid down his office as a minister, he was one of the principal leaders of those who go by the name of Prophesiers or Collegiants <note>The Collegiants were a 17th-century Dutch spiritual movement that valued individual interpretation of Scripture and rejected formal clerical hierarchy.</note>, who champion the freedom of speech within the church and are accustomed to meet at Rijnsburg <note>original: "Renoburgi."</note> in Holland to celebrate the Holy Communion <note>original: "S. Synaxin," from the Greek term for a liturgical assembly or gathering.</note>.

**Theological Works.** 1657, in octavo.

Also, **at Amsterdam**, 1640, in quarto.

Also, **at Amsterdam**, 1672, in quarto, **consisting of three parts: 1. on infallible judgment; 2. in sermons; 3. in letters and excerpts.** These comprise the same three parts: 1. On infallible judgment. 2. Sacred sermons. 3. Letters and excerpts.

**Paraphrase of the Psalms of David, in Dutch rhymes.** Often published; the latest edition now available was printed in Amsterdam by Johannes Riewertsz and Petrus Arentsz in 1679, in duodecimo <note>A small, portable book format.</note>.

**Edifying Rhymes: of which the eighteenth edition has come out in Amsterdam by Jan Rieuwertsz and Pieter Arentsz**, 1680, in duodecimo. These are sacred songs, the eighteenth edition of which appeared in 1680.

Also, these were set to musical rules by Joseph Butler <note>original: "Josephum Buthlerum."</note>, an Amsterdam musician. Amsterdam, 1652, in folio.

**Some of these have been set in High German rhymes by Robert Robertyn, etc., in the Prussian Melodies.** That is, several of them have been translated into the German language.

## JOHANNES STOINIUS

**JOHANNES STOINIUS**, also called **STATORIUS**, was a Polish Knight, the son of Peter Statorius the younger and the daughter of Gregory Paul of Brzeziny <note>Gregory Paul was one of the most radical early leaders of the Polish Brethren</note>. He served as the pastor of the congregation at Raków, a duty he performed as early as the year 1612. However, when this church was suppressed in 1638, he was covered in infamy and banished; he first went into exile in foreign lands, but later lived as an exile within his own country until 1654, when he passed away in Czarków at the age of 64. Among those called <term>Socinians: a non-trinitarian group that denied the pre-existence of Christ</term>, he was the most eloquent preacher.

A Disputation held with a Jesuit in the year 1615.

An Account of a Disputation regarding the divinity of Jesus Christ and the remission of our sins achieved through him, held with Giovanni Maria, an Italian Carmelite monk, in the Carmelite house in Lublin, in the presence of the Judges of the High Tribunal of the Kingdom, on July 13, 1616. Printed at Raków in 1618, in quarto.

Another Disputation with the same man, held in the same church: published in 1620.

A conversation with a certain Frenchman named Claude, regarding the question of whether Christ can be adored since he is not the Supreme God: held in 1626. Manuscript.

Against the monk Paxillus. Manuscript.

A book of Polish Prayers, 1633, in <term>octavo: a medium-sized book format</term>. A "Preface to the Reader" is included at the beginning, in which he explains the manner of praying to God.

A Preface to Johannes Crellius’s Commentary on Matthew.

## JOACHIM RUPNOVIUS

**JOACHIM RUPNOVIUS**, of Rupnow, a Polish Knight and son-in-law of Andrzej Lubieniecki. He was a pastor at Raków, later at Lublin, and finally at Berestia, where he died in the year 1643 at the age of 53.

He continued the *Synods of the Polish Brethren*, or the ecclesiastical chronology, from the year 1628; this work was subsequently continued by his successors, the scribes of the Synods, until the year 1668. In Polish. Manuscript.

A dream he had around the year 1630 concerning the Judgment of Raków, representing the future calamity of this town—namely, the suppression of the exercise of Religion, the Church, the school, and the printing house. In Polish. Manuscript. <note>This "dream" likely refers to a prophetic or allegorical warning about the 1638 decree that destroyed the Socinian center at Raków</note>

Sermons. Manuscript. As well as...

->### Other manuscripts of various kinds.<-

**SAMUEL PRZYPKOWSKI** <note>original: "Samuel Przipcovius"</note> of Przypcowice, a Polish Knight. He died in Prussia while in exile for his religious beliefs, while serving as a Counselor to the Elector of Brandenburg, on June 19, 1670, at about eighty years of age.

An anonymous *Dissertation on the Peace and Harmony of the Church*: published by Irenaeus Philalethes <note>A pseudonym meaning "Peace-loving Lover of Truth"</note>, with a preface by the same addressed to the reader (from which it is clear that this editor shared nearly the same views as the Arians <note>A term often used by opponents to describe those who denied the Trinity, specifically those following the teachings of Arius, though here applied to the Polish Brethren</note>). Added at the end of the booklet is another address to the reader by the same author. Published in Eleutheropolis <note>A pseudonym for "Free City," likely Amsterdam or Raków, used to bypass censorship</note> by the printer Godfridus Philadelphus <note>Another pseudonym, meaning "God-fearing Brother-lover"</note>, in the year 1628. In <term>duodecimo</term>. Many believed the author of this small work to be Simon Episcopius, a Professor of Sacred Theology among the Remonstrants in Holland.

Also, a second edition in 1630, in <term>duodecimo</term>, revised according to the author's own manuscript and expanded in many places, printed in the same place by the same publisher.

Also in German: *On the Peace and Harmony of the Church.* <note>original: "Von den friede und eintrachtickeit der kirchen"</note>

A Panegyric <note>A public speech or text written in high praise of someone</note> in honor and glory of the Most Serene and Powerful Prince and Lord, Władysław Sigismund <note>Władysław IV Vasa</note>, King of Poland, Grand Duke of Lithuania, etc., as well as hereditary King of the Swedes, Goths, and Vandals; elected Grand Duke of Moscow; dedicated by a Polish Knight, in the year 1633.

*The Life of Faustus Socinus.* 1636, in <term>quarto</term> <note>A book size where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</term>.

The same work appears in the *Library of the Polish Brethren*, prefixed to the works of Faustus Socinus: in <term>folio</term> <note>A large book format made by folding a sheet of paper once</note>, 1668.

The same in Dutch <note>original: "Belgicè"</note>. In <term>quarto</term> without a year, and in 1663 (<term>quarto</term>) and 1664 (<term>octavo</term>).

*Dissertation on the Supreme Good of Christians*, which the author wished to be placed before the works of Faustus Socinus. 1636. In <term>quarto</term>. It is usually attached to the aforementioned *Life of Faustus Socinus*, with the author's name suppressed, but with the following address to the reader added:

> „ *The author conceals his name: you labor to know it:*
> „ *We have published the name: and yet we have not published it!*
> „ *The name of the author rearranged into an anagram:* **YOU ARE WISE MORE PURELY WITH ZEAL.** <note>The Latin anagram "SAPIS CUM ZELO PURIUS" is formed from the letters of "SAMUEL PRZIPCOVIUS"</note>
> „ *Is wisdom pure without a burning zeal?*
> „ *With zeal, O Wise Man, you therefore are wise more purely.*

The same *Dissertation* is prefixed to the works of Faustus Socinus in the *Library of the Polish Brethren*.

**JONAS SZLICHTYNG** <note>original: "Jonas Slichtingius"</note> of Bukowiec, a Polish Knight. Pastor at Raków, afterwards at Lusławice. **On the Holy Trinity**, on the moral precepts of the New and Old Testaments: likewise on the sacred rites of the Eucharist and Baptism. A disputation against Balthasar Meisner. Published in 1637, in octavo. There are also cited his

**Notes against Hugo Grotius's *judgment* regarding ecclesiastical power.** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist whose work *De imperio summarum potestatum circa sacra* discussed the state's authority over church matters.</note> Manuscript.

**Oration to George Rákóczi, Prince of Transylvania.** <note>George II Rákóczi (1621–1660); Transylvania was a rare haven of religious tolerance where Unitarianism was legally recognized.</note> Manuscript.

**All passages of the Old Testament cited by the Trinitarians for the defense of that dogma, explained by the "orthodox" (as they wish to be known) in the same manner as the Unitarians, commonly called Socinians, explain them.** Likewise, all passages of the New Testament, collected in the same manner: both written by the hands of Szlichtyng, Morszkowski, Stegmann, and others. Manuscript.

**On the true catholic faith by an anonymous author, and a refutation of the same, for and against.** Manuscript.

**On the true honor of the Blessed Virgin.** Manuscript.

**On the fundamental articles [of faith].**

All of these were previously unpublished. They are arranged in this order:

In the first volume, to which is prefixed:

*A copy of a letter by Stanisław Lubieniecki of Lubienietz, in which he composed for a certain great man a brief history of the Commentaries, and of the life and death of Jonas Szlichtyng, of pious memory. Written 14/24 June 1665.* <note>The double date refers to the Julian and Gregorian calendars.</note>

### OF THE ANTI-TRINITARIANS. ###

I happened to see the original manuscript of these works in the year 1681, just past, in the Netherlands <note>original: "Batavia"</note> at the house of Antonius à Hoek, into whose hands they came after the author's death; he also translated them into the Dutch language.

He translated Johann Crell's book *On the One God the Father* into German in the year 1645, in quarto.

In the <term>Library of the Polish Brethren Unitarians</term> <note>The *Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum* (1665–1669) was a massive multi-volume collection that preserved the theological writings of the Polish Socinians after they were exiled from Poland.</note>, his exegetical, didactic, and polemical works, along with several commentaries by Andrzej Wiszowaty, are arranged in this order:

Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, with Introductions and Appendices.

——— on the Gospel of Mark.

——— on the Gospel of Luke.

**ANDREW WISZOWATY** of Szumki <note>Andrzej Wiszowaty (1608–1678) was one of the most significant Unitarian theologians of the 17th century and the grandson of Faustus Socinus.</note>, a Polish Knight, grandson of Faustus Socinus through his daughter, and son-in-law of Joachim Rupnovius. Pastor of Unitarian churches, first in Ukraine and Volhynia, then later in Lublin, from there in Raków [at Radostów], and finally in Rożnów in the Palatinate of Kraków. Manuscript. <note>Johann Heinrich Bisterfeld was a German Reformed theologian who engaged in fierce debates with the Socinians.</note>

**A Response to the thirty reasons of the Jesuit Mikołaj Cichowski**, by which he attempted to frighten men away from the religion of the Arians (as they are called). <note>The term "Arian" was often used as a slur by opponents to link modern Unitarians to the 4th-century heresy of Arius.</note> Likewise written by order of the Synod. Manuscript.

All these works, as well as other short treatises elaborated by him up to this point, were [lost/dispersed] during the persecution of the Unitarian churches which occurred in the year 1655...

*The Second Scourge of the Peace-Maker, defeated and bound a second time, indeed falling silent; or, a new and memorable example of the most unfortunate battle of Master Johannes Amos Comenius against the Author of the 'Peace-Maker of Peace-Makers'.* <note>original: "Irenico-mastix posterior..." The title uses the word "mastix" (scourge/lash) to describe a rebuttal. Comenius, the famous Moravian educator, was a major opponent of Zwicker's rationalist approach to religious unity.</note> March 19, 1662. Octavo.

*The special part of the same, or the Final Refutation of Comenius, Hoornbeck, and others.* <note>Johannes Hoornbeck was a leading Dutch Reformed theologian known for his defense of orthodoxy against various "sects."</note> Around September 15, 1662; though the year 1667 is placed on the title page. In octavo.

*Compel them to enter, or concerning the contradiction shown to the Churches, and intended to reform them.* <note>original: "Compelle intrare." This phrase is taken from the Parable of the Great Banquet in Luke 14:23. While often used to justify forced conversion, Zwicker uses it here in the context of intellectual or spiritual persuasion to reform the church.</note> End of March 1666. Quarto.

*Against Joachim Stegmann the younger, concerning the Magistrate, War, etc.* After this "saw of contention" <note>An idiom for a repetitive, back-and-forth argument.</note> was several times renewed through manuscripts, Zwicker finally published such a book against Stegmann’s thirteen *Collections*.

*The Ancient Church Unarmed, after so many later centuries, finally asserted again by right; or the final Response of the Anonymous Annotator to the thirteen collections of the likewise Anonymous Collector, concerning the Magistrate, coercive power, capital punishments, and lawful Christian wars.* <note>original: "Ecclesia antiqua inermis..." This work argues for a pacifist view of the early church, opposing the state's use of force in religious matters.</note> October 27, 1666. Quarto.

The same in Dutch, **The Defenseless Ancient Church.** <note>original: "De weerloose oude Kercke."</note> March 16, 1668. Quarto.

**A candid demonstration that the 14th chapter of Corinthians has been very poorly explained by the "Free-speakers" until now.** <note>original: "Openhertige vertooning..." The "Free-speakers" (Vryspreekers) were a faction within the Dutch Collegiant movement who believed any member should be allowed to speak and prophesy during worship.</note> That is, *A demonstration that 1 Corinthians chapter 14 has been perversely explained up to this day by the champions of the freedom of speaking.* July 19, 1668; and in 1680, published at Amsterdam by David Ruarus. Quarto.

**Freedom of Church assemblies, powerfully proven from Scripture and the wonderful examples of Divine governance in these last 300 years.** <note>original: "Vryheyd van Kercklijcke vergaderingen..."</note> That is, *The liberty of ecclesiastical congregations, firmly demonstrated from Holy Scripture and the marvelous examples of Divine providence in these last 300 years.* September 11, 1668. Quarto.

**The Vanishing Non-Apostolic "Free-speaker."** <note>original: "De verdwijnende on-Apostolische Vryspreecker."</note> That is, *The vanishing Non-Apostolic champion of the freedom of speaking in the church.* July 28, 1666.

**The New Testament Josiah.** <note>original: "De Nieuwe Testamentische Josias." King Josiah was a biblical reformer; Zwicker uses the name to call for a modern restoration of "pure" Christianity.</note> March 28, 1670. Quarto.

**JOHN BIDDLE**, Englishman, Master of Arts from Oxford University. He was almost of the same opinion as Socinus, except that he believed the Holy Spirit was a person, and as it were, a certain prince of the Angels. <note>Biddle is often called the "Father of English Unitarianism." His specific view on the Holy Spirit—that the Spirit was a created, finite, yet holy person—differed from the standard Socinian view that the Spirit was merely the power of God.</note> His followers, called Biddellians, even now have their assemblies in Great Britain. He died in prison, into which he was thrown for his religion when Cromwell was in power. <note>Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658), Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland.</note>

*Two Catechisms:* the first of which can simply be called, *A Scriptural Catechism*; the latter, *A Brief Scriptural Catechism for Children*. In which the principal chapters of the Christian Religion, proposed by way of questions, are explained by suitable answers drawn from the very words of Holy Scripture, excluding [theological] consequences and commentaries. For the sake of those who prefer to be called "mere Christians" rather than men of this or that sect: since all sects of Christians, by whatever name they are distinguished from each other, have turned aside more or less from the simplicity and truth of the Holy Scriptures. Composed in English; but afterwards, so that they might also be read and understood by foreigners, translated into the Latin language by Nathanaël Stuckey, in the year of Christ 1664, in the 15th year of his age. <note>Stuckey was a precocious protégé of Biddle who died young shortly after this translation was published.</note> 8vo. *On page 153 the second Catechism begins, under such a title:*

*A Brief Scriptural Catechism for Children:* in which, notwithstanding its brevity, all things necessary for Life and Godliness <note>A reference to 2 Peter 1:3.</note> [are contained]...

# BIBLIOGRAPHY

various matters are contained, composed in English and rendered into Latin by Nathaniel Stuckey <note>Stuckey was a precocious follower of John Biddle who died young of the plague.</note> in the year 1665. Attached to this is a *Short Oration on the passion and death of Christ*, by the aforementioned Nathaniel Stuckey. As well as a sample of the *Letters of Jeremias Felbinger to John Biddle*, written in the year 1654.

A writing in which he proposes his opinion on the Holy Spirit, which (as far as my memory serves) was published with Cloppenburg’s <note>Johannes Cloppenburg (1592–1652) was a Dutch theologian known for his polemics against the Socinians.</note> refutation, in quarto format.

**JAN PIETERSZOON BEELDHOUWER**, that is, *The Sculptor*, for he supported his life by this craft; a Dutchman. He lived in Enkhuizen in Holland <note>The original uses "Batavia," a Latin term for the Netherlands.</note>, from where he was forced to depart because he was suspected of Socinianism <note>A form of non-trinitarianism that emphasized human reason and denied the pre-existence of Christ.</note>. He moved to Amsterdam, where he died around the year 1665. He was a man most skilled in the Hebrew language.

**The Shield of Christians against all non-Christians.** Amsterdam 1660, octavo; and 1671, octavo. <note>original: *Schild der Christenon tegen alle onchristenen*; Latin: *Scutum Christianorum contra omnes à Christiana religione alienos*.</note>

**Dialogue on God, Religion, and Holy Scripture, between a Theologian and a Philosopher.** Amsterdam 1664, octavo; and 1671, octavo. Appended here is the **Answer to the question posed to me by several preachers and others, regarding how closely or distantly today's Jews agree or disagree with Christians.** <note>original: *Dialogus over Godt / Godts dienst / en H. Schriftuure...* and *Antwoort op de vraage...*</note> That is: *A Dialogue on God, Religion, and Sacred Scripture between a Theologian and a Philosopher.* At the end is added a *Response to the question which certain preachers and others proposed to him: namely, in what ways the Jews of today agree with Christians, or differ from them.*

**The Highest and Last Meditations on God and Divine Matters.** Amsterdam 1661, octavo. <note>original: *De hooghste en laatste bedenckingen / over Godt en Goddelijcke saacken*; Latin: *Summæ & ultimæ meditationes, de Deo & rebus divinis*.</note>

**Adam’s Response to Joost van den Vondel regarding Adam in Exile.** Amsterdam 1671, octavo. <note>original: *Adams antwoord teegen Joost van den Vondel / over Adam in ballingschap*. Joost van den Vondel was the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright of the era.</note> That is: *Adam's response to Joost van den Vondel's tragedy entitled "Adam Expelled."* In this treatise, he attacks the opinion on original sin <note>The doctrine that humanity inherits a state of sin from Adam's first transgression.</note>. He also wrote various other things.

**A brief inquiry between two parties disputing over the Holy Trinity, to which of them, finally, after long contests, victory should be granted:** published with the name suppressed, under this anagram, *Magnus Amicus honesti* <note>An anagram for "Joachimus Stegmannus".</note>. 1649. Octavo.

**Responses to objections concerning the eternal divinity of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit.** <note>original: *Responfiones ad objectiones de æterna divinitate Filii Dei, & Spiritus Sancti*</note> Manuscript in Polish.

**Twenty-three articles** taught and handed down by the Holy Apostle Paul to the early Roman Church, which are diametrically opposed to the modern, new Roman Church. Manuscript in Polish.

**On the equal right, by ancient law, of all Bishops with the Roman Bishop.** <note>This work argues against the primacy of the Pope, asserting that the Bishop of Rome historically held the same legal standing as other bishops.</note> Manuscript.

**Sacred Sermons.** Manuscript in Polish.

**Letters to various illustrious and learned men**, as well as to **Anna Maria van Schurman**. <note>Anna Maria van Schurman (1607–1678) was a renowned Dutch scholar, poet, and theologian, famous for being one of the most learned women of her era.</note> Manuscript.

**Several other manuscripts.**

->**STEPHANUS PAULI**<-
A Hungarian, son-in-law of Adam Franck, and Pastor of the Saxon Unitarian church in Cluj. <note>original: *Claudiopolis*—the Latin name for Cluj-Napoca in modern-day Romania.</note> He died [if I am not mistaken] in 1672 at the age of 43.

**Treatise on the passages of Holy Scripture** that are disputed between Unitarians and Trinitarians. Manuscript.

**Latin Sermons.** Manuscript.

->**JACOBUS OSTENS**<-
A Dutchman, <note>original: *Belga*—while literally "Belgian," in this period it typically referred to a resident of the Low Countries or the Netherlands.</note> Pastor of the Mennonite Church in Rotterdam, specifically of the group known as the Waterlanders. <note>The Waterlanders were a more liberal branch of the Mennonites who were often among the first to engage in dialogue with other dissenting groups like the Remonstrants and Socinians.</note> He died there in the year 1679.

**Notes** (regarding the Confession of G. Aldendorp, A. van Heuven, J. Andriessen, and W. van Maurick, concerning the principal doctrines of the Christian religion) weakly and unsuccessfully defended by C. Gentman, a preacher at Utrecht, printed for his associates, 1665. In octavo format. <note>This is an English rendering of the Dutch title *De Aan-teickeningen...* and the Latin *Animadversiones...* which follow. It refers to a theological dispute between Mennonite pastors and a Reformed (Calvinist) minister named Cornelis Gentman.</note>

**The Sun of Peace.** <note>original: *Vreede-zon* in Dutch; *Pacificus Sol* in Latin.</note> And other works.

->**WILLEM DAVIDSZ REDOCH**<-
A Dutchman from Amsterdam, Minister of the Mennonites at Groningen. He died not far from the aforementioned city in the year 1680.

**The Vanity of the Weenigan Antidote.** <note>original: *Antidoti Weenigani Vanitas*</note> In Dutch. 1672, octavo. In this book, he defends the opinions of the Hamburg Mennonites regarding **Baptism by immersion**, the **Washing of feet** according to the command and example of Christ, and the **Lord's Supper** to be celebrated in the evening or at night, and that too with unleavened bread. He maintains these points against Sebastian van Weenigem, the Pastor of the Mennonite congregation in Rotterdam known as the "Flemish" group. <note>The Flemish Mennonites were generally more conservative than the Waterlanders mentioned on the previous page.</note>

->**CHRISTOPHER SANDIUS**,<- 
son of Christopher. Born in Königsberg on October 12, 1644. Died in Amsterdam on the last day of November, 1680, at 7:30 in the morning.

**The Core of Ecclesiastical History:** <note>original: *Nucleus Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ*</note> To which is prefixed a **Treatise on Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers.** Published in "Cosmopolis" [that is, Amsterdam] by Libertus Pacificus. 1668, octavo. <note>Authors of radical or controversial works often used the pseudonym "Cosmopolis" (City of the World) and fictitious printer names like "Libertus Pacificus" (The Peaceful Freeman) to avoid censorship or persecution.</note>

**The same Core of Ecclesiastical History, or the History of the Arians:** <note>Arianism is a Christological concept that asserts that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, created by God the Father, and is therefore distinct from and subordinate to the Father.</note> together with the mentioned **Treatise on Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers.** Second edition, enlarged and corrected by the Author. Published in "Cologne" [that is, Amsterdam] by Joannes Nicolai. 1676, quarto. It is preceded by a Preface to the Readers written by Christopher Philip Sandius, his father.

**A Century of Epigrams.** <note>A collection of 100 short, witty poems.</note> Amsterdam, 1669, octavo.

**Paradoxical Interpretations of the Four Gospels.** Amsterdam, 1670, octavo. *to which is attached:*
> A Dissertation **concerning the Word**, <term>περὶ τοῦ λόγου</term> <note>original: *De Verbo*. This refers to the "Logos" or "Word" mentioned in the Gospel of John.</note> *Also,*
> **An Appendix of Paradoxical Interpretations.**

**Treatise on the Origin of the Soul.** "Cosmopolis" [that is, Amsterdam] by Libertus Pacificus. 1671, octavo.

**Notes and Observations on Gerard Joannes Vossius’s Three Books on Latin Historians.** Amsterdam, published by Jansson-Waesberge. 1677, duodecimo.

**Confession of Faith of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, According to Scripture:** translated from Latin. Published at Leiden, by Jean le Francois. 1678, duodecimo. <note>original: *Confession de Foy, de Dieu le Pere, du Fils, & du Saint Esprit, Conformément à l' Ecriture*</note> That is, a **Confession of Faith concerning God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, according to Scripture:** translated from the Latin. The name of the author was not added.

...Baptista Cetis, Adam Gosławski, Samuel Golecki, Benedict Wiszowaty, Peter Statorius, John Völkel, Andrew and Stanisław Lubieniecki, Valentine Schmalz, Simon Pistorius, and Andrew Wojdowski. The aforementioned School <note>This refers to the Racovian Academy, founded around 1602, which became the international center of Socinian (Antitrinitarian) scholarship.</note> was established around the year 1600.

**Three Theological Problems.** 1. Whether those who are born again—or what is the same, true Christians—can abstain from sinning and fulfill the law or the precepts of Christ. 2. Whether Paul, in the 7th Chapter of Romans, from verse 7 to the end, speaks in his own person about himself as one already born again through the spirit of Christ; or whether he speaks of those who are still without steadfast grace and under the law of sin, describing the effects that the law of sin produces in them and the kind of people they are. 3. Whether under the Old Testament they had only physical promises, and none regarding eternal life. These questions were debated between a certain Evangelical minister, **Doxastes** <note>A Greek-derived pseudonym meaning "One who holds an opinion" or "The Praiser."</note>, and another seeker of divine truth, **Philalethes** <note>A Greek-derived pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth."</note>, in the manner of a dialogue. Manuscript.

**A Brief Account of the Martyrdom of Jan Tyszkiewicz**, who was overwhelmed by slander because he refused to swear upon a wooden image of the crucifix or by the Triune God; for this reason, he was removed by a cruel execution at Warsaw in the year 1611. Manuscript in Polish.

**A Solution to the Arguments concerning the Doctrine of the Trinity**, delivered in the year 1620 at Klausenburg <note>original: "Claudiopoli"</note> in Transylvania. Manuscript. The author of this treatise, Martin Z. Thaläus, says he prefers to intentionally hide the name rather than stain the paper with the mark of that name. This was stated in the dedicatory epistle of the book he wrote in opposition to the aforementioned arguments, under the title: *The Anatomy of Samosatenianism <note>Samosatenianism was a pejorative term used by orthodox Christians for Antitrinitarians, referencing the 3rd-century heretic Paul of Samosata.</note>, or a brief and modest censure of a certain response by N. N. of Transylvania, organized against almost all the arguments of the orthodox concerning the doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity; where at the same time the reasonings of other Samosatenians—namely Faustus Socinus, György Enyedi, Christoph Ostorodt, Valentine Schmalz, etc.—are examined.* Leiden, 1634. Octavo.

*A Short Discourse on the religious comparison <note>A "religious comparison" or colloquy was a formal meeting to discuss and settle theological differences.</note> arranged at Leipzig in the month of March, 1631, between the theologians of the Electorate of Saxony, the Electorate of Brandenburg, and the Princely House of Hesse.* Quarto. That is: A brief discourse concerning the assembly held at Leipzig in March 1631, for the sake of harmony in Religion...

# BY JAN STOIŃSKI
### Pastor of the Racovian Congregation,

*A chronology of the stages by which heavenly truth gradually reached its height in Poland: especially concerning God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

In the year of our Lord 1556, in January, Peter Gonesius <note>Piotr z Goniądza (c. 1525–1573), a pioneer of the Antitrinitarian movement in Poland</note> of Podlachia, at the Evangelical Synod held in Secemin (which was the second such meeting in Poland after the first at Pińczów under King Augustus on May 1, 1555), stated that he only approved of the Apostles’ Creed, but rejected the Nicene and Athanasian creeds and others "of the same flour" <note>idiomatic: of the same sort</note>; and he professed this openly. He denied that the Trinity was one God. He argued that the Son was less than the Father: that He was indeed God, but had always shown honor to the Father. He claimed that the Father was that "only true God" from whom Christ received all things. He argued that no "communication of properties" <term>communication of idioms (communicatio idiomatum): the theological doctrine of how human and divine attributes are shared in the person of Jesus</term> should be admitted. Gregory Pauli <note>Grzegorz Paweł z Brzezin, a radical reformer who later became a leader of the Polish Brethren</note>, then an Evangelical minister in Pełsznica, was also present at his examination, though he was still undoubtedly a Calvinist at that time. Although Gonesius attacked the consubstantiality <term>the orthodox belief that the Son is of the same "substance" or essence as the Father</term> of the Son with the Father, he is nevertheless said to have affirmed that the *Word* <note>original Greek: τὸν Λόγον (ton Logon)</note>—that is, *the invisible Word*—was turned into flesh in the Virgin: that is, God turned into man. Among other things, they say he remarked that Irenaeus <note>an early Church Father from the 2nd century</note> alone should be preferred over all modern writers. [In passing, Andreas Lubieniecius the Elder, a minister, relates that at the same Synod a report was made on the "union," as they call it, made with the Waldensians <note>a pre-Reformation Christian movement that emphasized poverty and simplicity</note> in Koźminek; however, he notes that after that union was formed, church discipline perished.] In a letter from that Synod to Philipp Melanchthon <note>the famous German Reformer and successor to Luther</note>, in which Gonesius is recommended, it is asserted that he believes the Word is less than the Father according to divinity: that the divine nature was converted into the human nature: and that God properly <note>or "literally"</note> died. But I would prefer to have this from Gonesius’s own mouth, or from his own writing,

# JAN STOIŃSKI
<header>Jan Stoiński</header>
<meta>catchword: amen</meta>

...lity <note>original: "lius", likely the end of "consubstantialitate" from the previous page</note>, to understand this. Yet what wonder is it that someone striving to emerge from deep filth and a labyrinth of darkness with great and difficult effort could scarcely—or not even scarcely—struggle out in those first beginnings of the reborn Gospel.

In the year 1558, George Blandrata, a Doctor of Medicine, came to Pińczów, a town of the Oleśnicki family. He was then said to hold the opinion of the Spaniard Servetus <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a physician and theologian executed in Geneva, whose writings against the Trinity deeply influenced the radical Reformation</note> regarding the preeminence of God the Father. There he found Gonesius of the same opinion, as well as Stancarus the Italian <note>Francesco Stancaro (1501–1574), a Hebrew scholar who caused controversy by arguing that Christ's role as Mediator applied only to his human nature</note>, who denied that Christ was Mediator according to his divine nature. While these men were debating, partly among themselves and partly with Lismanino of Corfu and Krovicius the Pole, a Synod was called in November for the purpose of settling these controversies. This Synod was attended by Jan Łaski <note>Johannes à Lasco (1499–1560), the influential reformer and Superintendent of Greater Poland</note>, Gregory Pauli, Stanislaus Sarnicki, and Felix Cruciger, besides many others and high-ranking nobles. Although these disputes were discussed for several days for and against, nothing was concluded; for those named above remained firm in their opinions. Meanwhile, Sarnicki and Lawrence Discordia, along with several dissatisfied nobles, departed, as they say. But the Lubieniecki Chronicle notes that this Synod was a major step toward demolishing the dogma of the Trinity.

In the year 1558, on December 15th, at a Synod in Brest in Lithuania, Gonesius—after publishing a book against infant baptism <term>paedobaptism (pædobaptismus): the practice of baptizing infants</term>, which was read publicly there—was met with attempts by almost everyone to refute him, except for Hieronim Piekarski, who defended Gonesius's opinion. Gonesius openly professed that he held other views which had crept into the church from the Papacy, such as the dogma of the Trinity, the Communication of Properties <term>communication of idioms (communicatio idiomatum): the doctrine concerning how divine and human attributes are shared in the person of Jesus</term>, the two natures in Christ, and many other things. [This was the ninth Synod.] And although he was forbidden from promoting such things under penalty of excommunication, he nevertheless affirmed that he could not go against his conscience. But this Synod was held only in the presence of the ministers of Podlachia and Lithuania. Furthermore, although in the tenth Synod of Poland, in the presence of Łaski and Sarnicki on April 25, 1559, it was concluded that there should be established an ex-

# EPITOME, etc.

...ment <note>original: "amen", likely the conclusion of a word like "certamen" (struggle) or "testamen" (testimony) from the previous page</note> of the Ministers regarding what they feel about God? What about the unity of the Trinity, and the persons in the Trinity? and so forth. Nevertheless, divine truth, despite this hindrance <note>original: "sufflamine", literally a brake or clog on a wheel</note>, finally shone forth by divine favor. For in the same year, 1559, on November 22, in the Synod of Pińczów <note>A central gathering place for the Reformed Church in Poland</note>, there was a long and extensive dispute with Stancaro regarding the Mediator, but nothing was accomplished. In that same place, letters were brought from Lord Remian [or Remigius] Chełmski (although he had not signed his name), in which he calls into doubt the invocation or the direction of prayers to the Holy Spirit. He argued that the unique rule of praying is that we ask all things from the Father through the Son, and thus we should likewise ask for the Holy Spirit. This was the twelfth Synod.

In the year 1561, on January 30, in the 19th Synod of Pińczów, Peter Statorius the Frenchman <note>Peter Statorius (Pierre Stator), a French scholar who became a key figure in the Polish Reformation and helped author the first Polish grammar</note> first indicated that Lord Chełmski was not well satisfied with the response given to his letters from the Pińczów Synod. Statorius was ordered to respond to him. He responded according to the instinct of the divine; but he did so in such a way that his own mind’s feeling on the matter did not appear. He only says that Blandrata <note>George Blandrata, the Italian physician and theologian mentioned on the previous page</note> had been marked by Calvin as if he were nurturing the poison of the impiety of Servetus <note>Michael Servetus, whose radical views on the Trinity led to his execution in Geneva</note>. Meanwhile, Statorius says that Blandrata's opinion, which he proposed in the Synod, was praised by everyone; nevertheless, Blandrata was asked whether he creates a plurality of Gods, since he says the Father is the one unbegotten, and believes the Son is begotten.

"But we all," (these are the words of the same Statorius the Frenchman), "*I know not by what means we come into suspicion of heresy, we who live with Blandrata. But if they are heretics who believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to the prescription of the Sacred Scriptures, I freely confess myself to be of their number. That ill-will regarding the Holy Spirit, which that evil Demon had stirred up against me, has not yet arrived [others read: has not yet subsided], but I rest in my good conscience.*" In this Synod, finally, Lutomirski <note>Stanisław Lutomirski, a prominent Polish reformer</note> was declared Superintendent of Lesser Poland, whereas previously he was considered only the leader of the Pińczów district.

In the Synod of Książ, number 17, in September of the year 1560, Blandrata begins to be called the "Elder of the Church of Lesser Poland." He is likewise so named in the 19th Synod of Pińczów on January 30, 1561 (in which mention is first made of Peter Statorius the Frenchman), and in the 20th Synod of Kraków on September 16, 1561. To this latter Synod, letters from Calvin were brought by Martin Czechowic <note>A Polish theologian and a future leader of the Polish Brethren</note>, in which Calvin urges the people of Kraków and Pińczów to guard themselves against Blandrata...

Jerome Ossoliński then burst out with these words: *I wish that writings on the Trinity had not been spread.* <note>original: "Utinam & scripta de Trinitate sparsa non essent."</note> By this he indicated that he wished those things which do not appear in the word of God had not been disseminated. Indeed, Lismanino, together with Blandrata, is reported to have said: *Let all the Doctors leave me one God, and let them not divide Him; let them have a Mediator such as they have fashioned for themselves.* <note>original: "Relinquant mihi omnes Doctores unum Deum, nec illum dividant: habeant Mediatorem qualem sibi confinxerunt."</note> The same Blandrata was ordered to commit his confession to writing. <note>NB: Note Well</note> It was objected against Lismanino that he had written letters to Lord Iwan Karninski regarding the pre-eminence of God the Father.

In the 21st Synod in the year 1562, in the month of March, Blandrata presented his recorded confession in Książ <note>A town in south-central Poland, a site of early Reformed synods</note>; but this was approved by some and utterly rejected by others, and it was only read privately. Finally, in the 22nd Synod, celebrated at Pińczów in April 1562, it was read publicly; and because it was conceived in the words of Scripture, it suffered the contradiction of only a few, and a reconciliation between him and Calvin was promised. Nevertheless, he [Blandrata] urged that Calvin should allow him to confess that Christ is the Son of the most high and great God, and to speak of that one God simply and without interpretation; or at least that he should acquiesce to the bare Word of God and the Apostles' Creed, and retract what he had prefixed to the *Acts of the Apostles* addressed to the Palatine of Vilnius <note>Referring to Mikołaj "the Black" Radziwiłł, a powerful Polish-Lithuanian noble and protector of the Reformation</note>. In the same Synod, it was concluded that ministers should abstain from philosophical ways of speaking—concerning the Trinity, the Essence, the Generation, and the manner of proceeding <note>These are technical scholastic terms used to describe the internal relationships of the Trinity</note>—but that everyone should keep themselves within the boundaries of the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Apostles' Creed. Hence it happened that Gregory Paul, a minister of Kraków, in the same year of 1562 after this Synod of Pińczów, accommodated himself to its decree, which prohibited making mention of the Trinity in a sermon. He preached publicly in such a way that the Holy Scriptures and the Apostles' Creed speak of one God; and according to the order in which the volume of the New Testament is arranged, he read and explained it to the congregation. This so displeased Sarnicki <note>Stanisław Sarnicki, a staunch defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy</note>, a most fierce champion of the Trinity, that he was not ashamed to demand of Gregory that he should not in the future occupy the listeners with the reading of the New Testament or the Evangelists, but should instead explain the Creed. # JOHANNES STOINIUS

5. He appointed **Gregory Paul of Brzeziny** <note>A leading figure in the Polish Reformation who moved toward Unitarianism</note> as the Minister of the Evangelical Church of Kraków. After the decree of the Synod of Pińczów in April 1562, he began to preach openly in the capital of Poland <note>Kraków</note>, setting aside the commonly accepted theological terms. Instead, he spoke of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit using the phrasing found in the **Holy Scriptures** and the **Apostolic Creed**. He also engaged in a spirited conflict with Sarnicki <note>Stanisław Sarnicki, a Calvinist opponent of the Unitarians</note>.

Our people <note>The Unitarians or Polish Brethren</note> in Lublin, Poland—a city where the Tribunal Courts are established annually—publicly conducted their religious affairs alongside the Evangelicals <note>The Reformed/Calvinist Church</note> for many years, until the year 1627. In that year, by a decree of the Tribunal, we were driven out and ejected following a great injustice arising from a specific incident. First, a riot of the common people broke out, who spent day and night demolishing the oratories <note>Houses of prayer</note> of the **Unitarian Christians** and the **Evangelicals** (or Reformed). Afterward, a most unjust judicial decree was issued against us. Even the General Sejm <note>The Polish Parliament</note> at Warsaw later recognized this injustice and passed a public law stating that Tribunal decrees must not establish new laws, but must be issued according to old laws that have been established and confirmed by custom. 

In this city, therefore, in the year 1616, while there was a gathering of our people and the Evangelicals for the sake of religion, and while the Tribunal sessions were being held under the presidency of Marshal Zborowski, the Castellan of Oświęcim, a significant event occurred. The **Church of the Holy Trinity**, located in the Lublin castle, was struck by lightning and burned down on the very Day of the Holy Trinity, just as the Dedication festival, Indulgence, and <gloss>Fair</gloss> <note>original: "Encœnia Odpust y Kiermasz"</note> were being held there. The entire city trembled and marveled at the fire. A massive crowd of townspeople and peasants of both sexes had flocked to that church for the sake of the remission of sins. The collapse of the temple killed two sacrificing priests <note>Latin: "sacrificulos," a term often used by reformers to disparage Roman Catholic priests</note> and several commoners. This event caused all the more wonder because, at that very time, our people had begun dialogues with the Evangelicals regarding a path toward Concord, union, and mutual tolerance; during these talks, the question of the **Trinity** was among the primary subjects of debate.

# GEORG SCHOMANN’S
## T E S T A M E N T
### Of his last will,

->Containing a brief history of his life, as well as of various ecclesiastical acts.<-

---

GEORG SCHOMANN, a Silesian from Ratibor <note>original: "Silefius Ratiborienfis." Ratibor is modern-day Racibórz, Poland, then part of the Duchy of Ratibor in Silesia.</note>, prays for grace and peace for his children, from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

Because we are mortal and the memory of past events is fleeting, and because tongues are poisonous at the instigation of Satan—for they are accustomed to blackening and tearing apart the Christian reputation of the most innocent men, so that by attacking men they might obscure the glory of God and Christ, and hinder the course of the Holy Gospel. Just as while we were still alive and publicly practicing our piety in Kraków <note>original: "Cracoviæ"</note>, two Roman Bishops did not hesitate to spread infamous printed pamphlets, as if we—forgetting God and shame—met in our assemblies to commit all kinds of outrages, and publicly celebrated marriages while naked <note>These were common "blood libel" style accusations leveled against radical reformers like the Polish Brethren to incite public anger.</note>. What do you think will happen when we are dead and no longer able to respond to such slanders? Therefore, it seemed necessary to me to leave for you a simple and unadorned short history <term>historiolam</term> of my life, written in my own hand: so that you may have at hand both an incentive to praise God and a very true defense to shut the mouths of foolish men. I pray to God the Father of our Lord <note>original: "D. N." for Domini Nostri</note> Jesus Christ—who was crucified, raised, and now reigns—that He might guide you by His Holy Spirit, that He might make you vessels of mercy for honor and not for disgrace, and that after this mortal life, He might give to us all life eternal and immortal, through the same...

# GEORG SCHOMANN’S

Jesus Christ our Lord, Savior, and defender. Amen.

In the year 1530 after the birth of Christ the Lord, I was born in Ratibor, Silesia <note>original: "Ratiboriæ," modern-day Racibórz, Poland</note>, to my father Stanislaus Lossel—whom the common people called Schoman—who came from a German village between Krosno and Rymanów. My mother was Ursula, daughter of the noble Christopher Tiachowski, Chancellor to the Duke of Ratibor. She was born under the *Starykoń* and *Topór* <note>original: "Starykon Ztoporem." These are Polish heraldic clans. The text provides the Latin translation: "Vetus equus cum ascia," meaning "Old horse with an axe."</note> coats of arms; however, she was robbed of her villages and all her worldly goods by her brother, the Canon Christopher. As a boy in my homeland, I drank in the rudiments of grammar and music along with the Popish religion <note>original: "religione Papistica." A common term used by Reformers to refer to Roman Catholicism.</note>.

In the year 1545, I saw extremely thick swarms of locusts.

In the year 1546, I came to Wrocław <note>original: "Vratislaviam"</note>, where I lived not among the city-dwelling Evangelicals <term>Evangelicos</term>, but among several canons on the Cathedral Island <note>original: "insulares Canonicos." Ostrów Tumski (Cathedral Island) in Wrocław remained a Catholic stronghold during the Reformation.</note>. There, I began to make some small progress in the arts. Eventually, from a stubborn Papist, I became some sort of Lutheran through the work of our teacher, the Lutheran Johann Cyrus. After this man went to Italy, he relapsed into the Papacy and attempted to drag me back into that same pit <note>original: "barathrum"</note>, even trying to thrust a Wrocław canonry <note>A "canonry" was a prestigious and profitable ecclesiastical office.</note> upon me. But, with God guarding me, I was so far from yielding to his flatteries that I even resigned my own canonry in Ratibor. As for Cyrus, after he had waited in vain to be appointed Bishop of Wrocław, he became a monk out of desperation, eventually becoming the Abbot of St. Vincent’s Monastery in Wrocław. As for me, while I was serving as a tutor to the Lords Joachim and Friedrich von Maltzan, and was expecting to be sent on a mission to France, the lands of the Lords Maltzan in Wartenberg were seized by King Ferdinand because of debts and an army was sent. Because of this, I was forced to return to my homeland.

In the year 1552, I came to Kraków, where I lived first at St. Mary’s school, then as a tutor for Hieronymus Becho, then in the "paupers’ hostel" <note>original: "bursa pauperum," a communal residence for poor students at the University of Kraków</note>, and finally at St. Anne’s school, making some progress in the liberal arts and philosophy.

In the year 1554, I went to the Wieliczka salt mines <note>original: "zuppas Velicenses"</note> to serve Lord Hieronymus Buzeński, the Salt Mine Administrator of Kraków <term>Zupparium</term>. He placed me in charge of teaching his nephews and other noble boys. I instructed them faithfully and diligently for six years, bringing back <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "referens."</note>

# TESTAMENT

...bringing from both the Lord and the parents of my pupils a gratitude that was not to be regretted; and I was not far from being submerged in the salt pit <note>The salt mines of Wieliczka, where Schomann had been working.</note>, and the allurements of the world and the abundance of such things, had not Divine mercy called me forth from that earthly salt to the heavenly salt.

In the year 1558, I led my pupils, some to Pińczów <note>original: "Pinczoviam"</note> and others to Wittenberg <note>original: "Vitembergam"</note>. There, the conversations of Petrus Statorius <note>Piotr Statorius-Stojeński (c. 1530–1591), a French-born reformer and author of the first Polish grammar.</note> and Philippus Melanchthon <note>A primary collaborator of Martin Luther and a key figure in the Protestant Reformation.</note> won me over, convincing me not to waste my life in the salt mines; for they judged that even then, we were lacking much in the way of true piety.

Therefore, having returned from Wittenberg, and driven by the luxury of the court, terrible dreams, the stings of conscience, and the word of God, I with difficulty obtained a release from Master Zupparius. In the year 1559, I went to that most godly man, Master Johannes à Lasco <note>Jan Łaski (1499–1560), the leading figure of the Polish Reformation.</note> in Dembiany, to make progress in Christian piety. There indeed I would have progressed much, had death not snatched that holy man from us—exhausted as he was by long labors—while I was present in Pińczów. There, I lived in close friendship with Petrus Statorius of Thonville (a Frenchman), Johannes Thenaudus of Bourges (a Frenchman), Master Franciscus Lismaninus <note>An Italian physician and reformer.</note>, Master Georgius Blandrata <note>Giorgio Biandrata (1515–1588), an Italian physician who became a leader of the Antitrinitarian movement in Poland and Transylvania.</note> the physician, and Bernardino Ochino <note>A famous Italian preacher and former head of the Capuchins who turned toward radical reform.</note>. It was there I clearly learned that the absolute equality of the persons of the Trinity was an error and not the Christian faith; rather, that there is one God the Father, one Son of God, and one Holy Spirit—though at that time we did not yet understand many things pertaining to this. Shortly before the death of Master à Lasco, we held a dispute with Franciscus Stancarus <note>Francesco Stancaro (1501–1574), a controversial Italian theologian who argued that Christ was mediator only in his human nature, not his divine nature.</note> regarding the humanity of the Mediator <term>Mediator</term> <note>The theological role of Jesus Christ as the bridge between God and humanity.</note> before God the Trinity.

In the year 1560, I was appointed Minister of the Church of Pińczów. But because the gift of continence <note>The ability to remain celibate.</note> was not granted to me, I married there a young woman of sixteen years named Anna, the daughter of a citizen’s widow, on the 18th of February. Doctor Blandrata presented to us the errors concerning the Trinity; when we gave these to Brother Gilovius to be judged, he confessed that he himself could not contradict them.

In the autumn of the year 1561, I was sent by the church and the Synod to the ministry of the church in Książ <note>original: "Xianz"</note>, in the domain of the Magnificent Lord Jan Boner of Balice, Castellan of Biecz and Great Procurator of Kraków, who had ordered...

# THE TESTAMENT OF GEORG SCHOMANN

...brought it about that I was expelled and stripped of all my goods because of my views on the Trinity.

In the year 1562, on January 15th at dawn, my firstborn son Paul was born to me; he was baptized as an infant, as we were still ignorant at that time concerning true baptism <note>Schomann refers to "believer's baptism" or adult baptism, a key tenet of the Anabaptist and later Socinian movements which he would eventually join.</note>.

In the year 1563, I was sent by the Church along with those noble and excellent heroes, Lord Jerome Philipowski and Lord Stanislaus Lasocki, to the Diet of Piotrków <note>original: "Comitia Petricoviensia." The Sejm or parliamentary assembly of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.</note> to preach the Gospel of Our Lord Jesus Christ. There, I was soon defamed by Sarnicius <note>Stanisław Sarnicki (1532–1597), a prominent Calvinist who became a bitter opponent of the Antitrinitarians.</note> and other senior brothers as being an adherent of Arianism <note>A fourth-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ; in the 16th century, this label was used as a slur against any who questioned the Trinity.</note>—a matter which I had not even thought of yet. At that place, they openly made a schism from us without any just cause. There, Lord Lasocki also died, whose body we buried at Pełsznica <note>original: "Pelesniciæ."</note>.

In the year 1564, on January 22nd at sunrise, a daughter was born in Książ <note>original: "Xianz."</note>; she was not baptized as an infant, for I had already learned and was teaching that infant baptism <term>paedobaptism; from the Greek 'pais' (child) and 'baptismos'</term> was a human command, not a divine one. In the same year, I was ordered to go with Lord Philipowski to the Diet of Warsaw. There, when Sarnicius openly called us heretics and blasphemers against the Trinity, a colloquy <note>A formal theological discussion or debate.</note> was organized through the efforts of the Magnificent Lord Nicholas Radziwiłł <note>Mikołaj "the Black" Radziwiłł (1515–1565), the Palatine of Vilnius and one of the most powerful nobles in Lithuania and a great patron of the Reformation.</note>, Palatine of Vilnius. But Sarnicius and his faction, professing a Triune God <note>original: "Deum Trinum."</note>, while we professed One God the Father <note>original: "Deum unum Patrem."</note>, we parted ways.

In the year 1565, I was again ordered to go with Lord Philipowski to the Diet of Piotrków, where a formal disputation was then established between us and the opposing party, lasting for fourteen days. But since they stubbornly defended a Triune God while we confessed One God the Father, we departed.

In the year 1566, we were again ordered to go to the Diet of Lublin with Lord Philipowski and Lord Stanislaus Cikowski. There, the opposing party grew so strong that we were forced to withdraw from the city. Nevertheless, through the intermediary Lord Nicholas Sienicki <note>Mikołaj Sienicki (c. 1520–1581), a famous orator and leader of the Polish nobility known as the "Polish Demosthenes."</note>, we experienced the King's mercy, which was promised to us until his death. From that time on, we abstained from the Diets, and our adversaries had become so powerful that, by their instigation among our patrons, we were forced to give up our positions. Around that same time—

# TESTAMENT.

<meta>catchword: concerning</meta>

...time, from the writings <note>original: "rhapsodiis." Literally "rhapsodies," referring to the collected miscellaneous notes and manuscripts of Lelio Sozzini.</note> of Lord Lelio Sozzini, certain brothers learned that the Son of God is not the second person of the Trinity, consubstantial and coequal with the Father; but rather the man Jesus Christ, conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified, and raised from the dead. Having been urged by these brothers to examine the Holy Scriptures, we were finally persuaded.

**In the year 1567**, I moved from our home in Pińczów to Chmielnik, to the estate of Lord Jan Oleśnicki.

**In the year 1569**, on the 20th of August after sunset, Martha was born in Chmielnik. Around that time, we had traveled with Lord Jerome Philipowski, Lord Simon the Apothecary <note>Szymon Pistorius (d. 1591), a pharmacist and influential leader among the Polish Brethren.</note>, and several others into Moravia, to compare our doctrine and moral discipline with the Moravian brothers <note>The Hutterites or Moravian Brethren, known for their communal living and strict discipline.</note>. There, we found the governance of the people of God to be excellent; however, all their sects defended a Triune God most stubbornly <note>original: "mordicus," meaning "with their teeth" or tenaciously.</note>. Likewise, many brothers from Lithuania and Poland, both nobles and ministers, had gathered at Raków for a comparison of the Scriptures. This Synod lasted for several years and ended in the most serious disagreements, which revealed men calling one another Pharisees, others Sadducees, others Jews, and others—it is painful to say—Atheists. It reached such a point that almost all of us, except for Marcin Czechowic, resigned from the ministry of the word; this was followed by the near-ruin of all our affairs. But God, having mercy on us, restored our collapsed affairs through that most excellent man, Lord Simon the Apothecary, as if through a new Ezra; in the midst of those tumults, he established the Ministry along with the baptism of adults <term>believer's baptism; the practice of baptizing only those old enough to profess faith, a hallmark of the Radical Reformation</term>.

**In the year 1572**, on the last day of August, at the age of 42, I was baptized in Chmielnik in the name of Christ.

**In the year 1573**, I was sent to Kraków to the ministry of the Minor Church <note>original: "ecclesiæ minoris." The Ecclesia Minor, or Minor Reformed Church of Poland, was the official name of the Antitrinitarian body often called the Polish Brethren.</note>. While we were traveling there, my wife was baptized in the Konarian garden.

**In the year 1574**, on the first of August, my wife's mother was baptized in Chmielnik.

**In the year 1574**, on the last day of August at first light, Peter was born in Chmielnik; he later became a Doctor of Medicine.

**In the year 1577**, I held a Colloquy <note>A formal theological discussion or debate.</note> with Lord Fausto Sozzini.

<summary>Georg Schomann describes his transition to Antitrinitarian theology influenced by Lelio Sozzini and his eventual adult baptism in 1572. He recounts the chaotic Synods of Raków and the subsequent restoration of the "Minor Church" ministry before his move to Kraków.</summary>

# OF GEORG SCHOMANN

<meta>catchword: H</meta>

...we held concerning Baptism: he approved of it in us, but said it was less necessary for himself, because he had not learned his religion from us.

**In the year 1585**, our Master Johannes Volkelius <note>Jan Völkel (died 1618), a leading theologian of the Polish Brethren and author of "On True Religion."</note> was sent by the Synod of Chmielnik to the school at Węgrów, and in Lithuania he was made a <term>Minister of the Word of God</term> <note>original: "V. D. Minister," abbreviation for "Verbi Dei Minister."</note>.

**In the year 1586**, I was sent from Kraków to the ministry of the Church at Lucławice <note>A village in southern Poland that became a major intellectual center for the Antitrinitarians; Faustus Socinus eventually lived and died there.</note>, at the beginning of January.

**In the year 1588**, I came from the foothills to Chmielnik by order of the Synod; there, a terrible hailstorm deprived us of all our produce.

**In the year 1589**, the terror of the Turkish war <note>Likely referring to the tensions leading up to the Polish–Ottoman War, as the southern borders were frequently raided by Tatar forces allied with the Ottomans.</note>.

**In the year 1590**, the most merciful God protected us from fire when a neighboring house was burning.

These, my dearest sons and daughters, sons-in-law, and little grandchildren, are the things I thought should be briefly and truly sketched out for you. From this you can judge both our religion and our poverty. Therefore I ask, warn, and implore you, through our Lord Jesus Christ, that you not only do not abandon this church in which I have lived my life, but that you even progress further in it than we have, as far as eternal life is dear to you. For if I had seen or heard of a purer church in my time, I certainly would have joined myself to it. But here, as you know, according to our Catechism <note>Schomann is referring to an early version of the Polish Brethren's confession of faith, which preceded the famous 1605 Racovian Catechism.</note> (which I first collected for you privately from the Holy Scriptures), I have worshipped God the Most High Father and the man Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord, in Spirit and in Truth. Having been washed by the baptism of repentance, I have labored in the Lord's vineyard with the pious brothers, according to the talent entrusted to me from heaven, through prayers, the preaching of the Word of God, and the practice of holy discipline. For although I was gifted with only a common and grammatical education, yet by Divine mercy and an understanding of the purer Word, I was a guide to the path of true piety for both myself and others. And although many tried to knock us away from our conviction, as much by open force as by foxy deceits, defections, and disagreements; nevertheless, with our God and Christ the Lord defending us, we have stood firm thus far, and we hope that by His help we shall persevere until the end of our lives, Amen.
