# TESTAMENT

<sig>N 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: field (original: "gellum", completing "agellum")</meta>

Indeed, I would wish you to be seriously warned of this: if, after we have died, God should deign to open a way to a more perfect state of the church through anyone at all (as we hope He will), you must not—whether snatched away by ambition, any desire of the flesh, envy, or hatred—retard the course of the Gospel. Rather, you should pray to God, as we used to do, that **all Israel may prophesy** <note>A reference to Numbers 11:29, expressing a wish for universal spiritual gifts.</note>, and that not only the **Lutherans**, but even the **Papists** <note>original: "Papistæ," a common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics.</note> might equal or surpass us in all piety. It is a matter of grief that the Papists envy the Lutherans, the Lutherans the **Calvinists**, and the Calvinists us, as if for the prize of victory. We, however, have made it our work to gather a church for the Lord out of all sects of Christians—indeed, even from the Gentiles and the Jews—and to far surpass in innocence of life those whom we have long preceded in the knowledge of the truth. Let us burn with the fire of charity and draw them with the **cords of love** <note>A reference to Hosea 11:4.</note>, so that, whether they wish it or not, seeing our good works, they may glorify our heavenly Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, His beloved Son; so that when our course is finished, we may attain the unfading crown of life. Amen.

As for what concerns our small means <note>original: "facultatulas," a diminutive suggesting very modest assets.</note>, I ask you through God and His Christ not to be vexed that we have led a poor life; for you shall have many things if you fear the Lord, as **Tobias** says to his son <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit 4:21: "And fear not, my son, that we are made poor: for thou hast much wealth, if thou fear God."</note>. For my part, ever since I spent some money collected from the **salt mines** <note>original: "Salinis," likely referring to the royal salt mines at Wieliczka or Bochnia, where Schomann may have worked as a clerk or collector.</note>—at **Pińczów**, where I served for a whole year at my own expense—I spent 30 gold pieces on a house after I was married and laid out 40 gold pieces on books. I was never able to acquire anything for you, because I shared our daily food liberally, not only with you but also with the poor. Nevertheless, I give thanks to my God that, through the generosity of the brothers, I have raised most of you to adulthood so that you have experienced neither hunger nor shameful nakedness. Finally, I have married off three daughters, giving ten **marks** <note>original: "marcis," a unit of currency or weight.</note> as a dowry for each; but our household furniture felt the weight of how much I spent in providing sufficient woolen and linen clothes, furs, bedding, and other such **paraphernalia** <note>In this legal context, "paraphernalia" refers to the personal property of a married woman that did not form part of her dowry.</note>. Indeed, unless my brothers and sisters had helped us, my own resources would not have sufficed for such great expenses. Now, since I have nothing more besides this home and a small field...

# ON THE PRINTING HOUSES
### Of the Unitarians in Poland and Lithuania.

Our community <note>original: "nostrates"; literally "our countrymen," referring here to the Polish Brethren or Unitarians</note> had two printing houses in Poland: one in Poland proper, and the other in the annexed territory of Lithuania. The first was moved from Krakow to Raków. The printer was Aleksy Rodecki, who lived in Krakow and practiced the art of printing while Stephen Báthory was still reigning in Poland. He printed many books, especially some by Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), the Italian theologian whose ideas shaped the Unitarian movement in Poland</note>, though he suppressed Socinus’s name <note>likely to avoid censorship or persecution</note>. Later, in his old age, he moved to Raków, where among other works he printed the New Testament translated into the Polish language by Marcin Czechowic in the year 1577. At that time, Raków was owned by Jan Sienieński, the Palatine <term>Palatine: a high-ranking regional governor, also known as a Voivode</term> of Podolia and father of Jakub Sienieński. Jan was originally a follower of the Reformed <note>Calvinist</note> rites. However, in the year 1600, he joined our church and greatly supported and improved our Christian community. In that same town of Raków, after a church and school were built in a more orderly fashion, the printing house was also expanded. This happened when Sebastian Sternacki married the only daughter of Aleksy Rodecki and received the printing types <term>types: the individual metal letters used in a printing press</term> as a dowry. That workshop remained active until the year 1638.

The Lithuanian printing house seems to be even older, having been first established by Maciej Kawieczyński. The Polish Bible in the version by Budny <note>Szymon Budny (1530–1593), a scholar famous for his critical translation of the Bible</note> was printed in Zaslavye, a Lithuanian town. The expenses were paid by the same Kawieczyński and his brother, at the shop of the printer Daniel of Łęczyca in the year 1572—nine years after the Reformed Bibles were published in Brest. This workshop was later moved to the town of Losk, which was owned by Kiszka, the Castellan <term>Castellan: a governor of a city or castle and its surrounding territory</term> of Vilnius, who shared our faith. Later, it moved to Vilnius, where the printer was a man named Karcan. After that, it was moved to Lubcz (a town situated by the river called the Chronon, otherwise known as the Niemen, which the same Kiszka then possessed) when Piotr Blastus Kmita married Karcan’s daughter and inherited the printing types. After him, his son Jan Kmita took over; and after him...

<summary>This page catalogs the primary printing houses used by the Unitarians in Poland and Lithuania, noting key printers like Aleksy Rodecki and the influential noble patrons who supported them.</summary>

<header>OF THE UNITARIANS, &c.</header>

Johannes Lang, a Lutheran <note>original: "Iohannes Langius Lutheranus"</note>. At that time, Lubecz <note>A town in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, modern-day Belarus</note> was already subject to Janusz Radziwiłł, the Duke and Palatine <term>Palatine: a high-ranking regional governor, also known as a Voivode</term> of Vilnius and the Supreme General of the army of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. He was a descendant of the niece—the daughter of the brother—of the previously mentioned Jan Kiszka. This printing house lasted longer than the one in Raków; for even after the Raków press was destroyed <note>in 1638</note>, the *Response to the Books of Meisner* <note>Balthasar Meisner was a Lutheran theologian who wrote polemics against the Unitarians</note> was completed there, and Jonas Schlichting’s lengthy preface was printed in the same place. However, this press also ceased its operations, partly due to a horrific plague and partly because of the invasion of the Muscovites <note>The Russian army during the Russo-Polish War, circa 1655</note> in the year 1655 or 1656.

Certain old booklets by our people <note>original: "nostratium"; refers to the Polish Brethren/Unitarians</note> are still to be seen; one was printed at Pinczów by Mikołaj Oleśnicki, and another at Lusławice, while Sigismund Augustus was still reigning as King of Poland. These include the *Explanation of Difficult Passages of Holy Scripture* by Grzegorz Paweł <note>Grzegorz Paweł of Brzeziny (c. 1525–1591), a radical Reformation leader and early advocate for Unitarianism in Poland</note>. He served as a minister of the Word of God in Krakow, and later became the first minister at Raków while it was still owned by the "Reformed" <note>Calvinist</note> Jan Sienieński. However, Sienieński’s wife was already a member of our church.

# A BRIEF ACCOUNT
### Of
### The Martyrdom of Jan Tyszkiewicz.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Jan Tyszkiewicz <note>original: Johannes Tyſcovicius</note> was a citizen of the town of Bielsk in Podlachia <note>original: Bielſca Podlachiæ; located in modern-day eastern Poland.</note>, and a man of no small wealth. His relatives, who were greedy for his possessions (which had recently increased through a family inheritance), laid a trap for him. Among these relatives was the town’s own Consul <note>term: Consul | The head of the municipal council, similar to a mayor.</note>. They forcibly appointed Jan to the office of Treasurer <note>term: Quæſtor | A public official responsible for managing finances or taxes.</note> without requiring him to take the usual oath of office.

However, after a year had passed, they demanded that he take an oath to confirm that he had served faithfully in his post. At first, he declined. But as they grew more insistent and began to spread suspicions of his dishonesty, he stated that he was willing to swear by Almighty God. Yet even this was not granted to him. Instead, he was pressured to swear either upon a wooden image of a crucifix or by the Triune God <note>The "Triune God" refers to the Holy Trinity. As a member of the Polish Brethren, Jan believed in the unity of God but rejected the doctrine of the Trinity.</note>. When he utterly refused to do this, he was overwhelmed by false accusations. It was claimed that he had thrown a crucifix to the ground and trampled it underfoot, and that he had uttered blasphemies against the Trinity, saying he would not swear by it because he did not know whether it was male or female.

These and similar lies were falsely attributed to him. Consequently, he was mistreated and beaten by the town’s magistrates, condemned, and cast into prison. Trusting in his own innocence, he appealed to the High Tribunal of the Kingdom <note>term: Tribunal Regni | The highest court of appeal in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.</note>, as the King was then away from the realm. This honorable Tribunal, having examined the case, declared Jan Tyszkiewicz innocent and fully acquitted him. Furthermore, they imposed a penalty and a fine upon the Bielsk magistrates for their unjust judgment.

In the meantime, however, his enemies persisted in their malice. They brought the case before Queen Constance, the wife of King Sigismund III, as the governorship <note>term: præfectura | The administration of a royal district, often called a 'starosty'.</note> of Bielsk had been granted to her. The Queen approved the original decree of the local magistrates and commanded that it be carried out. Later, even the judgment of the King himself and his judicial advisors <note>term: Aſſeſſores | High-ranking legal counselors who sat in the royal courts.</note> decreed that Jan Tyszkiewicz should be punished with death...

<summary>This page recounts the legal persecution of Jan Tyszkiewicz, a wealthy citizen of Bielsk, whose refusal to take a Trinitarian oath led to false charges of blasphemy and desecration. Despite being acquitted by the High Tribunal, his enemies successfully appealed to Queen Constance and King Sigismund III to secure a death sentence.</summary>
<keywords>Jan Tyszkiewicz, Bielsk Podlaski, Polish Brethren, Socinians, martyrdom, religious persecution, Crown Tribunal, Queen Constance of Austria, Sigismund III Vasa, Trinitarian oath</keywords>

# MARTYRDOM

...decreed. And so at Warsaw, where he had come to clear his name, he was captured and thrown into the deepest part of the prison. Shortly thereafter, a horrific death sentence was pronounced against him, formulated in these words: 

*“Since he blasphemed, his tongue is to be torn out; since he stubbornly defied the Magistrate to whom he was subject and the decree of Her Royal Majesty the Queen <note>This likely refers to Constance of Austria, the Queen of Poland at the time.</note>, by which he was sent back to that same Magistrate, and since he dared to appeal and flee to the judgments of the Royal Tribunal <note>term: Tribunalis Regni | The highest court of appeal in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.</note> as a stubborn rebel, he is to be beheaded; since he threw down and trampled upon an image of the crucifix, his hand is to be amputated and his foot cut off; finally, since he is a heretic, he is to be burned.”* 

Once these things were pronounced, both before and especially then, he was urged by the Jesuits and monks to change his religion, with them promising that they would change the death sentence passed upon him and restore his property. But these words were sung to deaf ears <note>original: ſurdo hæc canebantur; a Latin idiom meaning his ears were closed to their persuasion</note>: for the closer he saw the end of his life approaching, the more strongly he resisted them. Since they could entice him to their side neither by threats nor by promises, they led him to a pyre prepared for that purpose in the Warsaw market square. Having tortured him <note>original: excarnificatum; literally "stripped of flesh," referring to the various disfigurements ordered in the sentence</note> in the manner decreed, they deprived him of his life. This tragedy reached its final resolution <note>original: Cataſtrophen; a term from classical drama meaning the final turning point or conclusion</note> on the 16th of November, at nine o’clock in the morning, in the year 1611.

# A CONCISE NARRATIVE,

### *Concerning how the Unitarian Christians in Poland were separated from the Reformed Trinitarians.*

->By the Author:<-

## ANDREW WISZOWATY.

<note>original: "Andrea Wissowatio." Andrew Wiszowaty (1608–1678) was a prominent Polish Socinian theologian and the grandson of Fausto Sozzini.</note>

Since long ago, from the times of the early Apostolic church—that "uncorrupted virgin"—the clear instruction concerning God and His son Christ announced by the Apostles was held by simple Christians, such as the <term>Nazarenes</term> <note>Early Jewish Christians who followed the Law of Moses and held a "low" Christology</note> and some of the better sort of <term>Ebionites</term>. However, when certain philosophers, especially the <term>Platonists</term>, began to join Christianity, this doctrine began to be corrupted by the admission of foreign dogmas. At that time, as these newer opinions were gaining strength, some who held fast to the original doctrine resisted and struggled against them. Such a person, around the year 190 AD, was Theodotus of Byzantium; then Artemon, with several others adhering to him, around the year 200; Beryllus, the Bishop of Bostra, around 240; and Paul of Samosata, the Bishop of Antioch, around 260, along with his followers. Later, after the Council of Nicaea, there was Photinus, the Bishop of Sirmium, around 350, with those who followed the same opinion. Concerning these men, one may consult the writers of Ecclesiastical History, such as Eusebius, Ruffinus, Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen—though these authors, in their usual manner, represent them as heretics.

After that dark night of errors, which had been gradually introduced into religion, had lain upon the Christian world for several centuries, the day of divine truth began to shine forth again by the breath of divine grace, returning gradually as is its custom. The appearance of Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, and <term>Menno</term> <note>Menno Simons, the leader of the Anabaptist Mennonites</note> preceded like the dawn and the first light of day; the brighter rays of the returning sun followed after these in succession.

Around the year 1546, in the territory of Italy...

<summary>Andrew Wiszowaty provides a historical justification for Unitarianism, arguing that the "simple" Apostolic faith was corrupted by Greek philosophy and only restored during the Reformation.</summary>

# ANDREW WISZOWATY

In Venice and Vicenza <note>original: "Vincentiam"</note>, meetings and assemblies regarding the matter of religion were begun by nearly 40 associates who called the accepted opinion concerning the Triune God into question. When two of these, Julius Trevisanus and Franciscus Ruego, were captured and suffocated <note>The Venetian Inquisition often executed heretics by drowning or strangulation in private to avoid the public spectacle of the stake.</note> in Venice, the rest, fleeing Italy because of this crime, betook themselves partly to the empire of the Turks—where liberty for any religion is permitted—traveling to Thessalonica and Damascus; and partly into Switzerland.

The most prominent of these was Lælius Socinus of Siena <note>Lelio Sozzini (1525–1562), a humanist scholar and uncle to Fausto Sozzini, whose name became the basis for "Socinianism."</note>, who, having entered the study of human law as was the inheritance of his family, turned to the sacred books, believing that law ought to be drawn from the fountains of divine law. While studying, he noticed that the commonly accepted dogmas of the Church, especially that of the Holy Trinity <note>original: "SS. Trinitate"</note>, differed from the scriptures. He revived that opinion concerning Jesus Christ, the Son of God—that He did not exist before Mary, His mother—which had been hiding as if under ashes. In the year of Christ 1547, in the twenty-second year of his age, having left Italy, he lived in voluntary exile in Zurich <note>original: "Tiguri"</note>. He first visited Poland in the year of Christ 1551, and again in 1558, where he instilled certain ideas against the accepted errors in Francesco Lismanino <note>A former Franciscan friar who became a leader of the Reformation in Poland.</note>—who was the confessor to Bona Sforza <note>The Italian-born Queen of Poland and wife of Sigismund I.</note>, the wife of King Sigismund I of Poland—and in others. From there, he returned to Zurich by way of Moravia, where his associates Alciati, Paruta, Ochino <note>Bernardino Ochino, a famous Italian reformer.</note>, and others were then staying, and there he met his end in the year of Christ 1562.

Around the time when Lælius Socinus departed Italy, it is related that a certain Belgian named Spiritus <note>His identity is debated; some suggest he was the Dutchman Adam Pastor.</note> came into Poland. There, in Kraków, having taken the opportunity among certain friends from a book in which distinct prayers were directed to three distinct divine persons, he raised the question: "Do you have three Gods?" When he had criticized that error with many words, he cast a doubt into the minds of some, and among these, Andrew Frycz Modrzewski <note>Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski (1503–1572), a preeminent Polish Renaissance thinker and political writer.</note>. Since he was a secretary to King Sigismund Augustus, by the command of the same King—who was kind and curious about various matters—he investigated the controversies then stirred up regarding the divine <term>Trinity</term> <note>original: "Triadem"</note>, and wrote books on that subject titled *The Woods* <note>original: "Sylvarum"</note>. In the first book of *The Woods*, in the second treatise, he recorded this story concerning Spiritus the Belgian.

It highlights the influence of these ideas on the Polish royal court and the intellectual Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski.</summary>

Those in Poland who distrusted the accepted opinion on the Trinity were at that time called **Pinczovians**, named after the town of Pinczów. It was there, under the protection of the illustrious patron **Nicholas Oleśnicki**, that several notable figures resided: **Francesco Stancaro** of Mantua (famous for the controversy regarding Christ being a Mediator only according to his human nature <note>original: "Secundùm humanam tantùm naturam Mediatore." Stancaro argued that Christ could not be a mediator in his divine nature because that would imply he was inferior to the Father.</note>), **Francesco Lismanino**, **Pierre Stator** the Frenchman, and **Giorgio Biandrata**, an Italian physician who arrived after leaving Geneva. **Jan Łaski** <note>Also known as Johannes à Lasco, a major figure in the European Reformation who returned to his native Poland from England.</note>, having returned from England, also stayed there with several others. In that same place, a Polish version of the Bible was prepared by several Reformed scholars; it was later printed in the Lithuanian city of Brest <note>original: "Brestia"</note>, where he served as governor, through the care and at the expense of **Mikołaj Radziwiłł**, Duke of Olyka and Nesvizh and Palatine of Vilnius.

**Peter Genesius** <note>Piotr z Goniądza (Peter of Goniądz).</note>, a Pole from the region of Podlachia, having returned to his fatherland from his travels abroad, presented his views at the Synod of Secemin in 1556. He spoke on the pre-eminence of God the Father over the Son, drawing his opinions largely from the teachings of **Michael Servetus** and **Valentino Gentile**. Later, at Brest in 1558, he spoke on the baptism of adult converts <note>original: "Baptismo Catechumenorum"</note> in opposition to the practice of infant baptism, and despite many contradictions, he moved the hearts of several people.

In the year of Christ 1562, at the Synod of Pinczów held by the Reformed, an occasion arose from the controversy regarding the Holy Trinity—or rather, whether God is one in essence and three in persons. It was decreed that the preachers of the Divine Word should, in their holy sermons on divine matters, abstain from using terms introduced from elsewhere that were not found in the Holy Scriptures or the Apostles' Creed. **Gregory Paulus of Brzeziny**, who was serving as the Reformed minister in Kraków, followed this rule. However, he was denounced as an "Arian" and "Servetian" heretic by **Stanisław Sarnicki**, who envied Gregory’s administration of the church in the capital and burned with a bitter zeal that lacked true knowledge. Meanwhile, the patron of the Kraków Reformed church, **Jan Boner** (Castellan of Biecz and Great Proctor of Kraków), suddenly passed away. After his widow remarried, the meeting place for the congregation was moved to the house of **Stanisław Likowski**, who was then the High Chamberlain of Kraków and later became the Castellan of Biecz and a military leader in the Muscovite war. Later, under the leadership of Sarnicki and his associate **Lawrence Prasnysz**—who was named "Discord" both by surname and by his very nature <note>original: "cognomine & re Discordiæ." A pun on the Latin name 'Discordia' (Prasznicki), suggesting he lived up to his name by causing strife.</note>—whom Sarnicki [had previously, on account of his dishonorable life...

...[Sarnicki] arranged for a superintendent he approved of to be appointed for the churches of Greater Poland <note>original: "majoris Poloniæ"</note>. Gregory Paul, though neither summoned nor heard, was condemned for heresy and stripped of his holy ministry; nevertheless, he was retained by his patron Likowski <note>Jan Likowski</note> and other listeners. The same Sarnicki, plotting a schism, worked with certain patrons of the Reformed churches to ensure that other preachers who proclaimed the pre-eminence of God the Father over the Son were also removed from their office.

In the year of Christ 1565, at Piotrków <note>original: "Petricovia"</note>—a royal city in Greater Poland—during the time of the Sejm <note>original: "Comitiorum regni," the Polish parliament</note>, while many Reformers (including Senators of the realm) were present, Gregory Paul and his associates attempted to restore the unity of the Church, which had been damaged by Sarnicki and discord. These associates included Stanisław Lutomirski (Superintendent of the churches of Lesser Poland and Royal Secretary), his brother Jan (Castellan of Sieradz), Mikołaj Sienicki (Speaker of the House of Deputies), Jan Niemojewski (Judge of Inowrocław), and others. They delivered a speech on the matter in the assembly and requested a friendly dialogue. 

This dialogue did indeed take place for several days; however, Sarnicki insisted most strongly on the authority of those called the "Fathers of the Church." A promised response was not given to Gregory; instead, without the presence of the other party, it was concluded that discussions concerning these controversies should no longer be held with them. The more powerful side prevailed, and the opinion more pleasing to the common people won out. Thus, with the schism now breaking out openly, that church was split into parts: the **Major**, which professed the Trinity of the Most High God, and the **Minor**, which professed His Unity. The former considered it a sin to have communion with the latter. 

Furthermore, those more powerful men incited their common Catholic <note>original: "Pontificii," literally "those of the Pontiff"</note> adversaries and their bishops against these weaker ones, calling them "blasphemous Arians." <note>The term "Arian" was used as a slur to link the reformers to a 4th-century heresy, though the Polish Brethren had distinct views.</note> They even cast slanders of treason against the fatherland upon certain noble patrons who disagreed with them, such as Stanisław Lasocki (Chief Chamberlain of Łęczyca) and Hieronim Filipowski (Treasurer of the Kraków Palatinate).

...and as this was being urged, at Krakow on the very day of the Holy Trinity, at noon—while Gregory Paul was preaching against this very opinion of the Trinity—lightning struck the Church of the Trinity and knocked down the globe placed on its summit.

Meanwhile, John Sigismund <note>John II Sigismund Zápolya (1540–1571)</note>—son of John, the elected King of Hungary <note>original: "Iohannis Scepusii," referring to John Zápolya, Count of Szepes</note>, and nephew by his sister to Sigismund II Augustus, King of Poland—established a ten-day colloquy <note>a formal theological discussion</note> on the heads of religion, and especially on the Triune God, in his principality of Transylvania at Alba Julia <note>modern-day Alba Iulia, Romania; also known as Gyulafehérvár</note>. He approved the opinion of those who confess that the Most High God is one in person as He is in essence, namely the Father alone, and that His only Son was conceived of the Holy Spirit of God and born of the Virgin Mary. From this, they are called Unitarians <note>original: "Unitarii"</note> in that region, and they enjoy the freedom of their religion as established by that Prince. He also summoned the physician Giorgio Biandrata <note>Georgium Blandratam</note> to his court from Poland to Transylvania; Biandrata was loathed by Calvin and his followers for his views on the one God. These things took place around the year 1567.

Among those who, having rejected the common opinion on the Trinity of God, embraced the view of the Father's pre-eminence over the Son, some fell plainly into Arianism <note>original: "Arianismum," a belief that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God</note>. One such person was Stanisław Farnowski (or Farnesius), who created a schism from the other Unitarians around the year 1567. After his death, his followers departed, some to those other Unitarians and others to the Calvinists.

Faustus Socinus of Siena <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), the namesake of Socinianism</note> was the grandson of Alessandro (brother of Laelius <note>Laelius Socinus</note>) and born to Agnes, daughter of Petrucci, Prince of Siena. After the death of his uncle, from whom he had been imbued with a particular knowledge of divine matters, he spent twelve years in honorable service at the court of Francesco, Grand Duke of Tuscany. However, by his own choice, he left the favor of the Prince in which he flourished and, scorning both his present and hoped-for fortune, was driven by a zeal for his own and others' salvation to leave Italy for Switzerland in the year of Christ 1574. While staying there in Basel, he began his *Disputation on Jesus Christ the Savior*. But in the year 1578, he was summoned to Transylvania by Giorgio Biandrata, Chief Physician to Prince Christopher Báthory, to refute Francis David <note>Franciscum Davidis, a founder of the Unitarian Church in Transylvania</note>. David, having rejected the error concerning the Son of God being consubstantial <note>of the same substance</note> with God the Father, had fallen into another more...

# ANDREW WISZOWATY

...fell into a pernicious error <note>The previous page ended discussing those who leaned toward Arianism</note> regarding the refusal to religiously honor or pray to Christ. From there, Faustus <note>Fausto Sozzini, or Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), the Italian theologian whose ideas gave rise to "Socinianism"</note> moved to Poland in the year 1579. At the Synod of Raków in 1580, when he publicly requested to be joined to the churches that confess only the Father of Jesus Christ as the Most High God, he suffered a rejection. He was not admitted to the holy communion <note>original: "sacram synaxin"</note> because he did not hide his disagreement on certain dogmas—specifically concerning the satisfaction of Christ <note>the idea that Christ’s death was a legal payment for human sin</note>, justification without all works, predestination and "slave-will" <note>original: "servo arbitrio," the belief that human will is not free to choose good without divine grace</note>, and water baptism. Despite this, he fought strenuously through his writings to defend these churches against their antagonists. Among other works, he wrote a book against the Calvinist Andrew Volanus regarding the nature of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and also concerning the expiation of sins through Him. He dedicated this to Jan Kiszka of Ciechanowiec, then the General Governor of Samogitia <note>a region in modern-day Lithuania</note> and later the Castellan of Vilnius, who was a patron of nearly twenty Unitarian churches.

Andreas Dudith, formerly the Bishop of Pécs <note>original: "Quinque-ecclesiensis"</note> in Hungary, had been present at the Council of Trent. Having observed the schemes of the Popes and the Papal Church there, he left them and joined the Reformed <note>Calvinists</note>. But later, moved both by the weight of logic and by the bitterness of the Calvinists toward the Unitarians, he became a supporter of the latter. He saw that the Unitarians' peaceful embassy was treated with contempt by the Calvinists, as appears in some of his letters.

In the year 1580, when 150 Reformed preachers were gathered at Lubartów <note>original: "Levartoviae"</note>, a colloquy <note>a formal theological discussion</note> with them was expected by the Unitarians, as hope for one had been offered. But the Unitarians who arrived there, with Socinus present, were frustrated in their hope. The Reformed replied that it was a sin <note>original: "nefas"</note> for them to hold a discussion or any business with these men, claiming they were followers of Ebion, Arius, and Samosatenus <note>Early Christian figures whose views were declared heretical by the central Church</note>, who had long ago been excommunicated by the church.

Around the year 1600, Jakub Sienieński of Sienno, the son of the Palatine <note>a high-ranking regional governor</note> of Podolia and Lord of Raków, who was previously a Calvinist, recognized that the Unitarian opinion was more in agreement with the truth and embraced it. In that town, he established a School and a Printing Press for the use of these churches.

Afterward, another attempt was also made by the Unitarians with the Reformed...

### ANDREAS WISSOWATIUS

### APPENDIX

Containing a fuller history of "Spirit the Dutchman," who was mentioned above.

*Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski <note>original: "Andreas Fricius Modrevius" (1503–1572), a renowned Polish Renaissance scholar, diplomat, and social reformer often called "the father of Polish democracy."</note> in the first book of his Miscellanies <note>original: "Sylvarum" (meaning "Woods" or "Miscellanies"). This refers to his major theological work *Silvae*, in which he discussed the nature of the Trinity and church reform.</note>, treatise 2, chapter 2, reports the following:*

> "In the year of Christ 1546, unless my memory fails me, a man of the Dutch nation came to Krakow. He was, as it appeared, very well-versed in the Holy Bible and most ready in citing passages from it. While he was a guest in Krakow for a few days, he was received at a banquet by a certain man of great renown; I was also a guest there at that time. Before we began the banquet, we were led into the host’s library, which was filled with every kind of writing. As each of us (for there were not a few of us) turned to the books we preferred for our own study, Spirit (for that was the name of that Dutchman) <note>This "Spiritus" is a semi-legendary figure in the history of the Polish Reformation, often credited with planting the first seeds of anti-Trinitarian doubt among the Polish nobility.</note> happened upon a certain small book of Christian prayers. In it, he found prayers: one to God the Father, another to God the Son, and a third to God the Holy Spirit. 'Hah!' he said, addressing us, 'Do you good people have three Gods?' When we replied that we had *one* God, who holds three persons in the unity of essence, he said, 'But that which possesses and that which is possessed are different things. Therefore, He who possesses the three is different from those three who are possessed by Him.'
> 
> 'But you, Spirit,' we replied, 'are playing the sophist <note>a "sophist" is someone who uses clever but fallacious arguments to deceive.</note>. Our confession is simple: God is *one in essence, three in persons*.' 'Therefore,' he said, 'God is both three and one to you.' 'Certainly,' we said, 'but in one respect and then another.' Then he said, 'If, therefore, this "Three" is "One," why do you address them with different prayers? Why in these prayers do you seek from them different benefits to be bestowed upon the human race?' These things were then said back and forth between us. Since we believed the matter to be most certain, and were restrained by religion from sowing contention over it, we turned the conversation to other matters. But later, as I weighed the matter more carefully, I wondered in silence how it could be...

# COMPACT NARRATIVE

> “...as if, even though all external actions of the [divine] persons were considered undivided, we should address them with different prayers: praying to the Father separately, to the Son separately, and to the Holy Spirit separately; and then imploring the help of the Trinity in a single prayer. It is no different than if someone were to ask for something from Peter, Paul, Andrew, James, and Philip with distinct prayers, and then demand help from all the Apostles with one single prayer: for just as their persons are distinct, so too are their essences. In common prayer books, such distinct prayers to the three persons still exist. *These things and similar matters Frycz [wrote] in the place cited.* <note>original: "Fricius d. l." referring to Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski’s *Silvae*.</note>”

Budziński <note>Stanisław Budziński (c. 1530–1595) was an early historian of the Polish Reformation and served as a secretary to various Protestant nobles.</note> recorded the same story in writing in Chapter IV of his manuscript *History*. He reports that the aforementioned host was Jan Trzecieski <note>original: "Johannes Tricessius" (c. 1499–1567), a leading Polish humanist, poet, and friend of Erasmus.</note>, a disciple of Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536), the "Prince of the Humanists," whose calls for biblical reform deeply influenced the Polish elite.</note>, who was renowned for the nobility of his family as well as for his knowledge of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages. Furthermore, among the guests he lists—besides the aforementioned Frycz—were Bernard Wojewódka, a printer and official of Krakow, likewise a disciple of Erasmus; and Jakub Przyłuski <note>original: "Jacobus Prilusius" (c. 1512–1554), a jurist who authored important works on Polish law.</note>, a notary of the Krakow Castle and a most famous legal scholar.

Budziński adds that at the words of "Spirit the Dutchman," everyone indeed fell silent; they brought up other subjects and proceeded to the meal. Nevertheless, there were those present into whom that "hook" was driven deeply: noting what they had heard, they carried this question home with them, which in its own time would rise up across Poland. However, who that "Spirit the Dutchman" was, where he came from, and what happened to him or what he did after this, the mentioned authors do not record. I suspect that Adam Pastor <note>Adam Pastor (died c. 1560) was a Dutch radical reformer and former Mennonite elder who was one of the first in the region to publicly deny the Trinity.</note> might have been hiding under that name.

*Most excellent Sir, and Friend to be honored for many reasons!*

The love with which **ANDRZEJ WISZOWATY** <note>original: "Andreæ Wissowatii." Wiszowaty (1608–1678) was a prominent philosopher and theologian of the Polish Brethren, a group known for their early advocacy of religious tolerance and Unitarian views.</note>, whom we have recently lost, embraced you, always counting you among his first-rank friends, is too well known to need many proofs. You, in turn, gave no small evidence of your favorable disposition toward him while he was alive. That the heat of your devotion was not extinguished by his death is proven by your burning desire to remember the man with a grateful mind, wishing to know his deeds from his earliest infancy. 

You demand a work beyond my strength, if it were to be handled as is fitting. For the dignity of such a man requires those endowed with more mature age and judgment, who will not let his praises die, but will pass them down to late posterity. However, lest I completely frustrate the constant urging of you and those like you, the love to which I am bound to you has forced me to produce something; I judged it better to follow the famous deeds of the man briefly than to wrap them entirely in silence. 

Therefore, I shall cast onto paper, as if into a heap, those things I have drawn both from his own writings and from the records of other trustworthy people, as well as what I have learned from his family and friends, or seen myself. And so, sketching an idea of his life with a rough brush according to my small measure, I will supply the material so that those suited to such a task may form something worthy of so great a man from it. I do not doubt, most upright Sir (since you are aware of how meager my resources are, and that for someone distracted by other matters there is scarcely time for such things), that you will grant pardon to my rough style, and will care less for exquisite words than for the matter itself. Accept these things, therefore, for the present.

The homeland of this man (to begin from there in the usual manner) was that most noble region once known by the name of <term>Sarmatia</term> <note>A historical name for the lands of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, often used in a scholarly or poetic context.</note>, but now known as Poland. The town of **Filipów** <note>original: "Philipovia."</note> gave him his place of birth; it is located in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania on the borders of Prussia. It is certainly not without its own charms, yet it is not so famous that it should not be counted among its chief honors that it produced such a man: whose fame, as long as it lives—

# THE LIFE OF ANDRZEJ WISZOWATY

[...he] will live, and we hope the name of Filipów <note>original: "Philipoviæ"</note> will never perish. Before it could be called the birthplace of Andrzej Wiszowaty, it was numbered among its chief honors that it had as its Great Governor <term>Satrapam</term> the famous Krzysztof Morsztyn <note>original: "Christophorum Morstinius." A Polish nobleman and diplomat who supported the Reformation.</note>: a man renowned in his fatherland, and, because of his merits, enriched and decorated by the King with the governorship of this place; he was no less famous in the ecclesiastical republic than in the civil one. Even his adversaries testify to his integrity, and the churches he established bear witness to his zeal for promoting divine glory. Among these was the church of Filipów, which flourished greatly under the wings of his protection, enjoying a pastor (among others whom I respect in silence) the famous Jan Völkel <note>original: "Johanne illo Volkelio." A German-born theologian and a leading figure of the Polish Brethren.</note>, renowned for his writings. This, too, was a significant ornament of Filipów.

The nobility of his lineage matched the excellence of his homeland. He was born of a family of the equestrian order <note>The Polish *szlachta* or noble class.</note> (illustrious, as is well known, for many great immunities in this Kingdom), from the coat of arms known as "Roch" or "The Column" <note>original: "stemmatis Roch seu Columna."</note>. Its origin is traced back to that Imperial Column <note>The Colonna family of Italy.</note> who, as our Annals have recorded for memory, crossed over from Italy with his companions to the shores of Sarmatia <note>original: "Sarmaticas oras." A historical and poetic name for the Polish-Lithuanian territories.</note> many centuries ago (specifically around the year nine hundred) and stood as the author and parent of many illustrious families. The father of our Andrzej was Stanisław, the vice-governor of the aforementioned Filipów district; his grandfather was Abraham, the Lord <term>Toparcha</term> of Szumsko, who performed the duty of Chamberlain <term>Camerarii</term> of the Brańsk region. His other ancestors and kinsmen also held a prominent place among their countrymen in the Palatinate of Podlachia (a region which from ancient times was the nest and home of the Wiszowaty family). Nor were they less noble in the church than in their country: for Benedict, our subject's uncle, is numbered among the first founders and directors of the Racovian Academy <note>original: "Athenæi Racoviensis." The center of learning for the Polish Brethren, famous throughout Europe for its scholarship and printing press.</note>; while Stanisław, his father, fulfilled the office of Deacon of the church.

Through his mother, a no less distinguished nobility had come to him: she was Agnieszka Socyn <note>original: "Agnes Socina."</note>, the only offspring of the famous Faustus Socinus <note>original: "Fausti illius Socini." An Italian theologian whose ideas on religious tolerance and the nature of God led to the movement known as Socinianism.</note>: a man noble as much for the splendor of his birth and deep erudition as for the multitude of his adversaries and their deadly hatreds. Because his deeds were so greatly renowned (despite the vain resistance of envy), those of the incomparable Samuel...

By the care of Przypkowski <note>original: "Przypcovii cura." The former, Antonio, because of his vigorous service rendered to Ferdinand, King of Aragon and Naples, in Sicily, obtained the Duchy of Amalfi through Maria, the daughter of the said King, and transmitted it to his posterity. This lineage also reckons among its honors Camillo, Supreme Roman- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, referring to Camillo Borghese, who became Pope Paul V.</note>

# ANDREW WISZOWATY

...in this respect, nothing was lacking from his praise.

Having set forth his homeland and lineage, it will not be out of place to touch briefly upon the state of the church and religion in which he was born and educated, which he embraced, and of which he stood as a strenuous champion. This church was, as it were, his spiritual homeland and foster-mother, in which he was joined to many distinguished men—not by the bond of blood, but by the bond of the Spirit. For our Wiszowaty always held the dignity of these spiritual matters in greater esteem than those of worldly rank. Therefore, it is no cause for shame to indicate here at the very outset—for he himself was never ashamed of it—that he worshipped **GOD THE FATHER** according to that "Way" which, both then and now, is known by the name of heresy <note>This is a biblical allusion to Acts 24:14, where the Apostle Paul defends his faith by saying, "I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect [or heresy]."</note>. Understand this to be the religion which, in his homeland, is commonly (though unfairly) known by the name of the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arius, an early Christian priest who taught that Jesus was a created being, distinct from God the Father.</note> and *Anabaptists* or *New-Baptizers*. Although they themselves, acknowledging Christ the Lord as their only master, wished to be named simply *Christians*. For others in the same Kingdom, both Roman Catholics and Evangelicals <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to other Protestant groups like the Lutherans or Calvinists.</note>, prefer to be called *Chrześcijanie* <note>The Polish word for Christians; the author notes that it sounds like the word for "The Baptized."</note> (from *Chrzest*, which denotes *Baptism*).

Furthermore, in the Kingdoms of Hungary and Transylvania (where they enjoy established liberty granted by John Sigismund <note>John Sigismund Zápolya (1540–1571), the first Prince of Transylvania, who was the first monarch to embrace Unitarianism and issued the Edict of Torda, a landmark of religious tolerance.</note>, a Prince devoted to their sacred rites), they assumed the name of *Unitarians* to distinguish themselves from those who favor the name of the Trinity. This was because, following in the footsteps of Holy Scripture, the Apostles' Creed, and the primitive Church, and considering it wrong to establish any division or multitude in the Supreme Deity, they confess only **One** Supreme God (one in essence as well as in person), the Creator of heaven and earth, and Him alone as the **FATHER**. Moreover, they adore one unique Lord (in person as well as in essence or nature), **JESUS CHRIST**, the only-begotten Son of that Most High. For this reason, the names of Ebionites, Samosatenians, Arians, and Photinians <note>These were all early Christian groups whose views on the nature of God and Christ were later declared heretical; the names were often used as insults against the Unitarians to link them to ancient "errors."</note> were imposed upon them as a reproach. They also acquired the title of *Anabaptists* or *New-Baptizers* (who in the Polish language are *Nowochrzczeńcy*) because they did not initiate infants, as is the common custom, but adults capable of faith, into this sacred rite. They did this not by sprinkling or pouring water over them, but by baptizing—that is [submerging]—them according to the command of the Lord and the practice of the primitive church, to express the pattern of burial or...

# EPISTLE ON THE LIFE [OF WISZOWATY]

...by immersion <note>original: "mergendo"</note>. And these were the primary "crimes" on account of which they were always exposed to the hatred of everyone and to the persecutions flowing from that hatred. For as to the morals of the church and what pertains to its order and discipline, these were such (especially in its early days) that they were approved of even by their very adversaries. Because they held a firm hope that there would be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust, they applied themselves with the greatest care to always maintain a blameless conscience before God and men.

This religion fixed its seat and home especially among the noble nation of the **Sarmatians** <note>The Latin term *Sarmatae* refers to the Polish people, based on the historical belief that the Polish nobility descended from ancient Sarmatian warriors.</note>, a people distinguished for their liberty among other kingdoms; it provided a safe asylum and refuge for others who were fugitives for the sake of these same sacred rites.

Indeed, being no strangers to misfortune themselves, they knew how to help those in misery <note>An adaptation of a famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid*: "Non ignara mali, miseris succurrere disco" (Not unacquainted with woe, I learn to help the unfortunate).</note>. Following the example of others, they had embarked—though later, yet more thoroughly—upon a **reformation** of the Church, which was then obscured by errors like thick clouds. They drew the blade of the spiritual sword (not the carnal sword, as many have perversely done) against those in error. Because of this, bolts of excommunication (though at that time they were "brute" or harmless bolts) were hurled against them. Scarcely had they emerged from the pit of the **Papacy** <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note>, when behold, they were traduced as heretics in a similar manner by the followers of **Calvin** <note>John Calvin, the French reformer. In Poland, his followers formed the Reformed Church, which initially included the Brethren before the two groups split.</note>, their own associates in reforming the church. This was due to their open disagreement regarding the dogmas and rituals mentioned above, and they were subsequently excluded from brotherhood and communion. And so, with everyone repelling and avoiding them, they were forced to hold separate assemblies.

These assemblies, which were then quite weak, were made even weaker by both external and internal adversaries. On one side, the madness of the **Budnyists** <note>Followers of Szymon Budny, a radical reformer who argued that Jesus was a natural human and should not be worshiped or prayed to.</note> disturbed the church; they diminished the honor of Christ the Lord by refusing to offer him the worship of adoration and invocation, and by asserting that he was conceived from human seed. On the other side, the **Farnovians** <note>Followers of Stanisław Farnowski, who broke away from the main body of the Polish Brethren. They held a "semi-Arian" view, believing that Christ existed before the creation of the world, though he remained subordinate to God the Father.</note> split the church by establishing separate congregations. Although the main church did not bar them from communion but rather freely invited them to it, the Farnovians claimed to increase the honor of the Son of God by asserting that he possessed a dual nature from before the ages (in addition to his human nature) and by defending his existence prior to his mother. However, as many of the former group returned to a better way of thinking along with their **champion** <term>hyperaspista|A Greek-derived term meaning 'shield-bearer' or 'protector,' used here to describe the primary defender of a specific theological sect.</term>, they vanished into thin air. The latter, the **Luslavicians**... <note>Referring to the inhabitants or the church center at Lusławice, a village that became a major intellectual hub for the Polish Brethren.</note>

# [THE LIFE] OF ANDREW WISZOWATY
### P 2

...the leader of their assemblies, together with their patron, that most noble Stanisław Taszycki <note>A Polish nobleman who supported the Unitarian movement and served in the court of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note> (formerly a courtier of Emperor Charles V). As others joined them, they too—having been deprived of their leaders—for the most part returned to the same place. Even Martin Czechowic <note>original: Martinus Czechovicius (1532–1613), a prominent theologian of the Polish Brethren known for his pacifism and biblical scholarship.</note>, a man of no ordinary learning, who had fostered dogmas different from the rest and was attempting a schism, had died in the same year that Wiszowaty first saw the light of day. He died warning and imploring his followers to persevere, behaving quietly and modestly in the **Minor Church** <note>original: "minori ecclesia." This was the official name of the Polish Brethren (Unitarians) to distinguish them from the "Major Church" of the Trinitarian Calvinists.</note>, which was the name for the assembly of those who worshiped one God, in contrast to the Major Church of the Trinitarian Reformed religion.

And so this religion, having struggled with internal adversaries and having finally pacified its domestic affairs, was now breaking out from small sparks into a great flame. It spread in every direction and seized the Christian world with admiration, daring to oppose all others, prevailing not so much by its numbers as by its intellectual strength. That time was one most practiced in spiritual men and weapons—namely, the writings which had now permeated the entire world—and the Church had reached, as it were, a certain robust maturity. 

There shone in it then, like bright stars (whose splendor was not limited only to their native soil, but reached even to foreigners), those men distinguished for their piety and learning. As the historical memory has been passed down to us, we have learned that these men were: the three Lubienieckis—Andrzej, Stanisław, and Krzysztof (who, having cast off the splendor of the court, had magnanimously taken upon themselves the ministry of the divine word); and just as many of the Stoinis family—Krzysztof, Piotr, and Jan (born to Piotr Statorius the younger and the daughter of Grzegorz Paweł of Brzeziny); along with Smalcius, Licinius, Kalissius, Nieciecki, Twardochleb, Moscorovius, Goslavius, the Radeckis, and Krzysztof and Daniel Rudnicki. This Daniel had reached such exceptional erudition that he was even appointed a Professor of Scholastic Theology and the Greek language in Rome itself. <note>It is remarkable that a member of this radical "heretical" group achieved such high standing in the center of the Catholic world.</note> There were also Ostorod, the Wojdowskis, Völkel, Pistor, Piasecki, Crell, Przypkowski, Rupnowski, Schlichting, Ruarus, the Stegmanns, Gittich the Venetian, Praetorius Lehocki, Ryniewicz, and not a few others...

# [LETTER] ON THE LIFE
### P 228

...few: through whose care and diligence churches and schools flourished and grew, not only in several Royal cities of both nations <note>The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, consisting of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.</note>, but especially in the towns and estates of the magnates and nobles who enjoyed sublime liberty in this Kingdom and were devoted to these sacred matters. For this church—although it did not overflow with members as much as others—was never lacking or destitute of wise, powerful, and noble men.

In this truly golden age, Wiszowaty was brought into the light to be the hope of the church, having so many and such great predecessors (as we have seen) to imitate, whose illustrious deeds and triumphs could stimulate and lift him up. The church had also recently received no slight wound, having lost in the year 1604, on the third day of March, that **Faustus Socinus** <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), the Italian theologian whose ideas formed the basis of Socinianism/Unitarianism.</note>. He was followed in death by **John Statorius Stoinski** <note>Jan Stoiński (1561–1604), a prominent minister and Socinus's close associate.</note> (who was like his very voice and inseparable companion), that strenuous defender and propagator of the truth, for which he did not fear to provide testimony even in the midst of the Turkish lands <note>original: "in medio Turcismo"</note>, in the very Byzantine citadel <note>Constantinople/Istanbul.</note>. The birth of Wiszowaty compensated for this loss; he emerged for the benefit of the church as if from the ashes of his grandfather. In the decade following Socinus's death, his only daughter <note>Agnes Socina.</note>, having been given in marriage to **Stanislaus Wiszowaty** by her uncle **Christopher Morstinus** (who, holding her guardianship, acted as a parent to her), gave birth on the 26th of November in the year 1608 to a grandson worthy of such a grandfather and such ancestors. The name **ANDREW** was bestowed upon him after Andrew Morstinius, his mother’s uncle; he proved through his own deeds that he did not bear this name in size or spirit in vain.

We have proclaimed that the state of the church at the time of Wiszowaty’s birth was happy. However, we do not assert this in the sense that it was entirely immune from all adversity. On the contrary, it had reached such a bloom, as we have seen, through the cross and through sufferings. Nevertheless, the times pressing upon the youth were no less full of danger and persecutions, and a darker age would follow that golden one. The calamity and blood of many taught how great a task it was to build such a church. Striving for brevity and sticking to our purpose, we reserve these tragedies for a more suitable time and place. # [A BIOGRAPHY] OF A. WISZOWATY
### PAGE 229

<margin>P 3</margin>

...[the church] was [provided] with men endowed with a firm spirit and heart, who could both endure such things themselves and teach others to bear similar trials: not only by commanding but also by demonstrating how to tolerate labors. Therefore, the first care of his parents—who considered that evil days were pressing in—was to imbue our Andrew with integrity and truth, and at the same time with the liberal arts <note>The "good arts" or liberal arts were the traditional core of a gentleman's education, including grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</note> (which he could carry with him always and everywhere). They handled the former [integrity] mostly by themselves; for the latter, they advanced his progress with the help of others.

To facilitate this more conveniently, his father (among other reasons) sold his possessions in Podlachia <note>A historical region in eastern Poland/western Belarus.</note> and migrated to Lesser Poland, as it was a more cultured region. Having fixed his residence in the Palatinate of Krakow, the premier province of the Kingdom, he held the village of Jankówka, which he rented from Christopher Morstinius, his wife's maternal uncle. From here he sent his son to nearby Racoborsko, so that there he might apply himself to his studies along with the sons of the aforementioned Morstinius (for whom he maintained a tutor at home). 

Here, under the oversight of the excellent Morstinius—whom our Wiszowaty, recalling the man's memory with a grateful mind, was rightly accustomed to call a **Senator of the Church of God** <note>A title of respect for prominent lay leaders in the Polish Brethren movement.</note>—he progressed so much in those first rudiments of character and learning through industry and diligence, that he was judged by his teacher to be fit for promotion to a more illustrious school. He was sent, therefore, in the year 1619, mature not so much in age as in intellect, into the recently established **Racovian Gymnasium** <note>The famous academy of the Polish Brethren in Raków, known for its high academic standards and religious tolerance.</note>.

At that time, this school flourished, noble even to the point of provoking envy, like a **Sarmatian Athens** <note>"Sarmatian" refers to the Polish nobility's identity; "Athens" marks the school as a center of supreme wisdom and philosophy.</note>. It rejoiced in founders and school directors who were men most deserving of their country and church. Among these, **Jacob Sieniński** stood out, the son of the Palatine of Podolia, and the heir and lord of Raków, the town founded by his father. To these should be added the Rectors and Teachers, endowed with the highest wisdom and learning. Among them, not necessarily by seniority but by merit of dignity, that great **Johannes Crellius** <note>Johann Crell (1590–1633), a renowned German-born theologian and leading figure of the Socinian movement.</note> rightly claims the first place. When Wiszowaty entered this academy, Crellius was steering the helm with the highest praise, following those men of distinguished learning: Brokajus, Manlius, Nieciecius, and Paul Crokier. In this office he had as successors those renowned men, **Martin Ruar** and then **Joachim Stegmann**, whom (after Wiszowaty had already left this gymnasium) Adam [Francus succeeded...]

# EPISTLE ON THE LIFE [OF WISZOWATY]
### PAGE 230

...[through] Francus the Silesian <note>Likely Adam Franck, a noted educator of the era.</note>, a man second to none of his contemporaries in integrity and learning. We understand that he was followed in this office by Peter Teichmann, Georg Nigrinus, and finally Lawrence Stegmann (who, toward the end of his time there when the school was being suppressed, was touched by the influence of Tribander <note>Likely referring to a specific theological faction or individual involved in the internal disputes of the Polish Brethren.</note>), all of whom were men of outstanding spirit. Happy were the families of that time whose sons were born into those years, for they could be sent to Raców <note>Raków was the "Sarmatian Athens," the intellectual center of the Polish Brethren (Socinians) and home to a world-famous academy and printing press.</note> as if to a great market of the liberal arts. This was done not only by those called Arians and Anabaptists <note>Terms often used by outsiders to describe the Polish Brethren (Unitarians).</note> (who held the reins of that town’s school), but also by the leading men and nobles of the Evangelicals <note>Protestants, usually Reformed/Calvinist or Lutheran.</note> and even the Roman Catholics. As a result, usually three hundred young men of the nobility, in addition to the sons of the townspeople (who together often exceeded a thousand in number), were counted as diligent students in this academy.

In this school, our Wiszowaty made great progress in the humanities, and in a short time was promoted from the lower to the highest class by applying himself tirelessly to his studies. He was so diligent in these pursuits that for several years he did not even find the leisure to visit his father's house. However, an opportunity for his parents to see him arose when his father, a Deacon of the Church of Robków, traveled to the Synods which were celebrated annually at Raców. After some years spent in study, when his parents saw that in a short space of time he had made enough progress to live an honorable life among his fellow citizens, they considered recalling him from the school. According to the custom of the nation, they intended to hand him over to the service of some great nobleman, so that from there a path to greater honors might lie open to him. 

But through the care of several men who excelled in the school and the church—most especially the great man Martin Ruar <note>A prominent humanist and theologian of the Polish Brethren.</note>—these efforts of his parents were restrained. His friends persuaded them that a boy endowed with such great talent should be turned toward higher things. They hoped that the first-born son of the only daughter of the great Socinus <note>Wiszowaty’s mother, Agnieszka Socyn, was the daughter of Fausto Sozzini (Socinus), the famous Italian theologian whose ideas shaped the movement.</note> might, by devoting himself to theological studies, represent his grandfather to them in the course of time. Therefore, when the church offered its own resources to advance his studies, his parents gave their consent.

### A. WISZOWATY
### PAGE 231

...[at] Raków <note>Raków was the intellectual center of the Polish Brethren, known for its progressive Academy.</note> therefore, proceeding tirelessly in his purpose. His progress in these studies was aided in no small way by the fact that he enjoyed the hospitality and table—and thus the daily conversation—of the famous Johannes Crellius <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633) was a leading Socinian theologian and rector of the Raków Academy.</note>. Crellius, having laid down the office of Rector to serve as the minister of the Raków congregation, devoted his efforts to instructing several students in the faculty of Theology by interpreting the sacred scriptures. He was a man most eminent in both learning and piety; Wiszowaty always acknowledged with a grateful mind that he had gained no small increase in both character and doctrine from him.

Having departed from the Academy of Raków, at the request of the Most Illustrious Lord Alexander Peter Tarło, the Palatine of Lublin <term>Palatine: a high-ranking official or provincial governor in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</term>, Wiszowaty undertook the care of instructing his eldest son in the liberal arts in the year 1629 (while the younger sons were pursuing their studies at the school in Raków). In the court of this nobleman (who was a Roman Catholic by religion), although many allurements presented themselves, Wiszowaty did not allow himself to be moved even a step from the right path. He not only refused to be led away from the sacred truths he had embraced as true, but he also busied himself with propagating them and instilling them in others whenever the opportunity arose. Eventually, when he was urged by the aforementioned Lord to travel to foreign lands as his son’s <term>ephorus: a traveling tutor or guardian responsible for a young nobleman's education and conduct</term>, he was unwilling to be the guardian of a youth of a different religion so far from his paternal home. Waiting for a better opportunity to visit foreign lands, he expressed his thanks to the Palatine and recommended another man, who was a follower of the Roman Catholic religion, to undertake this duty. Thus, having seized this opportunity, he gladly disentangled himself from that court.

Shortly after this, in the year 1631, he found a more convenient opportunity for traveling to foreign parts. He was sent by the church and his parents, who were diligently intent on him making the best possible progress in the noble arts. On this journey, he gained several distinguished companions (some of whom joined the pilgrimage in their homeland, others abroad), such as: Martin Ruar <note>A prominent Socinian diplomat and scholar.</note>, Joachim Pastorius of Hirtenberg, Georg Niemirycz <note>Jerzy Niemirycz, a powerful politician and leader of the Polish Brethren.</note>, Alexander Czaplic, Nicholas Lubieniecki, and Peter Sucho- <note>original: "Petrum Sucho-". The name is likely Suchodolski, interrupted by the page break.</note>

### PAGE 232

...[to] Suchodolski <note>original: "Suchodolium"; likely Stanisław Suchodolski, a member of the Polish Brethren</note>, and other men dedicated to the same sacred rites. Setting sail from **Gdańsk** <note>original: "Gedano"</note> by sea, and sailing past various coasts, he landed in **Holland** <note>original: "Bataviam"</note>. There, he stayed primarily in **Leiden** <note>original: "Lugduni"</note>, devoting himself to his studies at the University of that place, which at that time boasted of most illustrious men. He also occasionally visited the newly established **Athenaeum of Amsterdam**, and its renowned professors, **Vossius** and **Barlaeus** <note>Gerard Vossius and Caspar Barlaeus were giants of 17th-century Dutch humanism and scholarship</note>, to whom he always had free access. He also encountered in Holland at that time **Krzysztof Arciszewski**, a Polish Knight, who was serving the **West India Company**. Arciszewski was being dispatched by its directors to **America** with a band of soldiers, both to protect **Brazil** and other places subject to their jurisdiction, and to acquire new ones. Since his youth, he had been dedicated to the sacred rites of those whom they call **Arians** <note>Arianism, in this context, refers to the Polish Brethren/Unitarians who denied the Trinity</note>; however, living among the Reformed, he had joined their communion. Yet he did so on this condition: that he be allowed to dissent from the common opinion regarding the dogma of the Trinity, and to retain his former view on the unity of God. He was accustomed to confessing tirelessly that the Arians or **Photinians** <note>Photinians: another historical label for those holding Unitarian views, named after the 4th-century bishop Photinus</note> (as they are commonly called) held a purer view of God than others. He did not fear to include this even in his letters to **King Władysław IV**, written when he returned to his fatherland.

As a sign of the old friendship he had cherished with our **Wiszowaty**, Arciszewski invited him to set sail with him and cross over to America, suggesting that there would be no lack of a "harvest" there for promoting divine glory. Nor would he have had difficulty in swaying Wiszowaty’s mind—which had long been inclined toward such things—had he not been pulled back from such a distant and danger-filled journey by both his parents (left far behind and unaware of this matter) and the church to whose care he had committed himself. He did not wish to innovate anything without consulting them. Therefore, having thanked Arciszewski for his favor, he reserved these plans for more mature consideration.

Continuing then in his purpose, he crossed over into **England**, where it was his good fortune to see and speak with several distinguished men of that kingdom. From there, he sailed across to **France**; having traveled through its various provinces and cities, he devoted himself to studies in **Paris** <note>original: "Lutetiæ Pariſiorum"</note>...

# A. WISZOWATY.
P 5

...stayed primarily for the sake of these [learned men]: attending the **Sorbonne** <note>The famous theological college of the University of Paris</note> and other colleges of professors and doctors. There, he had the opportunity to form acquaintances and friendships with the great **Hugo Grotius**, **Pierre Gassendi**, **Marin Mersenne**, and several other most illustrious men. On every occasion, however, he was not unmindful of propagating and instilling in others the religion he embraced as true; he did not hesitate to publicly propose and defend it in academies and centers of learning <note>original: "Athenæisque"</note>.

After a stay of several years in western lands, he returned to his homeland, not without the fruits of his labor, in the year 1637. At the request of the mother and friends of the young **Adam Suchodolski** (who was later the Governor <note>original: "Satrapæ," likely referring to the office of Starosta</note> of Horodło), he took up the care and management of the youth's character and studies—an arrangement that turned out successfully according to the wishes of both parties.

The following year, 1638, proved to be most disastrous for the **Unitarians**, and indeed for all men who hold fast to what is right and just. At that time, the very "eye of Poland," the asylum and refuge of exiles, and the sanctuary of religion and the muses, was torn out: the Church, the School, and the Printing Press of **Raków** <note>The intellectual heart of the Polish Brethren, known for the "Racovian Catechism"</note> were abolished. The occasion for this irreparable loss was provided by the insolence of certain students, who used stones to break a wooden image of the crucified Christ located outside the town. Because of this, their adversaries found the pretext for slandering and harming that they had long sought. Even after the youths had been sent away (having been punished by their parents for their petulance), the adversaries attacked the whole society of those they call **Arians** <note>A pejorative term for the Unitarians/Polish Brethren used by their opponents</note>. **Sieninski**, the Lord of Raków, was overwhelmed by slander and charged with the crime of treason against both Divine and Royal Majesty. Similarly, the school's professors and the church's pastors were accused of being the authors of the crime and the instigators who prompted the youth to carry it out. Nothing availed against this: not the demonstration of the accused’s innocence proven by strong reasons; nor the "holy purgation" <note>A formal legal oath to clear one's name</note> of Sieninski himself. He was a seventy-year-old man, a nobleman who had served his country most excellently at the cost of his own inheritance, and who had often been hailed as the "Father of the Fatherland" in the Diets <note>original: "Comitiis," the Sejm or legislative assemblies</note> of the Kingdom. This oath was extorted from him to testify that these acts were perpetrated without his knowledge. Nothing [availed] of the many...

...of the delegates of the **equestrian order** <note>The *szlachta*, or Polish nobility, who held significant political power</note>, which included those devoted not only to the **Arian** (as it is called) religion <note>A term used by outsiders for the Polish Brethren/Unitarians</note>, but also to the **Greek** <note>Orthodox</note>, **Evangelical** <note>Protestant, usually Reformed or Lutheran</note>, and even the **Roman Catholic** faiths, a protest was lodged against the extraordinary summary judgment and the process of this trial—a new and unheard-of example in a free Republic. These orders, carried out with unflagging zeal, soon led to a dismal outcome.

But our subject [Wiszowaty], undeterred by this disaster, traveled to **Warsaw** the following year [1639] with several others of noble birth as the celebration of the Diet was imminent. There, in the Chamber of Deputies of the equestrian order, as opportunities arose, he was deterred neither by shame nor fear from giving an account of the faith he professed, even near the side of the **King** and the **Senators**. He engaged in discussions regarding the articles of religion for which he and his fellows were most hated, debating with both Roman Catholics and Evangelicals. Similar opportunities for propagating the truth in the presence of illustrious men often came to him, and he never allowed them to pass by despite the dangers; but as we strive for brevity, there is no room to recount all these things.

In the year 1640, at the earnest request of the mother of the aforementioned **Suchodolski**, although she was a member of the **Reformed** church <note>original: "Reformatorum," referring here to the Calvinist nobility</note>, he again undertook the care of the youth (whom he had already thoroughly instructed in the liberal arts) as a tutor <note>original: "ephorus"</note>, primarily for the sake of visiting foreign lands. Having traveled, therefore, through **Germany**, **France**, and the **Netherlands** (in which regions he had already formed acquaintances with several distinguished men), he returned to his homeland after some years. He presented **Suchodolski** safely to his mother, and himself to the church. But indeed, shortly after their return, the plans made regarding **Wiszowaty** and the hopes conceived for **Suchodolski** came to nothing. # A. WISZOWATY

...ministry <note>original: *ministerium*</note> (though some of his relatives and companions resisted in vain) toward which he was inclined, so that he might better promote the divine glory; (yet he was neither premature nor hasty in such matters) to place him in charge of the church which was gathered in **Suchodolski’s** hereditary town of **Piaski** <note>A town in eastern Poland that served as a significant center for the Polish Brethren</note>. But **Suchodolski**, having been drawn toward the **Calvinist** <note>The Reformed or "Evangelical" church, which often competed with the Unitarians for the loyalty of the Polish nobility</note> rites through the efforts of his mother and kinsmen, ordered the aforementioned church to be closed. When **Christopher Lubieniecki** and our **Wiszowaty** (for they had been commissioned for this task by the church) protested to him regarding this matter, he responded, following the advice of his friends through one of his ministers, that he would not open the church, for he feared that the **Unitarians** would convert the citizens of **Piaski** to their own religion.

Since this proposal of the Brethren had not succeeded, provision was made for **Wiszowaty** in another place. Thus, **Ukraine** saw him performing his first duties as a pastor: there, in the year 1643, by a decree of the Church Senate, in the town of **Szerfznie**, under the patronage of **Stefan Wojnarowski**, the **Royal Huntsman** <note>A high-ranking official title in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth; original: *Venationis Regiæ præfecti*</note> of the **Kiev Palatinate**, he was assigned as a colleague to **Jan Stoiński**, a preacher most eminent for his learning and eloquence.

While **Wiszowaty** thus worked tirelessly in the Lord’s vineyard in one corner of the **Kingdom of Poland**, a terrible calamity overwhelmed his father’s house in another—namely, in **Lesser Poland** near the borders of **Hungary**. His father’s estate, named **Wrocmirowa**, which he had purchased and held in the foothills of the **Cracow Palatinate**, was invaded at night by bandits and wicked men. His father—who was well-regarded by some inhabitants of that region for his fairness and modesty, but hated by most due to his different religion—was cruelly beaten after the men plundered his money and household goods. Wanting to extort even more than they had found, they tortured and scorched him with glowing coals; from these injuries he departed this life a few days later, specifically on the eighth of October in the year 1643.

The sad news of such an end to his father’s life certainly struck the mind of our **Wiszowaty**, as was only natural, but it by no means utterly prostrated him. For he knew that sorrow...
