# LETTER ON THE LIFE
### [OF WISZOWATY]

->236<-

...to show restraint in adversity: which at that time, especially, he managed and overcame by dedicating himself to the sacred duties and the office to which he had been called. Because of his diligence in his role, he was esteemed by both his listeners and the patron of the church himself, **Wojnarowski**.

Nor did the **Niemirycz** family <note>A powerful noble family in Ukraine and Lithuania, known for their support of the Socinian/Unitarian cause</note> (heirs of significant wealth and men of great authority in those regions) favor him any less. The eldest of them, **George**, the **Arch-Chamberlain of Kiev**, had long since requested of the church that they grant him **Wiszowaty**—upon his return from abroad—for the sake of ministering in divine matters. At that time, he invited him to cross the **Dnieper** <note>original: *Borysthenem*, the ancient name for the Dnieper River</note> with him and set out for his town of **Orel**, situated on the bank of this river, encouraging him with these words: *"Saint Andrew the Apostle, your namesake,"* he said, *"is said to have preached the Gospel to the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of southeastern Europe/Asia; here referring to the inhabitants of the Ukrainian steppes</note> and their neighboring peoples; you, come with me to those same shores to do the same."* 

But the mind of the Brethren was otherwise; in the year 1644, they transferred him from the **Kiev Palatinate** <note>An administrative region of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note> to the neighboring **Palatinate of Volhynia**. They placed him in charge of the church which was gathered partly in **Haliczany** under the patronage of **Alexander Czaplic** (son of **Martin**, the Lord of **Beresteczko**, a man most beloved by both the church and the fatherland and born of noble blood) and partly at the estate of his kinsman, **Tobias Ivanicki**, in his ancestral home of **Ivanicze**. In addition, the neighboring churches of **Kisielin** and **Beresteczko**, founded by the brothers **Martin** and **George Czaplic**, were added to his care, so that by traveling there, he might look after the visiting brothers and assist the pastors in their duties (especially during the season of the holy communions).

While the **Unitarian Christians** were thus strenuously watching over their sacred rites, their adversaries were not resting in the meantime. In that same year of 1644, the state of the churches was disturbed by a non-trivial and grave persecution (which is accustomed to follow the pious like a shadow follows the body), and the course of religious practice in those regions was slowed. Those twin churches just mentioned were attacked, whose growth had stirred up envy in the malevolent and, from there, a desire to do harm. **George Czaplic**, the Lord of **Kisielin** and patron of the church there, was dragged into court. He was charged with the crime of [uttering] **Arian** <note>A term used by opponents to label Unitarians as heretics, referring to the 4th-century priest Arius</note> blasphemies...

# ANDREW WISZOWATY

->237<-

...[accusing him of] transferring the academy from **Raków** to **Kisielin**, and of harboring the outlawed and infamous ministers and teachers of **Raków** at his home. Although this was a mere fabrication (for the pastors of the church in **Kisielin** and the teachers of the school had never taught at **Raków**), it did nothing to protect these innocent men from the malice of their adversaries.

They gave no small proof of this when they excluded **Adam Hulewicz of Wojutyń** (with whom our **Wiszowaty** later formed a family bond by marrying his wife's sister) and **Alexander Czaplic** (son of George) from the judgment of this case. Although they were members of the **High Tribunal** <note>The highest appellate court in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note> to which this matter had been referred, they were barred because they were devoted to the rites of the **"Arians"** <note>A label used by opponents for the Polish Brethren (Socinians), who denied the Trinity</note> (as they are called). Once this was done, **Czaplic** was fined a sum of one thousand **Hungarian gold pieces** and ordered to present the church ministers and gymnasium teachers before the Tribunal. Since these men did not appear (having been moved out of danger by friends), he was again stripped of several thousand florins. Furthermore, the church in **Kisielin**, and even the neighboring one in **Beresteczko**, were completely destroyed, and it was strictly ordered that the exercise of religion should never again be conducted there.

In addition, **Matthias Twardochleb**, who had served as pastor of the **Kisielin** church for thirty years, and **Joachim Rupniowski**, pastor at **Beresteczko** for several years—both of whom were already deceased—were proclaimed "infamous," and a fine was ordered to be paid on their behalf. Consequently, all the fines and expenses at that time cost **Czaplic** at least twenty thousand florins. Furthermore, while fines were not imposed on **Andrew** and **Alexander Czaplic** (the sons of the late **Martin**, Lord of **Beresteczko**), they were forbidden, under heavy penalties, from practicing their religion within their own territories.

Many people in those regions were deeply dismayed by this bitter event. Nevertheless, **Wiszowaty** continued to perform his duties in the places mentioned above, enduring many hardships brought against him by his opponents. # EPISTLE ON THE LIFE
### OF ANDREW WISZOWATY

->238<-

...[he was ready to] depart from his beloved [homeland], had he not been held back by the brothers, who tirelessly supported these labors of his with both counsel and assistance.

After these dangers had been happily endured, with the supreme deity breathing favor upon him, he breathed again for a short while; and in this quietude, now in his fortieth year, he turned his mind toward taking a wife, so that he might have a companion in prosperity and a relief in adversity. He joined himself in marriage to a maiden he had long sought, recommended to him for her uprightness: **Alexandra Rupniowska**, born to **Joachim Rupniowski** and **Elisabeth**, daughter of **Andrew Lubieniecki**. It would be enough to say she was born of these parents, whose virtue and merits in their homeland and the church were hidden from no one. However, I think it not out of place to indicate who her ancestors and kinsmen were, so it may be clear that in this regard she was worthy of such a husband—although he took account not so much of ancestors and relatives as of her own personal virtue. 

Her father, **Joachim Rupniowski** (a man, as his contemporaries testify, well-versed in every branch of knowledge), in the first flower of his youth, led by love for divine glory, took upon himself the sacred ministry. He worthily performed this in various places, such as **Lublin**, **Kryłów**, **Raków**, and **Kisielin**, preferring it to the honors of this world, despite the multitude and splendor of his kinsmen who were powerful within it. The parent of the lineage is said by chroniclers to have been **Mirosław, Count of Nakiel**, from whom many illustrious men have sprung, counted among the pillars and ornaments of the homeland both then and now. Indeed, the **Lubomirskis** (honored with the title of Princes), the **Kmitas**, Counts of **Wiśnicz**, as well as the **Stadnickis** and other celebrated families, trace their origin to this same stem. Her mother was of the **Czajkowski** family, and she herself was from the most noble **Bali** families. These, as we have learned, were the ornaments of her paternal house.

# THE LIFE OF ANDREW WISZOWATY
### BY BENEDICT WISSOWATIUS

->239<-

Rupniowski’s wife, and indeed the mother of our Alexandra, was **Elisabeth**, descended from the very ancient **Rola** line of the **Lubieniecki** family. She was born to **Andrew Lubieniecki**, a man who voluntarily left the King’s court (where he enjoyed great favor) and turned his back on both his current and expected fortune. He even disregarded the prestige of his own kinsmen—among whom he counted the great **Jan Saryusz Zamoyski**, the "Phoenix of Sarmatia" <note>Sarmatia was a poetic historical name for Poland; Zamoyski was one of the most powerful statesmen and military leaders in Polish history</note>—to join the ranks of that sect, hated by many, which they call the **Arians** <note>The "Arians" or Polish Brethren were a Nontrinitarian Christian group known for their rationalist approach to scripture and advocacy for religious tolerance</note>. 

Indeed, at his own expense (an example followed by few), he served the churches of that same faith as a pastor in various places and stood out as its most fierce defender and propagator. This is abundantly proven by the many debates he held with adversaries and the many people he led to those same sacred rites—among whom were his younger brothers, **Stanisław** and **Christopher**. 

His father was **Stanisław**, the lord of Krzesimów and Treasurer of the Lublin region, who also served as a delegate for the administration of justice from both that province and the Sandomierz Palatinate. His mother was a descendant of the **Sobieski** family, who were as illustrious then as they are today <note>The Sobieski family would eventually produce King Jan III Sobieski, the famous victor of the Battle of Vienna</note>. 

Andrew Lubieniecki's wife was **Christina Ostrowska**, a matron known for the dignity and integrity of her character, born of the very ancient **Gryf** clan. Our Alexandra prides herself on having spent the flower of her youth under the supervision of this woman, her grandmother. Christina’s brother was the renowned **Peter Ostrowski**, who served with great distinction as an envoy to the Monarch of the Turks <note>The Sultan of the Ottoman Empire</note>. Her sister was the wife of **Jan Niemojewski**, that great ornament and pillar of the church, from whom she had a daughter who married **Sieniński**, the Palatine of Podolia. Furthermore, the aforementioned Christina counted among her ancestors and relatives the most excellent lineages of the **Suchodolski** and **Orzechowski** families (the former being her mother’s line, the latter her grandmother’s), from which many famous heroes emerged in both the service of the homeland and the church.

It was with this maiden—who rejoiced in such ancestors and kinsmen and was a true imitator of their virtue—that **Wiszowaty** contracted marriage, and through her, established a kinship with the men mentioned above. The wedding was celebrated after the mother (for the father had already died) gave the maiden away, with the sacred rites performed according to the usual custom of the church. The ceremony took place in **Haliczany**, in the home of the most distinguished man of virtue and noble birth, **Alexander Czaplic**, who was the bride’s maternal uncle and guardian...

# EPISTLE ON THE LIFE OF ANDREW WISZOWATY

...of the guardian, on the third day of May in the year 1648.

In the same year, by a decree of the Synod, he was transferred from Volynia to Lesser Poland, and the care of the Lublin church, which gathered in **Siedliska**, was entrusted to him. The first to provide a home for the purer doctrine <note>A term used by the Polish Brethren to describe their Unitarian theology, which they believed was a return to the "pure" teachings of the early church</note> in Lublin was the illustrious **Tenczyński**, who served as the Palatine <term>Palatinus: a high-ranking regional governor, or Wojewoda</term> of Belz and also the Governor of Lublin; in his house (on the very site where the Jesuit college was later built), that church had once flourished. However, after both the patron himself and the church's pastor, **Paclesius**, passed away, a change followed, and the practice of religion ceased for a time. 

Later, however, it was resumed by others and flourished until the year 1627: in that year, this church was destroyed in a wicked manner by ill-wishers. Moreover, in place of any comfort, a severe decree was issued by the High Tribunal forbidding it from ever being restored hereafter. Because of this, the citizens of **Lublin** and their neighbors began to gather for worship in the village of **Siedliska**, near the city, under the protection of **Nicolaus Suchodolski**, the Steward <term>Dapifer: a court official, known in Polish as a Stolnik</term> of the Chełm territory. The pastor of this place was **Christopher Lubieniecki the Younger**, a man burning with zeal for divine glory, who served until the year 1648, when he left this office along with his life.

To succeed him, **Wiszowaty** was judged by the society of brothers to be the most suitable person to lead such a populous church (despite the brothers in Volynia trying in vain to keep him with them); **Paul Myślicki** was appointed as his assistant.

In the year just passed, the church had again received a blow that was not light, though not unusual. **Jonas Schlichting**, that great light and ornament of the church (who was also related to our Wiszowaty), because of his published confession regarding the words of Holy Scripture—a book which was publicly burned by the hand of the executioner in Warsaw—was entirely outlawed from the kingdom with infamy, and was "forbidden fire and water" <note>original: "ignique ac aqua ei interdicitur"; a Roman legal formula indicating total exile and loss of civil rights</note>. Desiring to heal this wound to the church, or at least to ensure it did not spread further, the society imposed on Wiszowaty the duty of an embassy to the brothers of the Kraków and Sandomierz Palatinates, for the sake of strengthening them, so that they might delegate suitable men to the Diet <term>Comitia: the national parliament or Sejm</term> of the kingdom to plead the church's cause. Scarcely had he returned home (which was in **Suchodoły**, near Siedliska) from this successful embassy...

...having completed his duties, he returned; and behold, upon the death of King **Wladislaus** <note>King Władysław IV Vasa, who died in May 1648</note>, a servile war flared up in Poland. He went there to celebrate the Holy Communion <term>Synaxis: a Greek term for a religious assembly or the Eucharist</term> in the Polish language, while Ruar conducted the same in German. Having spent the winter in Prussia in this manner, and as the storm of unrest in the kingdom subsided, he returned to his post in the **Lublin** region in the year 1649, and once his listeners were gathered back together, he performed his duties once again.

As the year turned, by a decree of the Synod (despite the patron and the brothers of the Lublin congregation struggling in vain against it with many prayers), he moved from the Lublin Palatinate to the **Sandomierz Palatinate** <term>Palatinatus: a high-ranking administrative province or Województwo</term>, to serve as the pastor of the citizens of **Raków**. ...received <note>original: "excepit"</note> him and took him into her home, and as long as she lived, she treated him with singular kindness. First, he drafted a letter to **Wiszowaty**, warning him as if he were a friend to cease performing sacred rites, claiming that dangers were imminent for him because of this matter. Our friend, following the dictates of his conscience, wrote back that he would by no means allow himself to be deterred from his zeal for promoting divine glory by any threats or dangers; he further pointed out the injustice of the afflictions they so often suffered at the hands of the priests. 

The priest <note>original: "sacrificus," a term often used by reformers to emphasize the Catholic focus on the sacrifice of the Mass</note>, provoked by these words and burning with a desire to do harm, hurried to **Warsaw**. There, he presented **Wiszowaty’s** letters to be read before the delegates of the noble order <note>original: "equestris ordinis," the szlachta or gentry</note> at the general Diet <note>original: "comitiis," the Sejm or parliament</note> of the kingdom. Striving to destroy this church in the same manner as the previous church at **Raków**, he fabricated a slanderous claim: he alleged that the citizens of **Raków**, while going to **Radostów** for religious services, had broken the foot of a statue of the crucified Christ, and that this had been done at the instigation of their pastor, **Wiszowaty**. 

These lies were welcomed by ears eager for harm, and soon a mandate was issued, protected by the Royal hand and seal, and delivered to **Wiszowaty’s** home. By this decree, he himself, as well as the patroness of **Radostów** and the leading citizens of **Raków**, were summoned to the Diet of the kingdom to give an account of this alleged crime. Without delay, several inhabitants of **Raków** appeared in **Warsaw**, with the intention of summoning **Wiszowaty** (who wished to do the same) if his presence should be required. However, when they presented themselves, the judgment of this case was deferred to another time. 

In the meantime, that virtuous matron, the patroness of the aforementioned congregation, passed away. **Radostów** then passed to **Lord Sieniuta**, the husband of her eldest daughter (for the younger daughter was married to **Stefan Niemirycz**, the High Chamberlain of the **Palatinate of Kiev** <note>original: "Archicamerari Palatinatus Kyoviensis"</note>...

# A. WISZOWATY. #
<sig>Q 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: eo</meta>

...rashly <note>original: "temerario," continuing from the previous page</note> a Catholic by religion <note>original: "religione pontificius," literally "papal in religion"</note>, came into the inheritance by law and took that church away from the **Christian Unitarians** <note>Also known as the Polish Brethren or Socinians; they rejected the Trinity</note>. Because of this change, **Wiszowaty** found it necessary to depart from there; once he had done so, his adversaries ceased pressing the legal matter they had begun. With the sacred rites at **Radostów** silenced in this manner, Wiszowaty looked for another location. In the year 1652, he moved to the **Kraków Palatinate** <note>A high-level administrative province in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note> and, by the unanimous decision of the brethren, he was substituted into the ministry of the **Robców** congregation. He succeeded **Serinus Morsztyn**, the worthy son of that great **Governor** <term>Satrap: a title used here for a Starosta, a high-ranking regional official</term> of **Filipów**, to whom the care of the church at **Raciborsko** (erected by his father) had been entrusted. 

This church was founded by **Sebastian Chronowski**, the lord of Robców, who was honored with the name of the **"Christian Cato"** <note>A reference to Cato the Elder, symbolizing moral gravity and strictness</note> because of the seriousness of his character. By taking upon himself the burden of ministering to this congregation, he had, by a laudable example, acted as both its patron and its pastor. At that time, however, after others had served, **Abraham Mierzeński**—the son-in-law of the aforementioned Governor of Filipów and a man of similar character—was overseeing its protection. Wiszowaty spent four years in the ministry of this church. 

Furthermore, he undertook the care of inspecting and visiting the **Lusławice** church, which had been committed to him by the brethren. The minister there at the time was **Jan Moszowski**, who had once been condemned to the stake in **Hungary** by the **Lutherans** (whose rites he had abandoned) because of his religion. Similarly, Wiszowaty used to travel across the **Dunajec** river to the village of **Łużna**, where certain pious matrons lived who, due to their advanced age, were unable to attend the Robców congregation, so that he might perform sacred rites for them. 

While making these journeys, he encountered many adversities (which we will omit for now) from his opponents, who did not look upon these activities with friendly eyes; yet he emerged safely from these troubles by divine help. By stealing time from these regular occupations, he devoted himself to writing books. To say nothing of other works, he illustrated the entire **New Testament** <note>original: "Novum Instrumentum," a term famously used by Erasmus for his New Testament edition</note> with notes; he rendered the **Psalms** into Polish verse at the request of the brethren for use in the churches, adding many hymns for the same purpose. # ->A. WISZOWATY.<- #

...the manuscripts he had worked on thus far, along with his other books, perished in the persecution of which we shall soon speak. In that same place, **Robców**, on January 20, 1654, he lost his mother, **Agnes Sozzini** <note>original: "Agnetem Socinam." She was the daughter of Fausto Sozzini, the famous Italian theologian whose name gave rise to the term "Socinianism"</note>. In his home, after pouring out a generous blessing upon him, his wife, and his children for the kindnesses shown to her until her death, she commended her spirit to the Savior. She rests there, committed to the earth by her son.

We now enter the year 1655, which proved disastrous for **Wiszowaty’s** homeland, and especially for those who practiced the same faith as he. For that was the year in which **Charles Gustav**, King of the **Swedes**, invading **Poland** like a torrent, occupied almost the entire country. This occurred to such an extent that, with **King Casimir** <note>John II Casimir Vasa, who fled to Silesia during the invasion known as "The Deluge"</note> fleeing the kingdom, most of the **Palatinates** <note>High-level administrative provinces</note> and the leading Senators, as well as the royal army with its commanders and even the capital city of **Kraków** itself, found it necessary to submit to his protection. They did this primarily so that they might be protected from the **Muscovites** and **Cossacks**, who were savagely devastating the kingdom from another side with fire and sword. 

Consequently, when the whirlwind of war ceased and a proclamation of liberty was issued for everyone to return to their own estates, Wiszowaty returned from the fortress of **Rożnów** <note>original: "Roznoviana arce"</note>—where he had fled with his family to avoid this storm—to his station. During this time, he did not neglect the observance of fasts on account of the changed state of his homeland. Scarcely three months had passed in peace when, behold, a new whirlwind shattered this quiet. The Polish peasants were incited by certain individuals against the Swedes, urged to drive their garrisons out of the towns in violation of the oaths of surrender they had given. 

In place of a reward, however, the goods and villages of the **Arians** <note>original: "Arianorum." This was a derogatory term used by opponents to describe the Polish Brethren/Unitarians, suggesting they shared the ancient heresy of Arius in denying the Trinity</note> (as they are called) were promised to these peasants. It was publicly proclaimed from the pulpits in the marketplaces and churches throughout the towns that they should attack them and—as if they were sacrificial victims for the sins of others—slaughter them and plunder their possessions and goods. Incited by these words, the peasants—the subjects of many of these men—acted with great haste against their own masters. A mob of more than three thousand gathered. After the town of **Nowy Sącz** <note>original: "Sandecia"</note> was captured through treachery and the Swedish garrison there was butchered, the peasants unexpectedly attacked the villages and estates of the **Unitarians**. With the Catholic priests themselves showing the way, and equipped with axes, hoes, and fire-hardened stakes, they threw everything into a chaos of fire and sword. ...they slaughter others, leaving some bruised and half-dead, sparing neither the weaker sex nor infants: to recount all these things, and thus to renew such great grief, my mind shudders <note>original: "horret animus" — a classical allusion to Virgil’s Aeneid, used here to emphasize the trauma of the events</note>, nor do the place and time permit it. Furthermore, in snatching his life and those of his family from immediate danger, he was forced to leave behind almost all his property, and among it a library excellently furnished, exposing it to the madness of the spiteful. 

But **Rożnów** did not provide them a safe refuge for long, indeed scarcely for a single day; for the lord of the place (a Catholic <note>original: "religione pontificius" — a term used by Protestants to refer to members of the Roman Catholic Church</note>), fearing it might go badly for him if he sheltered such guests while a crowd of peasants was approaching, asked Wiszowaty to free him from fear and himself from danger by departing from there as quickly as possible. Therefore, Wiszowaty soon prepared for the journey; he was forced to travel by night, in mid-winter <note>original: "media bruma"</note>, with the frost and cold being extremely intense, as if moving through the very flames of those pursuing them, crossing the **Vistula** for almost twenty miles. Having struggled out of these dangers by a peculiar divine grace, after crossing the **Vistula** river, he moved to a village named **Czarkowy**. 

The heir of the place and patron of the church was **Hieronim Grat Moskorzowski**, the grandson of that incomparable **Hieronim Moskorzowski** (whom even the adversaries of the truth, compelled by its force, admitted was a man of whom these churches might rightly boast) through his son **Andrzej**; he was also the great-grandson of the great **Andreas Dudith** <note>Andrzej Dudycz (1533–1589), a famous humanist, diplomat, and bishop who became a leading figure in the Reformation</note>. He was also related to our Wiszowaty by blood, being born of the daughter of Wiszowaty's paternal uncle, **Benedict Wiszowaty**. Under his patronage, in the church built by the elder Moskorzowski whom we mentioned, the pastor at that time was **Stanisław Lubieniecki** <note>Stanisław Lubieniecki (1623–1675) was a prominent Polish Unitarian historian and astronomer</note> (who died in exile in **Hamburg** on May 21, 1675), a man of profound learning. Here Wiszowaty breathed again for a little while with his family, and spent the time he was permitted to stay there performing sacred duties; for his former listeners, having heard he was there, had flocked to **Czarkowy**. Daily, sermons and admonitions were held there, both during the day and in the hours before dawn; and at fixed times, as the occasion required, they devoted themselves to fasting and prayers.

### ->LETTER ON THE LIFE<- ###
<meta>catchword: but</meta>

But truly, they did not enjoy these circumstances for long; for it was reported that a crowd of stupid plunderers, egged on by more cunning individuals and lured by fresh spoils, was heading toward **Czarkowy** (where they had learned many **Arians** <note>original: "Arianos" — A term used to describe the Polish Brethren or Socinians, who were frequently targeted during this period for their non-trinitarian beliefs</note> had gathered). They were said to be crossing the **Vistula** near the town of **Witowice**, which was only a short distance away. It was unanimously decided by the brothers that they must flee from there immediately. 

They had scarcely traveled one or two miles when, behold, those idle troublemakers fell upon **Czarkowy** with fire and sword: they burned the church to the ground, plundered goods, and tore apart the library of the aforementioned **Lubieniecki** <note>Stanisław Lubieniecki (1623–1675), a notable historian and astronomer of the Polish Brethren</note>, even paving the road all the way to **Pińczów** with his books. These and similar atrocities were being committed everywhere at that time. Placed in such narrow straits, and having poured out prayers to God, they deliberated where they should go. They saw that they were by no means safe from their own countrymen in their homeland; nor did it seem more prudent to withdraw outside the country into neighboring **Silesia** or **Hungary** (as many desired). For all the passages were occupied by robbers and assassins, and no idle rumor reported that some who had already attempted it had been snatched away by a horrific death. 

In such a situation, since no better remedy could be found, neighboring **Kraków** was chosen. This city (as we mentioned above) had entrusted itself, along with the other inhabitants of the region, to the patronage and protection of the **Swedes**; and many from the neighborhood—both Roman Catholics and Evangelicals—had fled there, seeking to avoid the fear of war, as it was considered safer and more fortified than other places. Therefore, the aforementioned brothers, compelled by a more serious necessity and having obtained permission from the city's governors, turned their course there. 

Entering the city, they commissioned **Wiszowaty** to greet the governor—who was the renowned **Paul Wirtz** <note>A famous German officer and diplomat who served as the Swedish governor of Kraków during the occupation</note>—on behalf of everyone and to thank him for the promised defense and protection. This he did, delivering an oration to him. Nearly thirty families entered **Kraków**; and because, contrary to what they had hoped, no opportunity was given to depart or return to their own homes due to seditions and military movements, their first priority was the exercise of their religion. They had once enjoyed freedom of religion in this city, secured by royal charters, nor during the past century [had] that church [been] from the troublemakers (who [acted] against both the living and the dead laid in their tombs...

Now, however, having seized this opportunity, they obtained the freedom to conduct their sacred rites from the aforementioned governor <note>Likely the Swedish commander in Krakow, Paul Würtz, who was known for his relative tolerance toward various religious groups during the occupation</note>, just as the others did. This was the greatest consolation after so many adversities. It was no small help in such a good undertaking that they had with them several men trained in divine matters; because of the great size of the city, they divided the work among themselves, with each one conducting sacred rites twice daily in his own quarters. On Sundays and fast days (which were observed every week), they all gathered in one place; they did the same at the time of ecclesiastical discipline and for the breaking of the sacred bread <note>The Lord’s Supper or Communion, a central rite for the Polish Brethren</note>. 

Moreover, they met at fixed times to investigate and draw out the meaning of the Holy Scriptures; through the help of these gatherings, **Jonas Schlichting** <note>Jonas Slichtingius (1592–1661), a preeminent theologian and biblical critic of the Socinian movement</note> illustrated a large part of the **New Testament** <note>original: "novi fœderis"</note> with commentaries there. They spent their time in these pursuits throughout the following year. Amidst the distress and the noise of the siege, which was renewed three times, they often struggled with hunger and cold; yet, by divine grace, they were never reduced to the final extremity and persevered with patience.

Finally, in the year 1657, the city [Krakow] was surrendered to the **King of Poland**, its former and legitimate lord, after it had been surrounded by him in a fourth siege. As the **Swedes** were departing the kingdom and permission was given to everyone to return to their own homes, **Wiszowaty** also departed from **Krakow** with his people. He betook himself to the sub-mountainous region <note>The Podgórze or Beskids region in southern Poland</note> and made for **Robków** <note>original: "Robcoviam"</note>. 

But indeed, he found there a far different state of affairs than he had left: his house was ruined and devastated, and his furniture and all his goods had been carried off. His library—the loss of which struck him most severely—which had been furnished with excellent books, both printed and handwritten, had been plundered and torn apart by priests and peasants. Therefore, distressed by such a state and finding only the ruins of the pastoral house in **Robków**, he moved to his hereditary village named **Wrocmirowa**, situated half a mile from there. Mindful of his duty, he used his letters to gather the brothers, who were scattered both within the homeland and outside it, to celebrate their sacred rites together once more.

Thus, that church, which had made its home in this kingdom for a hundred years, was utterly rooted out from there; yet, just as it had grown through blood and persecutions, it grew in a similar manner <note>A reference to the common Christian motif that "the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church."</note>.

The year was 1658, during the reign of **John Casimir** <note>King John II Casimir Vasa, whose reign was marked by the Swedish invasion and the subsequent expulsion of religious minorities</note>, when a decree of a harsh nature <note>original: "horre carminis"—literally "a dreadful song," an idiom for a harsh or grim law</note> was said to have been enacted against those commonly called **Arians** <note>The "Arians" here refers to the Polish Brethren or Socinians, a Restorationist Christian group that rejected the Trinity</note>. > *Although public law has forbidden the **Arian** sect, or as some call it, the **Anabaptist** sect, to live and propagate in our domains, nevertheless, by some fatal misfortune of the Republic, the aforementioned sect has begun to spread in recent times in our domains of both the Kingdom and the **Grand Duchy of Lithuania** <note>The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was a dual state; the law applied to both parts</note>, a sect which diminishes the pre-eternity of the Son of God. Therefore, by reassuming and leaving in its full force the statute of our predecessor **Wladyslaw Jagiello** <note>King Wladyslaw II Jagiello (reigned 1386–1434), who issued early edicts against heresy</note> regarding heretics, we decree by the consensus of all orders: That if any such person is found who has dared to profess, spread, or preach this **Arian** sect in our domains, both of the Kingdom and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the provinces annexed to them, or to protect and cherish it or its supporters, and has been legally convicted of that matter; every such person must be subject to the aforementioned statute, and without any delay by our captains <note>term: "capitaneos" (starostas)—local administrative and judicial officials</note> and their offices, they must be punished with the **death penalty** <note>original: "pœna capitis"</note> under pain of being deprived of their office. But for their supporters, as a penalty for **high treason** <note>original: "perduellionis"</note>, we assign a hearing in the Tribunal among the cases of mixed jurisdiction at the instance of anyone, including the captains and their offices; in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, however, in the Tribunal in any register. Wishing nevertheless to show our clemency, if any such person is found who refuses to renounce this sect of theirs, we grant them a period of three years to sell their possessions, preserving the security of their goods and persons and the recovery of their debts. During this time, however, they must perform no exercises of their aforementioned sect.*

...shall be forbidden, *and shall be able to involve himself in no public duties, under the penalties expressed above.*

It is not our intention to pick apart this decree; nor does the time or place allow us to contrast it with that eternal law of the entire Republic—reaffirmed many times and sanctioned by the oaths of so many Kings—concerning peace and security for those who disagree in matters of religion <note>This refers to the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, which had guaranteed religious peace between different faiths but was effectively overturned by the 1658 decree</note>. In the face of such terrible events, it would be pointless to complain about the titles and names of **Arians** and **Anabaptists** that were so unjustly forced upon them. Regarding the disagreement over the dogmas of faith: did they believe rightly or wrongly? If wrongly, why were they not instructed in Christian charity? Why were they struck down by a physical <note>original: "carnali"—literally "fleshly" or worldly</note> sword rather than a spiritual one? This is especially true since they never refused such instruction, but were always ready and seeking opportunities to meet openly with their adversaries. They did not fear to give an account of their religion in the very churches and monasteries of their opponents, or before Kings, the highest courts, Bishops, and other high priests <note>original: "mystis"—referring to those initiated into religious mysteries, used here for the Catholic clergy</note>. But if they believed rightly, let the persecutors judge for themselves what a crime they have committed in pursuing the innocent; and let them consider what comfort and how great a reward awaits those who suffer such things for the sake of the **SON OF MAN**. Having committed these matters to the most just Judge, let us return to our subject.

This edict struck many like a lightning bolt. Fearing the miseries of exile and preferring an earthly homeland to a heavenly one, they changed their religion and were torn away from the rest like chaff in the wind. Some fled to the camp of the Roman Pope <note>Catholicism</note>, while others fled to the camp of Calvin <note>The Reformed Church</note>. The Catholics <note>original: "pontificiis"</note> soon forbade the latter from happening. But our **Wiszowaty** was not dismayed by this whirlwind. He did not cease in the performance of his duties, despising the dangers and snares that were laid for him daily because of this—especially by the neighboring parish priest of **Zbyszyce** <note>Latin: "Zbyscenfi"</note>. Setting aside the priest’s other schemes for harming Wiszowaty, I wish to recount one example of his ill-will and his efforts (in which a singular divine providence shone through). Many of the brothers had gathered at **Robkow** <note>Latin: "Robcoviam"</note> for fasting and church discipline, as well as to celebrate the rites of baptism and the breaking of the sacred bread. As soon as that parish priest found out—whose residence was scarcely one...

(was only a stone’s throw away from there) having gathered wicked men of no importance, he set out for **Robcovia** <note>likely the village of Robków or Rabkowa</note>, intending to capture **Wiszowaty** and to drive the rest away after stripping them of their property. Having spent two days in their religious duties, they departed peacefully, and continued to do the same afterward.

When such attempts at harm did not succeed as the adversaries hoped, they struck a heavier blow <note>original: "fulmen vibrarunt"—literally "hurled a thunderbolt"</note> by issuing Royal mandates (commonly called **Universals** <note>public proclamations or edicts issued by the Polish king to the whole nobility</note>), which strictly forbade such gatherings of the so-called **Arians**. At the same time, the **Governors** (commonly called **Captains** <note>original: "Satrapae (vulgo Capitanei)"—referring to the Starostas, local administrative and judicial officials in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note>) and other officials were commanded that wherever they found people of this sect, of whatever status or rank, whether men or women, gathered for worship, they were to seize them, throw them into prison in chains, and punish them.

This news terrified most people, but not our **Andrew**, who, as in all matters, behaved here with great courage. He was ready to perform his duties in the same place as before; however, the patron of the church <note>the local nobleman who owned the land and supported the congregation</note>, fearing he might lose his estates, no longer dared to allow a meeting place in his village. Therefore, **Wiszowaty** did not hesitate to invite the brothers to meet for worship at his own ancestral estate of **Wrocmirov** <note>Wrocimierz or Wrocimierowice</note>, opening his own home for this purpose. Some came to him openly, others, who were more fearful, came by night. Furthermore, he visited those who did not come, or reminded them of their duty and strengthened them in the faith through letters. In this way, worship was held in his house almost every day, for they no longer dared to gather all at once as they had done before. Thus, he had to provide for them both spiritually and physically (namely, through hospitality), and he performed both to the best of his ability...

# THE LIFE OF A. WISZOWATY

[He] stood firm, even amidst the dangers hanging over him; as for the lawsuits moved against him by the **clergy** <note>original: "Spiritualibus"—referring to the Catholic ecclesiastical authorities</note> (as they are called) because of his religious practice, we pass over these as not unusual, and move on to more noteworthy things.

The year was 1660, and as the deadline for the exile of those called **Arians** and **Anabaptists** approached, many—especially those whose great wealth and the distinction of their relatives did not allow them to be torn from their earthly homeland—were wavering in their religion. These men requested that a **charitable colloquy** <note>original: "colloquium charitativum"—a formal, peaceful debate between different religious groups intended to find common ground</note> regarding religion be established between the Roman Catholics and those who had been condemned and were known by the name of **Arians**. For this purpose, one of the primary senators of the kingdom, **Jan Wielopolski Szafraniec**, offered his home. At that time, he held the dignities of **Castellan of Wojnicz** <note>a high-ranking administrative and military office in Poland</note> and **Governor of Warsaw** <note>original: "Satrapae Warsawiensis"</note>, and later served as the **Palatine of Kraków**. Permission for this meeting was obtained from the Bishop of Kraków.

This undertaking was full of dangerous risk <note>original: "periculosae plenum hoc opus erat aleae," literally "full of dangerous dice," echoing the phrase "the die is cast"</note>. For if those challenged had not appeared, they would have been immediately accused of distrusting their own cause; on the other hand, those who were vacillating in their faith might have thought they now had a just reason for changing their religion. Furthermore, appearing seemed neither safe nor useful, for it was feared that the adversaries had instituted this out of a desire for their corruption rather than their correction. Considering these things, some stayed at home; others, who were already prepared to go, were restrained by friends; others were delayed by the difficulty of the journey and arrived only after the disputation was finished. 

But our **Wiszowaty**, putting aside all other considerations and despising the dangers and inconveniences, and relying only on divine help, descended into the arena. There, as if in a theater, he intended to give testimony to the truth for the last time in his homeland and to strengthen those who were wavering in their faith. He appeared, therefore, on the appointed day, accompanied by some of his friends, at the castle of **Rożnów**, where the mentioned **Castellan** resided and where the place for the disputation had been designated. There, contrary to the expectations of many—both adversaries and friends—everything went according to his heart's desire. He was received very kindly by the **Castellan** and humanely invited to his table, experiencing singular benevolence along with his companions; those who envied and growled looked on in vain...

->EPISTLE ON HIS LIFE<-

[...him whom] the priests had previously persecuted, and who had flown there at that time specifically to witness his ruin. A great many Roman Catholics gathered for this conference, including several who were prominent and famous in those regions: **Rychlovius**, Provincial of the **Reformed Bernardines** <note>a branch of the Franciscan Order</note>; **Henning**, the Jesuit Rector of Kraków; **Nicolaus Cichovius**, also a **Jesuit**, and others. With these men, **Wiszowaty** debated courageously and—as they themselves admitted—with solid reasoning for five whole days, from the 11th to the 16th of March in the aforementioned year of 1660, concerning the primary religious controversies (and especially the one for which they were being driven from their homeland). 

He frequently reduced his opponents to a standstill <note>original: "ad incitas," a metaphor from games like chess meaning to be unable to move</note>. Even the **Castellan** <note>Jan Wielopolski</note>, who served as the moderator of this debate, acknowledged this; he sometimes became angry with his own side when they failed to respond correctly. The Castellan (to mention nothing else) openly confessed that a specific argument produced by **Wiszowaty** from **1 Corinthians 8** <note>referring to verse 6: "yet for us there is but one God, the Father..."</note>—proving that the **FATHER** alone is that supreme and one **GOD**—had robbed him of sleep for an entire night. 

Similarly, when **Wiszowaty** was sharply pressing the priests to prove that the Son of God was not the supreme God himself—on the grounds that he was ignorant of the day of the last Judgment—**Cichovius**, that subtle Jesuit, fell into the trap of saying that it was possible for someone to be the supreme God (provided he was not the "first person" of the Trinity) and yet not know everything. Angry, the Castellan burst out with these words: *"I do not want to have such a supreme God,"* said the Castellan, *"who did not know about that day!"* <note>referencing Mark 13:32, a key text used by Unitarians to argue that Jesus, being ignorant of the timing of the end of the world, could not be co-equal with the omniscient Father</note>. 

However, for those who wish to know these matters more deeply, we refer them to the records of this conference. A summary of these acts, as recorded by the scribes' pens, was recently published as an annex to **Wengerscius’s** *Ecclesiastical History* <note>Andrzej Węgierski (1600–1649); his "History of the Slavonic Churches" was a standard reference for the era</note>. 

Among other testimonies from the opponents regarding this disputation, we found this written account, which is certainly worth noting. While the Lord Castellan was speaking with the most noble **Wladislaus Morsztyn**, he saw the **Superior** of a monastery (commonly called a **Guardian** <note>the title for a local superior in Franciscan houses</note>) approaching. He asked Mr. **Morsztyn** to step into the next room so he could overhear the priest's honest judgment of the debate. Once this was done, the Castellan asked the Superior how the debate had pleased him. To this, the priest replied: *"Even if all [the heretics] came up from hell,"* he said, *"they could not defend their religion more strongly than this one man alone."* The Castellan then asked: *"But what if there were more of them? For there are,"* he added, *"not a few like him."* The other replied: *"I do not know what should then be done with them..."*

### A. WISZOWATY.

Meanwhile, various rumors were striking the ears of **Wiszowaty's** wife and family. The envy and wonder of those who wished him ill was only increased when, a few days later, **Wiszowaty** received an invitation from the aforementioned **Castellan** <note>Jan Wielopolski, the local governor and moderator of the debate</note> to visit him during the time of **Carnival** <note>original: *carnisprivium*, the period of feasting before the fast of Lent</note>. He did not refuse the invitation, although he was again afraid; for he hoped that he would once again find an opportunity to achieve something good there.

During the greeting, the Illustrious Lord Wielopolski addressed him with these words: *“The first time,”* he said, *“I received you as a theologian; but now, your arrival is welcome to me as that of a friend and neighbor.”* The outcome proved that these were not just empty words. For several days he was treated most kindly by the Castellan, as they engaged in friendly conversations (principally concerning religion) in the presence of several priests and some knights.

I myself,”* the Castellan added, *“will give you a rich estate named Grodek for you to possess for the rest of your life. Furthermore, I promise that I will see to it that you receive a substantial annual sum of money from other magnates of the kingdom, my colleagues; for our country has need of learned men such as you are.”*

This was a weapon wielded against **Wiszowaty** no less forcefully than the threats of persecution and exile. But indeed, as in all his good purposes, so here too, he remained constant and immo—

### LETTER ON THE LIFE

...and then our **Andrzej** <note>Andrzej Wiszowaty (1608–1678)</note> showed his resolve. He preferred his virtues and the reputation of a good man over the loss of a good conscience; he chose rather to suffer *reproach with the people of God* than to enjoy the *fleeting pleasures of sin*. <note>A paraphrase of Hebrews 11:25-26, comparing Wiszowaty to Moses.</note> Briefly, therefore, he responded to the Lord **Castellan** with thanks for his kindness, stating that his conscience prevented him from satisfying the Castellan’s desire <note>The Castellan had likely urged him to convert to Catholicism to save his estate and status.</note>. When the **Castellan** saw that he could be moved from his purpose neither by harshness nor by kindness, he found it necessary to yield to these facts. Nevertheless, he dismissed him affectionately and promised his help (though it was now too late).

Finally, in that same year **1660**, that fatal day never to be forgotten by the **Unitarian Christians**, the tenth of July, dawned. On this day, if they wished to keep their lives, they were forced to leave their fatherland; they were abandoned to the hands of all as outlaws and infamous people, to be slaughtered and cut down with impunity if they remained beyond the appointed time. This deadline, accelerated by their adversaries, came unexpectedly for many; for in the legal decree <note>original: *constitutione*</note> of the year 1658, a period of three years had been granted for the selling of their property. But the wretched people were not even allowed to settle their affairs in peace: with one year taken away, their exile was hastened. 

Consequently, many received hardly anything for their possessions and goods. Some had to be content with a fifteenth or twentieth part of the actual value; others were left with nothing but bare hope and a promise of payment. Many were unable to sell their possessions at all, as the local inhabitants were well aware that these things would be left behind for them to take. Furthermore, while our **Wiszowaty** was distracted and intent on more serious matters, a soldier, having obtained permission from the **King**, occupied and took possession of his village, **Opalia** (as was the case for several others). At the same time, he suffered a heavy loss of other properties which had come to him by hereditary right, as well as money which it was then impossible to recover from his debtors. 

Thus, leaving behind his fatherland, but keeping for himself a good conscience and the hope of better things, he departed from **Poland** with men of the same spirit. Thus are driven out and scattered so many excellent citizens, many who served the fatherland best and were linked by blood to the most famous lineages—flesh of the flesh and bone of the bones of the **Republic** <note>original: *Reipublicæ*, referring to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note>—now stripped of goods and honor. They were treated as if they had suffered <term>civil death</term> <note>original: *capite deminuti*, a Roman legal term for the loss of status or civil rights</note>, placed not only below the commoners, but even below the **Jews** and **Mahometans** <note>original: *Mahometanos*; a historical term for Muslims</note>...

->## THE LIFE OF ANDRZEJ WISZOWATY<-

...regarded as worse than **Muslims** (who are allowed to live freely in Poland). At that time, many rejoiced and exulted as if a great deed had been accomplished, prophesying that the kingdom would be happy after the departure of the **Arians** <note>A derogatory term for the Polish Brethren or Unitarians, who rejected the doctrine of the Trinity.</note>. Others, moved by pity, did not dare to offer help to the wretches, knowing they would be liable to a greater punishment than the exiles themselves. For to those who conformed to **Roman** rites (as was done by not a few), their honors and possessions were restored; furthermore, for those convicted of having aided the **Arians**, or even of having had commerce with them, the guilt had to be paid for with the inevitable confiscation of their goods, and no remedy remained.

Therefore, one part of them—wherever each could conveniently hurry away and withdraw his life from danger—sought **Prussia**, another part the **Margraviate of Brandenburg**, others **Silesia**, and finally others sought **Transylvania** and **Hungary**. But a new disaster overwhelmed these last ones (although the others did not lack their own hardships). For scarcely had they crossed the **Carpathian** mountains into the **Maramureș** <note>A historical region now split between Romania and Ukraine.</note> County of the Kingdom of Hungary, intending to stay under the protection of the Illustrious Count **Francisc Ráday**, when—behold—by **Imperial** soldiers <note>original: *Cæsareano milite*; referring to the troops of the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> (incited, as was reported, by secret messages and provocations from ill-wishers in Poland), the wretched exiles, whose number was more than five hundred, were robbed in a most piteous manner of their travel money and all their goods (which they had rescued from their homeland as if from the midst of flames), even down to their clothes, leaving them naked.

Furthermore, our **Wiszowaty**, having been warned that there were many who were lying in wait for him, anticipated the fixed deadline and, leaving the threshold of his fatherland, went into **Silesia** with his family. He stayed there for six months and spent the time conducting sacred rites with the brothers who had moved to the same place. From there, towards winter, when the movements had subsided to some extent, he returned to his homeland; in which some of the brothers and sisters still remained—especially widows and orphans, who did not have the funds to migrate—whom he intended to help with counsel and aid as much as a man can. Upon hearing of his arrival, not a few flowed to him from their hiding places, and he ministered to them by performing his duties as long as he stayed there.

Having spent the winter in his homeland in this manner, amidst the dangers threatening him, just as the soldiers were moving from their stations...

...disturbances, as a more turbulent time loomed, by the advice of the brothers he left his homeland again in the year 1661. Having crossed the **Carpathian** mountains, which were full of danger and hardship, he was escorted by several brothers into **Hungary** to the town of **Cæsareopolis** (called ***Keszmark*** by the inhabitants) <note>Modern-day Kežmarok in Slovakia.</note>, located in the **Spiš** County, where the Illustrious Count **István Thököly** <note>original: *Stephanus Tekeli*</note> was the local Lord. As winter approached, he hurried back to his homeland to remind those brothers who were still hiding there of their duty and to strengthen them in their religion, especially several pious matrons whose husbands had become apostates <note>In this context, "apostates" refers to those who had converted to Catholicism to avoid exile or property confiscation.</note>.

In the following year, 1662, at the very start of the new year and as new troubles were pressing in, he again followed the advice of friends and left the borders of his homeland. Once more, he returned to **Cæsareopolis** over the high **Carpathian** mountains. He remained there for the entire year, for no hope now shone of accomplishing any good in **Poland**. Indeed, the fervor of their adversaries had reached such a point that they even brought to trial husbands who had defected to them, but whose wives remained stubbornly tenacious in their religion, imposing fines on them for the "crime" of cohabiting with **Arian** spouses.

Meanwhile, however, he was by no means idle in **Hungary**. He spent his time partly by performing sacred rites for those present who flocked to him, and partly by writing several works for the benefit of his friends and for common use, as well as drafting advisory letters to the scattered exiles. Nevertheless, because he did not have there the opportunity he desired for promoting divine glory, he turned over in his mind where he might go. Neighboring **Transylvania** (although it had its own disadvantages) flourished with a freedom for the religion to which he was devoted that surpassed other regions. For in that land, the Princes (following a custom established since the time of **John Sigismund** <note>John Sigismund Zápolya (1540–1571), the first Prince of Transylvania and a promoter of religious tolerance through the Edict of Torda.</note>) are accustomed to confirm by oath that they will preserve the religious immunity of the **Reformed**, the **Unitarians**, the **Saxons** of the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church.</note>, and the **Roman Catholics**. Among these, the **Unitarians** are especially prominent in **Claudiopolis** <note>Modern-day Cluj-Napoca, Romania.</note> (where they hold the governing reins of the city and its **athenaeum** <note>A college or center of higher learning.</note>) and in the **Szekler** County <note>original: *Siculorum Comitatu*</note>. ...[will remain] (for he used to read more than he wrote) and will never perish. Among his unpublished writings, he considered two works to be of the greatest importance—brief in length, yet of no small weight—which he would have polished further had he been permitted. One was titled *Rational Religion* <note>original: *Religio rationalis*</note>, the other *The Stimuli of Virtues and the Bridles of Sins* <note>original: *Stimulorum virtutum frenorumque peccatorum*</note>. As death drew near, he expressed a profound desire that these treatises, above all his other scholarly works, be brought to light. He hoped they might offer something to help mortals recognize the truth and perform good deeds. Indeed, he constantly regarded these two goals as the highest of all concerns; just as he applied himself to them with all his strength, he strove to instill the same purpose in others. 

To his youngest son (whom he left as his only survivor, his older children having already passed away), he gave this as one of his final deathbed instructions: "Peter," he said, "you have seen what I have done, my boy! You too, always care for the true and the good; seek it, and let your whole being be devoted to this." These and similar words were the chief things he impressed upon those standing by his side or visiting him. He especially commended charity and harmony, continuing until he lost his life along with his voice. Having finished the good fight, he reached his longed-for goal, weary <note>original: *satur*, meaning "sated" or "full of"</note> both of his years and his misfortunes.

In the following year, 1679, the wife of our Wiszowaty, Alexandra Rupnovia, aged fifty-six, followed her husband into death. Deprived of him, she had found life bitter. She followed him after being confined to her bed by illness for nearly the same amount of time as he had been. Remaining in full possession of her mind and memory to the end, and holding a joyful hope for a better life, she breathed out her soul—entrusted to the Supreme Deity—on the 23rd of November. On the 27th of that month, she was laid to rest beside her husband. 

There is no space here to list her praises (among which it is no small thing that she did not bear the name 'Alexandra' in vain until her end <note>A classic rhetorical play on names; "Alexandra" is Greek for "defender of men," suggesting her strength of character during their exile</note>). Let it suffice to mention this one honor, which she herself always held as her greatest: that she was the beloved wife of Andrew Wiszowaty. Fortunate are they both! If the cause for which they suffered so many evils remains true, they are blessed; if it were false, they would be the most unhappy of all mortals. For the latter would be merely the end of a life endured, but for them, it was truly the cessation of labors and a transition to a better life.

->A. WISZOWATY<-

And so we have guided this man through the cycle of his deeds, from his earliest cradle to the very finish line, and narrated the annals of his life. From the actions we have recounted, the remarkable qualities of his mind easily shine forth. We consider it less necessary to describe his physical attributes, for he never allowed them to be depicted <note>Wiszowaty, like many in the Socinian/Polish Brethren movement, likely avoided portraits out of a sense of religious humility or to avoid the "idolatry" of the individual.</note> while he lived.

The traces of his venerable face—worn down significantly by both cares and years—remain fixed in the fresh memory of many. Setting aside those things which he laid down along with his body, let us rise higher and contemplate the virtues of his soul a bit more deeply. By briefly recalling what has already been mentioned, we can easily assemble a model of all his virtues.

First, he had laid a firm and good foundation: namely, a love of what is right. He always maintained a mind inclined toward understanding the truth and performing good deeds. Aiming at the ultimate goal <note>original: *scopum*</note> of all actions, he examined everything that led toward it, always holding fast to what was good. To ensure he did not crash against the reefs of error, the torch of prudence and knowledge shone before him. He had added these qualities to his virtue, having been endowed with them as a divine gift. His physical eyesight was nearsighted and weak, but the sharp insight and prudence of his mind—the mother of all virtues—compensated for this; even so, these qualities were always tempered by his modesty.

Having embraced the religion he believed to be true, he worshiped God and His Christ with a pure mind according to the requirements of their law, setting aside all worldly considerations. His entire life, spent enduring various persecutions <note>original: *persepffiones*, likely a printing error for *persecutiones*</note>, bears witness to this. Placing firm trust in God and believing in His promises, he maintained an unshakable hope for the good to come. For this reason, he took care to maintain a blameless conscience before both God and men; he would have preferred to lose his possessions or his reputation as a good man rather than lose his integrity. Nor was his pure knowledge of divine things—which cost him dearly <note>A reference to the social, financial, and political sacrifices he made for his "heretical" Unitarian beliefs</note>—possessed in vain. Instead, maintaining an unwavering faith and hope, he built his charity upon these by acting according to what he knew. Every action he took began with a love for the Supreme Being <note>original: *Summi Numinis*</note>. He was diligent in daily prayers, and vigilant and fervent in his sermons and exhortations (in which he was greatly aided by his natural eloquence). In his debates—

[...devotions] <note>The Latin word *exercitationibus* (exercises/devotions) begins on the previous page and concludes here.</note> for the sake of religion with zeal, always ready for everything looking toward the glory of God. Nor is it more difficult to say than to see from his actions his justice and his charity toward his neighbors, which constantly accompanied his piety and love of God. He always displayed the duty owed to parents, loyalty to country, honor to the magistrate, love to relatives, obedience to the church, observance of the laws, and help to the wretched—always giving what was due. He acted toward all just as he would wish them to act toward him.

Now indeed, he joined temperance to the piety owed to God and the justice owed to his neighbor, keeping himself untainted by the world by fleeing its desires. He utterly shrank from the illicit pleasures of the flesh; in those that were licit, he conducted himself moderately, leading a life of sobriety and chastity. The "lust of the eyes" <note>A biblical reference to 1 John 2:16, usually meaning materialism or the desire for worldly possessions.</note> held no place in him; and although he could have enjoyed a more luxurious lifestyle, he preferred divine glory to earthly goods and lived content with his lot. Even when he was driven from his fatherland <note>Wiszowaty and the Polish Brethren (Socinians) were officially banished from Poland in 1658 due to their non-trinitarian beliefs.</note>, he did not take the loss of his possessions with a heavy heart, for he held the hope of a better treasure.

Furthermore, from what he possessed by the grace of God, he always gave to the needy according to his strength. He was never anxious about tomorrow; frequently, when he seemed to have been reduced to desperate straits <note>original: *ad incitas redactus*—a Latin idiom derived from board games, meaning to be cornered or unable to make a move.</note>, help arrived unexpectedly. He fled far from pride and ambition, both internal and external: for he cared very little for the splendor of clothing and houses; furthermore, an arrogant spirit was entirely exiled from him. And although he did not lack those things in which men of this world are accustomed to glory, he by no means exalted himself above others.

Although he did not seek honor, he was nevertheless held in great estimation among the great; he was pleasing and acceptable to all good men, who recall his memory with a grateful mind even after his death. He cultivated those sublime virtues of humility and modesty above all others; at all times, toward both inferiors and superiors, he exhibited a companionable manner. Upon temperance, he had built fortitude and patience (of which we have seen examples to the point of abundance): by abstaining from illicit things, he sustained adversity with a strong heart. In a good purpose (from which he allowed himself to be torn away neither by adversity nor prosperity), he constantly displayed a steady mind. In these matters, if it happened that he erred—for he was a man, and did not lack failings—he was by no means stubborn or persistent; but always mo[ved...]

# VINDICATION

## For the Religious Freedom of the Unitarians in Poland,

### *Written by a Polish Knight.* <note>In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, a "Knight" (Eques) referred to a member of the *Szlachta*, or noble class, who held significant political rights.</note>

We read in the records of the ancients that for those Philosophers against whom an impudent tongue thrust the venomous stings of accusations, it was judged not only impossible to remain silent, but even unseemly—indeed, a sin—to withdraw in the slightest from a fierce defense of those who had revealed to the human race the most precious treasure: the hidden knowledge of things divine and human. In the same way, as I see how the sacred bonds of that most beneficial covenant <note>Referring to the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, a landmark agreement that guaranteed religious peace and equality among the nobility regardless of their faith.</note> established at Warsaw by our Ancestors regarding those who differ in religion are being shattered; how the very oaths sworn by five of our most serene Kings and the bonds of public laws are being broken; and how (alas!) among Christians, such sacred faith wavers; it seemed entirely unworthy of me to remain silent. Instead, I have chosen to undertake a defense <note>original: *apologiam*; in this context, a formal legal and theological justification.</note> for the sake of posterity, for the faith and piety of our Ancestors, and for the sake of afflicted innocence. 

Truly, freedom of conscience <term>libertas conscientiarum: the right to hold religious beliefs without state coercion</term> is a priceless good granted from heaven, not to be traded for any royal purple or gold. Thus, justice—the pillar of laws and kingdoms alike—and a just peace—the steward and guardian of Commonwealths—and Christian Charity—the hallmark of the Christian people—and faith, sanctioned by the oaths of Kings and the Estates <note>The "Estates" refers to the social and political ranks of the Polish parliament, or Sejm.</note> as the unshakable foundation of the state; all these things, along with the sanctity of public law and the public safety (which all converge in this matter I now approach), demand by their own right the protection of every good man and easily obtain it. This is my current task: to demonstrate that all these values are being violated by a prevailing faction against a weaker one, under the unjust pretext of "heresy," and I do so without intending harm or offense to anyone, but to vindicate the innocence of the afflicted. Therefore, the UNITARIANS <note>The Unitarians, also known as the Polish Brethren or Socinians, were a non-trinitarian group that faced increasing persecution in the 17th century.</note>

<summary>A Polish nobleman begins a formal defense of the Unitarians, arguing that the religious freedoms established by the Warsaw Confederation are being illegally undermined by the majority. He frames freedom of conscience as a divine gift and an essential foundation of the Polish state.</summary>

# VINDICATION

...who in the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the annexed provinces—* no less than in the kingdom of Transylvania—profess **ONE GOD THE FATHER, AND HIS ONLY-BEGOTTEN SON JESUS CHRIST** our Lord with the Holy Spirit. By right and merit, they should be called **UNITARIANS** and **CHRISTIANS**, because of their faith in Christ and their call through him to the One God; yet, contrary to the conviction of their own faith and soul, † they are called by other hateful titles. They ought to enjoy peace and public liberty, which is based on the covenant of our Ancestors, the oaths of the Elected Kings, and the public laws. As long as that covenant of our Ancestors and their oath remain standing, along with due justice and equity, the rights of the Unitarians must also stand. This, I say, is what it falls upon me to prove with suitable documents. And indeed, I rightly undertake this defense of the faith of our Ancestors and Kings, and of our own innocence, since that unfair and reckless accusation does not fall silent even in this time—already so disastrous and in such need of divine grace—but rather charges that this [tolerance] neither can nor should be done. But rather, with that ancient and necessary law of oblivion <note>original: *lex oblivionis*; a legal concept similar to an amnesty, where past religious grievances are "forgotten" to maintain civil peace.</note> having been restored, the Unitarians...

<margin>
* [*No less than in the kingdom of Transylvania.*] For the Prince of Transylvania confirms by oath the rights of the Reformed, the Unitarians, the Saxons adhering to the Augsburg Confession <note>The "Augustan Confession" is the primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church.</note>, and the Roman Catholics <note>original: *Pontificiorum*, a term often used for those loyal to the Pope.</note>. The Unitarians are prominent in Cluj <note>original: *Claudiopolis*</note> and Turda <note>original: *Thorda*</note>, and they have more than 200 churches in Transylvania and the land of the Szeklers <note>original: *Siculia*; the Szeklers are a Hungarian-speaking ethnic group in Transylvania.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
† [*They are called by other hateful titles.*] Specifically, they are called *Anabaptists*. This is despite the fact that our practice—the baptism of Catechumens <term>Catechumens: adults receiving formal instruction in Christian doctrines before being baptized</term> (that is, those instructed in the Christian faith and professing the Apostles' Creed) by the immersion of the whole body in water—is confirmed by the authority of Holy Scripture and the practice of the ancient Church. Furthermore, the Unitarian brothers do not compel those who were baptized as infants to repeat their baptism. They are also called *Arians*; I believe this is used as a pretext to revive ancient grievances. But the Arians believed that the Son of God actually existed before his Mother, and even before Adam and the creation of the world; that he was created out of nothing, appeared to the Patriarchs and Prophets, and was finally incarnated. These were the things they argued, following Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, and other Fathers as the authors of their dogma. This in no way agrees with our confession of faith. Indeed, the Arians bitterly persecuted the disciples of Photinus (Bishop of Sirmium) and Paul of Samosata (Bishop of Antioch). These men, retaining the faith of the first Christians—the Nazarenes, the Ebionites, and others of the first and second centuries—upheld the primitive truth, which we also confess.
</margin>

### OF THE UNITARIORANS, etc.

...tarians, who are modest, quiet citizens devoted to the public good, there must be a promised observation of an equal peace and liberty—guarded and fortified in every better way—that is as strict and accurate as that which they experienced from their Ancestors. Nothing would be more fitting for the present state of our shared fatherland than if mutual concord in civil affairs and tolerance in sacred matters were restored to us, and if we consulted for the common good. Otherwise, the faith of our Ancestors, of all of us, and of so many Kings, the majesty of the Laws, our common peace, equal liberty, equity, and the Republic itself will not stand. 

Our common ancestors foresaw these evils of perjury and the oppression of minds. They were made cautious and fair by the calamities of France and neighboring Germany, which arose from "holy wars" <note>This refers to the French Wars of Religion and the conflicts in the Holy Roman Empire (like the Schmalkaldic War), which the author uses as a warning against religious intolerance.</note> that shook the most flourishing empires and filled all things with the sword, fire, blood, ashes, devastation, and wailing. Indeed, after the death of King Augustus <note>Sigismund II Augustus (1520–1572), the last monarch of the Jagiellonian dynasty, whose death triggered the first "free election" of a Polish king.</note>, the last of the Jagiellonians, when the people moved toward a freer election—one devoid of any hereditary right (the fame of which reached even as far as France, then burning with holy war, to find Henry Valois <note>Henry III of France (1551–1589), who was elected King of Poland in 1573 but famously abandoned the Polish throne to return to France after his brother died.</note>, upon whom they conferred the reins of government)—they formed a general treaty at Warsaw <note>The Warsaw Confederation of 1573, a landmark document in the history of religious freedom, which granted rights to "dissenters in religion."</note> on January 28, in the year of our salvation 1573. In this treaty, they provided above all else that in an equal Republic, regardless of the diversity of opinions on faith, an equal peace and liberty should be preserved, forever unshaken. It is pleasing here to insert the very words taken from the body of Polish laws and rendered into English: 

*“This especially the elected King shall confirm to us by oath: to preserve public peace among those split and divided in faith and religion.”* 

And shortly after: 

*“Since, however, in our Republic there is no small disagreement in the matter of the Christian Religion, we—meeting this challenge so that no harmful sedition arises among men for that cause (as we clearly see happening in other Kingdoms)—mutually promise for ourselves and our successors forever, under the bond of an oath, on our faith, honor, and consciences: that we who are dissenters in religion <note>original: *dissidentes de religione*; a technical legal term in Poland used to describe all those who did not belong to the state-sanctioned Catholic Church.</note> will preserve peace among ourselves; and because of different faiths and differences in Churches, we will not shed blood, nor will we inflict punishments such as confiscation of goods, infamy, imprisonment, or exile; nor will we assist any magistrate or office in such a deed in any way. Rather, if anyone...”*

...would wish to shed blood for that cause, we shall all be bound to oppose him, even if he wishes to do so under the pretext of a decree or some legal proceeding. That clause was also added: *We all mutually promise to preserve all these things constantly for our posterity and to hold them under our faith, honor, and consciences. Whoever, however, should wish to oppose this convention and to destroy public peace and union, we shall all rise up against such a person for his destruction.* This is that Union <term>Syncretismus: here referring to a political harmonizing or union of different factions for the sake of the state</term> of the Estates, this is the bond of the confederation, this is the uniquely necessary method for preserving everyone in eternal peace and liberty, and for keeping citizens who disagree in religion in their duty—a method rightly, prudently, and opportunely entered into by all the Estates. 

I do not deny, indeed, that this law—although passed with the unanimous consent and applause of the Political Estates <note>The secular nobility and officials in the Sejm (Parliament)</note> at the proper time, place, and in the proper manner—was not admitted or approved by the Sacred Order <note>The Roman Catholic clergy</note> and the Masovians <note>The inhabitants of the Masovia region, known for their staunch religious conservatism</note>, as new things are always subject to suspicion. In this matter, Piotr Myszkowski followed in his footsteps; while he signed the confederation of the Estates of Kraków during the time of the second interregnum in the year 1586—to which that blessed article concerning the preservation of peace among those dissenting in religion was joined—he reflected the legacy of Krasiński not only in the Bishopric of Kraków but also in this equity and benevolence of mind toward those dissenting from his Church, and indeed toward the public peace. So too did Wawrzyniec Goślicki, the Bishop of Kamianets and Bishop-elect of Chełm, sign the general confederation of all the Estates of Poland and Lithuania at Warsaw on the 7th of March in the General Convention the following year.
