# OF THE UNITARIANS, etc.

...was sanctioned and approved by the decrees of Kings. But it is even more significant that such a useful and necessary law of the Republic was repeatedly approved by the Political Estates <note>The secular nobility and officials in the parliament</note> as they renewed their ancestral alliance: for instance, on December 27, 1586; and in 1587 on March 7, May 8, and again elsewhere on May 9, August 19, and October 8; and in the year 1632. Among these instances, it was also sanctioned by the oaths of Kings, taken three times using this specific formula: 

*I shall protect and maintain peace and tranquility among those who disagree in religion; nor shall I permit anyone to be harmed or oppressed for the sake of religion by any means, whether by our jurisdiction or by the authority of any of our offices or Estates; nor shall I myself harm or oppress anyone,* 

as read in the *Code of Polish Laws*, pages 226 and 227. And the elected Kings of Poland took this oath many times—in order to grant even greater trust to this perpetual law—during the acts of election and coronation, and they approved this sanction of the agreed peace: 

As Henry <note>Henry of Valois, the first elected king of the Commonwealth</note> did in Paris <note>original: "Lutetia"</note> on September 10, 1573 (following the sharp challenge by Jan Zborowski, the Starosta <term>Capitaneus: a royal administrative official</term> of Odolanów and one of the envoys, who told the initially reluctant king: *“If you will not swear, you shall not reign”*); and in Kraków during the Coronation assembly on February 21, 1574. 

Stephen <note>Stephen Báthory</note> of Somlyó <note>original: "Meggiesii"</note> likewise did so on February 8, 1576, through several charters, and in Kraków at the Coronation assembly on May 4, in the presence of four Bishops. 

Sigismund III, in the confirmation of the *pacta conventa* <term>Agreed Covenants: the contractual conditions signed by elected kings</term> made between the Estates of Poland and the Swedish envoys near Warsaw during the Sejm <term>Comitia: the Polish parliament</term> on August 19, 1587; then in Kraków at the Coronation assembly on December 28 of that same year; and in the "recess" <note>The final resolutions or acts of a parliamentary session</note> of the Coronation Sejm in Kraków on January 30, 1588; and shortly before that, on January 8, in a charter confirming all rights in the presence of the Archbishop Primate, five Bishops, many Senators, nobles, and knights holding various offices throughout the kingdom and its several districts <term>Satrapias: provinces or administrative divisions</term>, as well as provincial delegates. 

Władysław [IV] also swore several times in November 1632 and February 1633, as did the most Serene surviving King, John Casimir, in 1648 and 1649, following the ancestral custom regarding election and coronation. I will pass over the fact that this law for maintaining peace among those who disagree in religion was approved and established by parliamentary law several times, specifically in Kraków on May 30, 1576, and December 28, 1587.

# DEFENSE

In the years 1631 and 1633: For these reasons, without a violation of the fundamental law, public faith, equality, and the just liberty of the common peace—as well as the Oath and conscience of so great a Kingdom—neither the alliance of the dissenters <note>The "Pax Dissidentium" or Warsaw Confederation, which granted legal status to non-Catholics</note> nor the article regarding the preservation of peace among themselves could be violated. If this had been observed as was right, the Cossacks <term>Cosaci: the semi-autonomous military societies of the Ukrainian frontiers</term> would not have rebelled; they would not have brought their Tartar and Muscovite <note>Allies from the Crimean Khanate and the Grand Duchy of Moscow</note> allies into the very heart of the kingdom, resulting in so many slaughters <note>original: "cladibus," transcribed as "clendis"</note> of the Polish and Lithuanian armies and the unspeakable calamities of the provinces. > We broke the laws; the winds have snatched away

> Exiled Equity has birthed for us

Hence, there are so many obvious examples of those who accelerated the destruction of themselves and their own people when they broke faith given even to Turks or Pagans (such as the Gibeonites and Babylonians of old). -># THE UNITARIORS, etc.<-

...of the Polish people, we have a clear and homegrown example. Indeed, the ancient Doctors of the Church—Ambrose in Books 2 and 3 of *On Duties*, Augustine in questions 13 and 14 on *Joshua*, Nicholas of Lyra on *Joshua*, and others—teach that faith must be kept even to those who are faithless <note>original: "perfidis"; here referring to those of a different or "wrong" faith</note>. It is not fitting for a Prince to endure saying to some barbarian or infidel, *My tongue swore, but my mind remains unsworn* <note>original: "Lingua iuravi mentem iniuratam gero." This is a famous line from Euripides often used to discuss the ethics of oaths.</note>, or, *Did you not know that my tongue is not made of bone?* <note>A proverb meaning that words are flexible and can be easily taken back or twisted.</note> For what remains to a Prince if he dares to violate that faith which must be kept and cherished as untainted, or that conscience which must be guarded more diligently than the pupil of one’s eye?

Therefore, if our ancestors and so many of our Kings had given and sworn their word to preserve peace even with Turks <term>Turcis: the Ottoman Empire</term> and Pagans—not only with heretics and schismatics—it still had to be kept. Those who disagree with the Roman Church—including the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox</note>, the Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note>, and the Unitarians—should not have been afflicted with so many injuries in violation of so many treaties, oaths, and laws.

And surely it is a beautiful thing, pleasing to God and to honest and prudent men, when subjects—though diverse in nation, customs, language, dress, and religion—nevertheless enjoy a harmony of minds, common liberty, and necessary equality. They live quietly under one sky, one sun, and one King, experiencing his equal favor toward them. They enjoy common goods, are held by equal right without discrimination, and equally suffer or repel common evils!

But who is there who does not see, on the contrary, that it is the height of injustice if a Prince is unwilling for his subjects to enjoy equal right and liberty (especially in a free Republic <term>Respublica: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</term>), and expects all to carry common burdens equally, but wants only some to enjoy the common benefits? By this reasoning, the hearts of the nobility are alienated from both the King and the Republic, if the former acts not as a Father but as a stepfather, and the latter acts not as a mother but as a stepmother.

And is it not as consistent with reason as it is healthy for the public state to join together citizens who are divided by dogmas of faith with the "tenacious glue of tolerance"? This prevents them from harassing and oppressing one another, and from not only shaking the Republic with internal hatreds and upheavals, but tearing it apart and overturning it entirely. Is it not also consistent with equity that, beyond the bonds of a common fatherland and obedience, they should love and tolerate one another, bound by the ties of blood, kinship, and friendship, and maintain a sincere con-

# VINDICIAE

...should they not maintain harmony among themselves and enjoy equal liberty, even if they differ in opinions regarding faith and consequently in their consciences (by which everyone is bound to God alone)? Does not piety, after all, demand this most of all? For what does the sacred page of the New Testament <term>novi fœderis: literally "New Covenant"</term> emphasize and commend more than love even for enemies, than harmony, and charity—the unique token of Christ’s true disciples, the bond of perfection, the fulfillment of the law, and the covering of many sins? And does not the Supreme Monarch <note>referring to God</note> lead the way for us, both by His example and His command, to tolerate rather than to eliminate and uproot those who disagree with us in faith? Therefore, Theodatus, King of the Goths, once rightly said: *Since the Divinity permits diverse religions, we do not dare to impose just one.* Princes have the rights of Majesty and the sword from God, but they do not have rights over consciences; God has granted this to no one. Indeed, He has reserved these three things for Himself alone, *in which He neither wishes to nor can have an equal: to create something from nothing, to foreknow the future, and to rule over consciences.* 

For this is truly a royal sentiment, worthy of the most praised King of Poland, Stephen <note>Stephen Báthory (reigned 1575–1586), a proponent of the Warsaw Confederation which guaranteed religious freedom</note>. Just as Emperor Maximilian II <note>Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1564–1576), known for his moderate and tolerant religious policies</note> most wisely said: *those who wish to dominate the human conscience are invading the very citadel of heaven.* When Henry of Valois <note>Henry III of France, who was briefly King of Poland before returning to France</note> was leaving Poland, and likewise most truly fifteen years later in France, as he was about to die from the blow of a murderous monk—having been taught by the very ones who harmed him—he said: *religion is a unique duty of man toward God, over which the carnal arm* <note>the "secular arm" or physical force of the state</note> *has no jurisdiction.* 

Therefore, to arrogate to oneself and cruelly exercise command over consciences—which belongs to God alone—is utterly contrary to God and to all equity. We will not now descend into the theological field to engage in a contest regarding the truth of the Catholic faith. However, this must be said, because it is useful for the public to know: a man should by no means be called a heretic—much less be harassed, killed, or at least deprived of public faith and liberty under the pretext of heresy—who adheres to the Apostles' Creed <note>original: "symbolo Apostolico"</note> as the most ancient, most true, and truly universal <note>original: "Catholico"; here used in its original sense of "universal" rather than "Roman Catholic"</note> confession, as the unique token of Christian baptism. If he holds it firmly and understands it just as it sounds, indeed resting in this simple and genuine faith, he prays to God and strives so that what in regenera- <note>The text continues on the next page with "regeneration."</note>

Furthermore, such a person is devoted to piety and justice, favors public peace and safety, obeys the civil magistrate, subjects himself to common laws, and pays public taxes. 

Such a man, I say, should be regarded as neither a heretic nor a seditious person in either an Ecclesiastical or a civil court, even if he disagrees with others on those specific points that either do not belong to the head and fundamental articles of faith contained in the **Apostles’ Creed**, or cannot be proven by the express words of Canonical Scripture, or cannot be comprehended by human reason. 

For, to provide divine testimony for these words: *Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God; and everyone who loves him who begot, loves also him who has been begotten of him. 1 John 5:1.* 

I say, therefore, that the Unitarians are included under the general name of **Dissidents in religion** <term>Dissidentes de religione: a specific legal category in Poland referring to those who disagreed with the dominant Catholic Church but were protected by the 1573 Warsaw Confederation</term> (who are protected by treaties, public laws, and the oaths of Kings in Poland). For they emphasize nothing more than faith in Christ Jesus, the Son of God, the Savior of the world, the heavenly King and Lord, the eternal High Priest, and the Judge of all. They adhere in all things to the **Apostles’ Creed**, with which alone the primitive Church was content. They receive, hold, and cherish in good faith everything in the sacred writings that abundantly teaches faith and the conduct of life. They condemn no one because of a different explanation of scripture, waiting until everyone is fully instructed by God; in the meantime, they sincerely testify to and prove by their actions love, equity, and modesty toward all. As Holy Scripture warns, they do not seek things higher than themselves; they do not dare to be "wise" beyond what is written, and they do not wish to violate with curious investigation those things which exceed all human understanding; and finally, they desire to live according to the laws of their fatherland. 

In the meantime, let them be considered heretics by those who dare to forget Christian faith and love. But because the basics of ancient simplicity are not believed to suffice for explaining such a great mystery, we therefore disagree in the explanation of these most holy names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—even though we are all baptized into them. Nevertheless, we cannot in any way justify depriving anyone of the name "Christian" who believes Jesus is the Christ, or rather, who believes and confesses the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that these three witnesses in heaven are one. Much less can we exclude such a person—provided they live piously and obey the laws—from the communion of the Church and eternal life, and certainly not from public peace and liberty, or from that **Warsaw Confederation** <note>The Warsaw Confederation of 1573 was a pioneering legal document in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth that guaranteed religious freedom and peace among different faiths</note>. 

To put it in a word: we all mutually agree and disagree—everyone who is counted as belonging to the faith in the name of Christ—according to whether each person, while holding to the rule of faith or departing from it, has embraced truth or falsehood. In the matters where we agree, it would be the height of impiety to harass and pursue one another in their name. But in the matters where we mutually disagree, we should not for that reason intend blows of persecution against one another. For our ancestors, by a sanctioned, holy, and perpetual covenant, took precautions for one another so that this would never happen under any pretext, whether of a decree...

# VINDICATION #

He denied, having experienced it himself along with others, that he had consented to that summary process in the Raków affair <note>original: "negoviano" — likely a variant for "Racoviano," referring to the town of Raków, the intellectual center of the Polish Unitarians</note> by a poorly-judged example, saying *Let it be for this one time* <note>original: "Fiat pro una vice"</note> during all the parliamentary proceedings of the year 1638. Nor is it far-fetched to say that the "Knightly Nymph" of that time <note>original: "Nympham Cavaleriam" — a poetic and perhaps sarcastic metaphor for the sudden, aggressive legal force or "cavalry" maneuver used in court</note>, who emerged from the fiery brain of the Vice-Chancellor <note>Likely referring to Jerzy Ossoliński, a powerful Catholic statesman who orchestrated the move against Raków</note> like an armed Pallas Athena <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom and war, said to have sprung fully formed and armed from the head of Zeus</note>, had declared war against the equal Polish liberty. She was seen while still tender and blushing from her parent, yet already oppressed and buried by others who were eager for her destruction. Her parent, having satisfied his desire for vengeance against the customs of the fatherland by hiding behind the oppression and burial of the liberty of a sect most hateful to him, achieved his goal. You have in hand the epitaph of this Knighthood written by a defender of ancient virtue and the faith of the Church (whoever he may be); you also have a worthy author...

<margin>*</margin> *Regarding the general Parliament of 1638.*] I shall explain this in a few words. Some students of the school of Raków <note>The Racovian Academy was famous throughout Europe for its high academic standards and radical theology</note>, through insolence, broke and cast down an image of the Lord's Passion <note>a roadside crucifix</note> with stones in a nearby field. Although those caught were brought to justice and suffered no physical punishment, the entire community, through a summary legal process <term>Summary process: An expedited legal proceeding that bypasses standard protections and delays</term> and a grave violation of precedent, was stripped of its church, printing house, and school. All innocent persons were proscribed and exposed to the whims of the malevolent by a decree full of ambiguities and injustice. Furthermore, against the decree issued in the Raków matter—as it was contrary to the liberty not only of the Unitarians, but also of the Greeks <note>Eastern Orthodox</note>, Evangelicals <note>Protestants such as Calvinists and Lutherans</note>, and even Catholics, and against the laws of the fatherland—the Land Envoys <term>Land Envoys: Polish "Nuncii Terrestres," the elected representatives of the nobility in the Sejm (Parliament)</term> or Delegates of the Provinces protested. These included not only Unitarians but also Evangelicals, Greeks, and even Catholics. Their names are listed here:

*   **Janusz Radziwiłł** <note>Janussius Radzivil</note>, Duke of Biržai and Dubingiai, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Grand Lord Chamberlain of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, etc., Delegate of the Vilkomir District.
*   **Jan Antoni Tyszkiewicz**, Cup-bearer of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Delegate of the Vilnius Palatinate.

*   **Jan Szlichtyng** of Bukowiec, Land Judge of Fraustadt, Delegate of the Poznań Palatinate.
*   **Zbigniew Gorzecki** of Góra, Delegate of the Lublin Palatinate.
*   **Mikołaj Woźniewicz** of Woźniki, Captain and Delegate of Starodub.
*   **Piotr Kolewski**, Land Judge and Delegate of the Brest Palatinate.
*   **Yurii Nemyrych** <note>Georgius Niemiritz</note> of Chernihiv, Delegate of the Kiev Palatinate.
*   **Yurii**, Prince of Chetvertyn <note>Georgius Dux in Cetwertyn</note>, Delegate of the Volhynian Palatinate.

-> UNITARIANS, etc. <-

The response opposed to that epitaph provides excellent documentation of this matter. One and the same infant, born for the ruin of ancestral liberty and wrongly suppressed and buried, lived again in those same assemblies; having cast off its Italian dress <note>A metaphor for foreign, specifically Roman or Jesuit, political influence</note> and put on Polish attire, it wished to be seen. Having been admitted into the midst, it prematurely reached maturity and, through the ruin of the Unitarians, advanced to the oppression of the Evangelicals <note>A general term for Protestants, including Lutherans and Calvinists</note>, and finally to the Catholics themselves. From that time, we see and still feel that the orbit of liberty—and of the entire Republic—has been overturned. 

For from that same birth was born that massive weight <note>original: "moles"</note> of the Turkish war, initiated without the consent of the Estates <note>The parliamentary orders of the Commonwealth</note> to test the limits of absolute rule. When this undertaking was undermined with a great loss of reputation and gold, the force of the Cossacks was stirred up to rouse and strengthen that same weight. Mindful of the injuries inflicted upon their social standing and their religion, and conscious of their own strength, the Cossacks unexpectedly turned their arms against the Republic and overwhelmed the leaders who were ignorant of the secret <note>Likely referring to secret diplomatic maneuvers or the "arcana imperii" (secrets of state) used by the King's faction</note>, and finally grew in power and audacity beyond their own desires. 

Therefore, even the saner men in our fathers' memory noticed that it is in the interest of the Greeks <note>Refers to the Eastern Orthodox citizens of the Commonwealth</note>, and especially the Evangelicals, that the rights of the Unitarians are not broken; otherwise, the Catholic party <note>original: "pars Pontificia"</note>—acting against those of us who labor under the greatest envy—will grow accustomed to harassing and persecuting those who differ from them, thereby strengthening their own arrogance. Certainly, equity persuades us of this, as does the necessity of preserving public peace and civil society: that fellow citizens should either agree or tolerate one another, treating each other with every kind of benevolence and duty, and diligently ensuring that the prevailing party (whichever it may be) does not oppress the weaker. 

**So in Transylvania**, where the Reformed <note>Calvinists</note> predominate, the weaker followers of the Augsburg Confession <note>Lutherans</note> and the Catholics live in concord with the Unitarians without any danger to their religion, and they work together so as not to be oppressed by the Reformed. By the same means of concord, the followers of the Augsburg Confession protect themselves alongside the Remonstrants in Holland. In such a Republic, where several religions already exist, there is no other way of preserving safety than for the more powerful party to be restrained by the concord of the weaker ones. In this, the weaker party does not sin in the least; rather, to say it as it is, it is in the interest of the stronger party to be kept within the boundaries of equity; otherwise, through its own powerlessness to resist its impulses, it may strike against <note>original catchword: "allidat"</note> the rocks of unbridled and confused license.

# VINDICIAE

It is necessarily strengthened. Who, moreover, would not see, even in the example of Solon <note>original: "Solonis"; Solon was the famous Athenian lawgiver who reformed debt-slavery to stabilize the state</note>, that no Republic is so strong that it does not have to fear danger from even the lowest slaves, should injury and opportunity arise? Therefore, the best method for preserving a state is this: that every person may enjoy their own right—whether inherited from their ancestors or acquired by their own merits—with equality. Nor indeed in the Polish Republic <note>The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note>, even though the Catholics <note>original: "Pontificii," referring to those loyal to the Pope</note> prevail, do those who dissent from them drag out a precarious life or obtain liberty by favor; rather, all enjoy common law, liberty, and peace, as is customary in a free Republic. We have learned, received, and read this law of living, sanctioned and fortified by our ancestors; we have been taught and made, instructed and imbued for this very purpose.

Let the Catholics not say that their religion in Poland is the steward <note>original: "oiconomam"</note> and mistress, while others are foreign and immigrant. For while it is true that every religion which differs from the Catholic or Greek <note>Refers to the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> is foreign and immigrant in Poland <note>In terms of historical arrival</note>, it is not so in the Christian world. But any religion which agrees with Holy Scripture and the Apostles' Creed, as our Unitarian faith does, should by no means be considered foreign, but should by right be judged the mistress and the only truly Catholic <note>The author is reclaiming the word "Catholic," which means "universal," arguing that their biblical faith is the true universal one</note> faith. Otherwise, the Samogitians <note>A group in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania who were among the last in Europe to be Christianized</note>, who are still in part devoted to the impious worship of idols and constitute a part of Lithuania, could rightly say to the Polish, Lithuanian, and Samogitian Catholics that their religion is foreign and immigrant, while their own [paganism] is the steward and mistress.

But indeed, *that is truer which is earlier; that is earlier which is from the beginning; and that is from the beginning which is from the Apostles,* as Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) often cited in debates about the antiquity and purity of faith</note> says. And all these same reasons fight for the liberty of the Evangelicals <note>Protestants, such as Lutherans and Calvinists</note>, as well as for the liberty of the Unitarians, against the arrogance of many Catholics (for not all are so unjust toward those who differ from them and toward our common liberty and peace). I say, therefore, that while the faith of our Confederate ancestors and our Kings remains intact, public tranquility and liberty are safe, and all our possessions are safe, provided that all those dissenting in religion—both Catholics and anti-Catholics (for both differ from each other in matters of faith, and the latter are as much dissenters to the former as the former are to the latter)—enjoy equal peace.

But truly, it is objected that the Unitarians cannot enjoy this, because...

### OF THE UNITARIANS, etc.

...[strengthened by the] public alliance of our Ancestors and the Royal oaths, as well as by the common peace and liberty. Why is this so? Because, our opponents say, that alliance and oath concern those who "dissent regarding the Christian religion," <note>The author refers to the *Dissidentes in religione*, the legal term for non-Catholics in the Warsaw Confederation of 1573</note> but these [Unitarians] are not dissenters *regarding* religion, but rather *from* the Christian religion. This claim is as true as saying that a man who professes only the **Apostles' Creed**, <note>original: "Symbolum Apostolicum"; the basic statement of early Christian belief</note> and therefore is nothing if not a Christian, is not actually a Christian. 

It is no wonder, then, that this distinction is a recent invention, unheard of by our ancestors. They decreed, in general terms, that peace was to be maintained among all who "dissent regarding religion," whoever they might be that profess themselves to be Christians and who already at that time constituted a part of the citizenry. Certainly, they never intended to create some discrimination among themselves under the pretext of religion. Acting with that ancient Polish faith and sincerity toward one another, they decreed that no one should ever be harassed for the sake of conscience in their common fatherland. Indeed, they determined that all who dissent regarding religion ought to enjoy public peace and tranquility, as is fitting in a free Republic. 

Otherwise, they would have openly excluded the Unitarians at the very beginning of the alliance—which they entered into together with the rest of the citizens and confirmed with their signatures—and thus they would have boasted of having "crushed the heresy in the bud." <note>original: "hæresin se in herbis oppressisse"</note> But far from this thought entering their minds, they instead entrusted **Senatorial dignities**, as well as various royal and provincial offices and duties, to Unitarians for the good of the Republic. This is a fact that must now be proven.

And first, it is ready to hand for me to state and demonstrate that nearly thirty years before that **Warsaw Alliance** <note>The Warsaw Confederation of 1573, a landmark act of religious tolerance</note> was sanctioned, the seeds of the restored Unitarian opinion were sown. These seeds were spread not only by learned and pious men coming from Germany, Italy, and Poland, but especially by the most noble citizens of the kingdom, where they took firm root and grew successfully while still in their early stages. I pass over in silence the secret supporters among the Canons of Krakow—men who, having spurned the truth they hated, turned toward atheism; some of their number were promoted to the highest ecclesiastical dignities while laboring under the suspicion and even the infamy of heresy, and were marked by the censure of the Pope. 

But truly, through **Jan Trzecieski** and his son **Andrzej**, **Jan Filipowski** (a Royal Courtier), and **Jakub Przyłuski** (the District Notary of Krakow)—men of the highest nobility and conspicuous learning—the beginnings of the reformation were made during the reign of King **Sigismund I**.

# OF THE UNITARIANS, ETC.

[They] were not only not excluded from that confederation <note>The Warsaw Confederation of 1573, a landmark agreement guaranteeing religious peace and equality among the nobility</note> at its very beginning, but a large part of those who then governed the Republic struck that treaty. They approved and fortified it—along with the acts of all subsequent Interregnums <note>The periods between the death of one king and the election of the next</note> and Elections—by adding their signatures alongside those of the other citizens. 

That the **Unitarians** retained this right of treaty without controversy during the reigns of Kings Henry <note>Henry Valois, r. 1573–1575</note> and Stephen <note>Stephen Báthory, r. 1576–1586</note>, while liberty of conscience and the Republic flourished, is proven by a significant number of examples. I speak of those who held the chief Senatorial dignities and courtly and provincial offices in the Kingdom and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. 

First among these is **Jan Kiszka of Ciechanowiec**, Governor of Samogitia <note>term: "Gubernator"; specifically the Elder/Starosta of Samogitia, a position with senatorial rank</note> and Cup-bearer <note>term: "Pincerna"; a prestigious court office</note> to His Royal Majesty in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, later Castellan of Vilnius. Counted among the principal Senators and lords of Lithuania by these dignities, he was a most generous patron of the Unitarians. 

He is followed by **Jan Czaplic of Szpanów**, Castellan of Kyiv; then **Mikołaj Kazimirski of Biberstein**, Lord of Lewartów, an outstanding man, most famous for his embassies to the Sejm <note>original: "Comitia Regni"; the national parliament</note> and his fierce defense of liberty. 

To these I add **Stanisław Lubieniecki**, Treasurer of the Lublin district <note>original: "Quaestorem Satrapiae"</note> and a Deputy appointed to the courts of Sandomierz and Lublin. His three sons, seized by an unusual fervor, cast off not only the splendor of the Royal court but also the love of this fleeting world to become open professors and heralds of the Unitarian faith, free from all fear of danger or ill-will. 

Some of these men lived into the time of **Sigismund III** <note>Sigismund III Vasa, r. 1587–1632, known for his strong support of the Catholic Counter-Reformation</note>, adding to the number of those who followed. For although Sigismund (who found seven Catholics in the Senate and left only five Protestants) promoted no Unitarian to Senatorial rank except for **Stanisław Cikowski**, he did not deny them court and provincial offices. Indeed, at his election, the Marshal of the Equestrian Order <note>term: "Mareschalcus Ordinis Equestris"; the Speaker of the House of Deputies, the lower house of parliament</note> was **Paweł Orzechowski**...

### VINDICATIONS

->### OF THE UNITARIORUMS, etc.<-

Even if I remain silent, the facts speak for themselves, and the abundance of examples provided—which was not suggested by boastfulness or a desire for vain glory, but forced out by necessity even against my will—proves the right and the exercise of the liberty of the Unitarian Brethren, in which they have rejoiced equally with other Polish citizens and still rejoice today. What of the fact that the Unitarians, along with the rest of the Polish citizens, have consistently and within the memory of our ancestors obtained, without contradiction, a place in the assemblies of the Equestrian Order <note>The *Equestris Ordo* refers to the Szlachta, the Polish nobility who held exclusive political rights</note> and the power of speaking their opinions, casting votes, and being chosen not only as officials, judges, and delegates, but even as electors of Kings, along with other rights of the nobility? 

Rightly, therefore, does wonder seize the mind of every upright and fair man as to how it happens that, while the Polish nation—to the envy of foreigners—retains and displays its enviable liberty, such inequality can nevertheless exist in so equal a Republic under the pretext of religion. To exclude the Unitarians (whose ancestors performed various most eminent senatorial duties, and many of whose brothers still hold most honorable offices) from the peace and liberty fortified by so many treaties of our ancestors, oaths of Kings, and public laws, is nothing other than to wish to turn an equal into an unequal, a Senator into a commoner, an elector of Kings into a slave <note>original: "mancipium"</note>, a knight into a stable boy, a commander and high officer into a camp follower, an heir into a household servant, a free and well-born man into a slave, and a Pole into a non-Pole. 

Behold where such injustice leads! Are such things to be endured in a free Republic, in a state that is popular and equal? That this or that man, prevailing and trusting in his own strength, should deprive a citizen—his equal—of his birthright and ancestral liberty because of a different opinion of faith? A liberty which he did not give to him, since both received it from their ancestors, and indeed with so many and such great protestations and oaths as we have seen. 

I appeal to your faith and equity, O CITIZENS, and by the common rights of our fatherland’s liberty, by the sworn faith of our ancestors’ treaty, by the public peace and safety, by the bonds of blood and all things sacred, I implore you: see what the enemies of liberty and equality are doing or what they are meditating—those minds serving ambition and hating the ancient state of the Republic! Under the cover now of this heresy, now of that, or of some crime, and even with a sought-after pretext, they [invade/infringe] the common rights...

They have undermined, violated, and weakened [these rights], either while you were not paying attention, or looking the other way, or even while you were secretly laughing and repeating, *“Well done, it’s not so bad after all!”* <note>original: "Euge, ne sic quidem male"</note> Believe me, these internal and domestic enemies provoke and stir up wars, wearing down the **Equestrian Order** <note>The *Equestris Ordo* refers to the Szlachta, the Polish nobility who held exclusive political rights</note> with disasters and taxes, while they themselves remain out of harm’s reach. They will concentrate all power into the hands of a few who are more easily corrupted and open to bribery. O fellow citizens, you do not yet lack the means to restore liberty to those citizens oppressed under the pretext of religion, nor to restore the state and public freedom. Look around for those who favor the liberty of our homeland; seek out and cultivate their friendship. If you return to the fairness and moderation of our ancestors, freely offering the reins of government to the most excellent and worthy man when the time for the **Election** <note>The Polish King was elected by the nobility, a cornerstone of their political system</note> arrives, then it shall be said among the nations:

-> OF THE UNITARIANS, etc. <-

See whether your own ancestors did not profess the **Evangelical** or **Unitarian** religion. Look for your own ancestors among these men: you will surely recognize—and I believe not unwillingly—that all these from whose blood you are descended enjoyed their ancestral birthright and the common liberty. What, then, prevents their descendants today from experiencing the same fairness? Truly, we depart far from the faith and equity of our ancestors if we exclude those who profess the Evangelical or Unitarian faith not only from Senatorial dignities and the principal offices, but even from the public peace and the enjoyment of our common liberty and light, stripping them of honor, reputation, inheritance, succession, and every right.

> Indeed, you bring home exceptional praise and ample spoils. <note>original: "Egregiam vero laudem & spolia ampla refertis." A sarcastic quotation from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (4.93), used here to shame the oppressors for their "victory" over their fellow citizens.</note>

Therefore, what was permitted to your ancestors, even though others adhered to the Roman Church, let it also be permitted to me—even if you yourself adhere to that Church, or have returned to it after abandoning the faith of your ancestors or parents. *For who (especially in a free Republic) may impose upon me the necessity of either believing what I do not wish, or not believing what I do wish?* says the eloquent <note>original: "lacteus," literally "milky," a common epithet for Lactantius referring to his smooth, sweet, and persuasive style.</note> **Lactantius**. If this or that faith is good and true and genuine, it ought to be instilled by teaching rather than by commanding—and much less by harming—by advising rather than by threatening, as **Augustine** writes elsewhere. By the judgment of that same man, <term>Heretics</term> <note>At this time, "heretic" was a legal and theological label used by the state church for anyone outside the Roman Catholic faith.</note> are not to be punished with death, nor killed by any laws, but ought to be cut off from the Catholic Church by the sword of the spirit alone. And this is the genius of the true faith, this is its character: that it desires to be instilled gently and taught calmly, and commends itself to all by its very modesty.

They remained loyal to him there, yet they did not take up arms against the fatherland. They did not involve themselves in war councils against their own people (to which they were never even called or admitted). They were satisfied with freedom of conscience and the free exercise of religion, which they had enjoyed in that capital city <note>Kraków.</note>, as in other chief cities, under King Stephen <note>Stephen Bathory, reigned 1576–1586, known for his religious tolerance.</note> and at the beginning of Sigismund's reign <note>Sigismund III Vasa, reigned 1587–1632.</note> (and sometimes nearly a decade before the death of Augustus <note>Sigismund II Augustus, died 1572, the last Jagiellonian king.</note>). They rejoiced and offered vows and prayers for the safety of the fatherland and public peace, submitting themselves in all things to God's providence and the times.

They provided no service to the Swedes, except that one man of German origin was occasionally employed by the Governor of Kraków to write Latin letters. Some, however, were sent with letters by that same Governor in whose power they then were; they preferred to lose their lives rather than break their sworn oath. And thus did that body of the Unitarian Brethren in Kraków conduct itself. As is indeed evident...

# OF THE UNITARIANS, etc.

household and private actions of certain individuals do not bind the entire Unitarian society, such that they should be held to answer for them, much less be made to suffer. Likewise, the deed of those who remained in Kraków under the sworn faith of the Patron King <note>Charles X Gustav of Sweden, who occupied Kraków in 1655.</note> does not obligate the community of Unitarians, nor can it deservedly excite suspicions and persecutions against all Unitarians in the minds of the common people. They await its peace, tranquility, and restoration to its former state, which divine and human laws teach should be open to everyone and not considered a crime. 

By this reasoning, they cast off neither their sworn faith nor the love due to the Fatherland (which, as someone has said, "embraces all affections" <note>original: *omnes charitates complectitur*. But indeed, hostility turns faith into treachery and virtue into vice. On the contrary, the constant and invincible faith of the Unitarians, which they kept toward the Swedish King (though he was a foreigner) as it had been given and sworn together with the Republic, ought to be proof that they can only be faithful to their own Kings and Lords—a fact they have always testified to until now.

For at that time, there was no other method of preserving safety available either to the Republic or to the Unitarians. Nor was it an option for the Unitarians to resist the whole Republic, as they were subjecting themselves to the Patron King—a King whom the entire Republic was not then resisting.

Many of the Unitarians living in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and in the Palatinates of Lublin, Belz, and parts of Ruthenia, being further removed from the Swedes, had no necessity to pledge their faith to them; indeed, they took up arms against the Swedes along with the rest of the citizens. Many also withdrew into Hungary or Silesia, waiting intently on the outcome of events. Undoubtedly, everyone would have departed for Hungary or Silesia if it had been permitted for these miserable people to snatch their lives and dear possessions—as if from the midst of a flame—and transport them to foreign lands. This was prevented by the provincial and peasant bandits <note>Refers to the "Chłopi" or local insurgents who often targeted non-Catholics during the Swedish "Deluge."</note> raging against the Swedes and slaughtering the "heretics" (for so all anti-papists <note>original: "Antipontificii"</note> were commonly called), but especially the Unitarians and Swedes alike, while also blockading the road passes.

But when no other way of preserving their safety was left, they betook themselves to Kraków under the protection of the Patron King, and there they remained under his authority. However, they did not take up arms against the fatherland, nor did they involve themselves in military councils against their own people (to which they were neither invited nor admitted). They were content with liberty of conscience and the free exercise of their religion, which they had enjoyed under King Stephen <note>Stephen Báthory (reigned 1576–1586), known for religious tolerance.</note> and at the beginning of the reign of Sigismund <note>Sigismund III Vasa (reigned 1587–1632).</note> (as well as nearly a decade before the death of Augustus <note>Sigismund II Augustus (died 1572), the last Jagiellonian king, who oversaw the height of the Polish Reformation.</note>). Just as they had held these rights in other royal cities, so they held them in that Metropolis <note>Kraków.</note>; and they offered vows and prayers for the safety of the fatherland and public peace, subjecting themselves in all things to God's ordinance and the circumstances of the time.

They provided no assistance to the Swedes, except that one man, a German by birth, was occasionally employed by the Governor of Kraków <note>The Swedish commander Paul Wirtz.</note> to write Latin letters. Certain others were sent with letters by the same Governor, in whose power they then were, and they preferred even to lose their lives rather than break their sworn faith. And thus the body of the Unitarian Brethren in Kraków conducted itself. Truly, as...

### OF THE UNITARIANS, etc.

T 3
<meta>catchword: No-</meta>

...particular and private actions of certain individuals do not bind the entire Unitarian society, such that they should be held responsible for them, much less be made to suffer for them. Thus, the actions of those who remained in Kraków, having sworn their loyalty to the Patron King <note>Charles X Gustav of Sweden, who occupied Kraków during the war.</note>, do not obligate the Unitarian community as a whole, nor can they rightly provoke suspicion and persecution against all Unitarians in the minds of the common people. In such great confusion of affairs and the fatal necessity of the Commonwealth <note>original: "Respublica"; referring to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.</note>, each person does what harsh necessity extorts from them for their own good or ill. 

Ultimately, some departed with the Kraków garrison because of the hatred of many nobles and commoners, amidst a thousand reproaches and horrifying threats. They lost their goods, possessions, and their reputations as honorable men and citizens, rather than lose their consciences, and so that they might withdraw themselves from this hatred for a time. And they indeed remain in the faith of the one to whom they once swore <note>They maintained their oath of loyalty to the Swedish King even in exile.</note>, but they act only for their own sake, without harm to anyone—much less to the fatherland—and they await its peace, tranquility, and restoration to its former state. Divine and human laws teach that this path should be open to anyone and should not be considered a crime. 

For in this way, they cast off neither their sworn faith nor the love due to the Fatherland (which, as someone once said, embraces all affections). But envy turns loyalty into treachery and virtue into vice; whereas the constant and unconquerable faith of the Unitarians—which they kept as given and sworn with the Commonwealth to the Swedish King, even though he was a foreigner—ought to be proof that they can only be faithful to their own Kings and Lords, as they have always testified until now. 

Therefore, against all the accusations of the malevolent, I offer nothing else to vindicate the faith and innocence of my Brothers, and the untarnished reputation of our religion, than what is contained in the speech delivered to the Prince of Transylvania <note>George II Rákóczi, a Protestant prince who invaded Poland in 1657 as an ally of Sweden.</note> when we greeted him on March 29, 1657, in the Royal Palace of Kraków (for it could not be done otherwise). *“We,”* the speech says, *“whose crimes our countrymen were going to expiate with our innocent blood <note>This implies the Unitarians were being used as scapegoats for the nation's misfortunes.</note>, had we not been snatched away and preserved to this day by the protection of divine providence. For it is no secret to your Most Serene Highness in what manner our leaders, our armies, and all the inhabitants of this Kingdom surrendered themselves under the patronage and protection of His Sacred Royal Majesty of Sweden by sworn faith. We were among the number of the other citizens.”* No-

# VINDICATION

[...continued from previous page] councils with the Most Serene King of Sweden, we never joined forces in arms; rather, we bore the greatest injuries, with which we were harassed on account of our conscience, with the utmost patience. We did only what everyone else did: when the King had been driven out of the kingdom, those in the most immediate peril of the fatherland believed they were plainly released from the oath of loyalty by which they had been bound to their King. We, however, preserved our loyalty to the Most Serene King Casimir to the very end; we aided him with all public taxes even beyond our strength, we were present for him in every military expedition, we risked our own lives for his safety in times of danger, and we lost many of our own people—some even their sons—who fought most bravely for the fatherland. We were all prepared to die for our King. 

But when he himself deserted the kingdom as affairs became desperate, and was in turn deserted by all the inhabitants of the Realm, what small portion of us remained? We would have been a burden to the King as he withdrew outside the kingdom, rather than any help. Therefore, we remained with the others in our native land, and when everyone else surrendered to the Most Serene King of Sweden, we alone could not resist this course of action.

What happened next, Most Serene Prince? Not long after, having found what seemed to them a favorable opportunity, our detractors changed their plan; they also changed the loyalty they had sanctioned by oath and raised arms everywhere against the Most Serene King of Sweden. They wished to sanction and consecrate this new undertaking of theirs—so that it might be successful and auspicious—with our blood. They did this for no other reason than that we appeared to them to be heretics. 

They published an Edict and caused it to be proclaimed everywhere, letting loose the unrestrained fury of peasants and bandits on all sides. It ordered that the "Lutherans" <note>original: "Lutheri"; the author notes that their enemies used this as a derogatory label for all Protestants and Unitarians.</note> (for so they love to call us) should be slaughtered wherever they could be found, just like the Swedes. They were to be plundered, their goods snatched, their possessions devastated, and every kind of hostility and cruelty was to be exercised against them with impunity. 

That Edict was immediately put into action. As many as were caught were all miserably slaughtered; some were even consumed by fire. Their goods were snatched, their houses despoiled, and to some who were cruelly murdered, no burial was granted other than the **burial of a donkey** <term>asini sepultura: a biblical reference to being left unburied or thrown into a pit like a carcass, considered a final, ultimate indignity.</term>, their bodies being thrown to the dogs and vultures to be torn apart. Thus, the rage against these wretched people continued even beyond death. 

What other choice was left to us here but to flee as quickly as possible—leaving behind everything that could not be carried away—and snatch our lives from a most cruel death? The fury of the peasants <note>original: "Paganorum"; referring here to the rural commoners.</note>, led by their parish priests, followed some even as they fled, so that they escaped only with the greatest difficulty, leaving behind their children and all their baggage...

# OF THE UNITARIANS, etc.

...they lost. But where were we to flee? The borders of *Hungary* and *Silesia* <note>A region then mostly under the Bohemian Crown, now largely in Poland</note> were closed to us with the same cruelty. No other refuge remained except to flee to those under whose protection and patronage we had been placed, and on whose account we, though innocent, suffered such unspeakable and cruel things. By them, we were also kindly received and humanely treated. 

Although we escaped the savage hands of our fellow countrymen, we did not escape their bitter hatred and persecutions, solely because they were unable to kill us. They defame us as deserters of the fatherland and as traitors; they demand our slaughter; they sought us out through the triple siege of that city <note>Likely referring to the sieges of Kraków during the Swedish occupation</note>. Of these sieges, when two had been repelled, a third fell upon us, much heavier and longer than the previous two. Indeed, because of the unhappy outcome of the first two, it was begun and managed with much greater force. We miserable refugees, having consumed what we had brought with us, were oppressed by a poverty and want that worsened daily, and matters reached the point of starvation. The fame of the arrival of your Most Serene Highness dissipated such great darkness and gloom, brought light, and restored our spirit.

Now let the Christian world judge whether the <term>Unitarians</term> <note>A Restorationist Christian movement that rejected the Trinity</note>—who either conducted themselves in this manner for their own preservation during that transformation of the Republic, without the infamy of treachery or harm to the fatherland, or fought with their fellow citizens against the Swedes—can, while preserving the faith of the Ancestors and Kings, be excluded from liberty and public peace. Truly, I believe no one who weighs the matter with a fair scale, without the religious prejudice (with which we are undeservedly pressed), would say so. 

For we do not dwell on what the author of the *Theatrum Europæum* <note>original: "Theatri Europæi"; a famous 17th-century chronicle of European events</note> writes—a man ignorant of Polish affairs and deceived by a false report. He claims that in that <term>Charitable Colloquy of Toruń</term> <note>A 1645 meeting intended to reconcile different Christian denominations in Poland</note>, we first wished to attach ourselves to the <term>Reformed</term> <note>Calvinists</note>, but were shamefully rejected by them as those not numbered among the dissenters in the Christian religion and not included in the <term>Confederation of the Realm</term> <note>The Warsaw Confederation of 1573, which legally guaranteed religious freedom for "dissidents in religion"</note>; and that later in that same meeting we professed the <term>Augsburg Confession</term> <note>The primary statement of faith of the Lutheran Church</note>. This is false. Indeed, all to whom truth and equity are dear both confess and know that the matter is plainly otherwise, and was handled differently at that time. We openly professed our Unitarian Confession (which had already been published in print in the year 1642, written according to the articles of the Apostles' Creed) before the Bishop...

# VINDICATIONS

...of Samogitia <note>A historical region in present-day Lithuania</note>. The Presiding Officer of that Colloquy, along with the entire circle of those sitting with him, and the King himself, when he understood that we had appeared at the first session in the year 1644, [decided that] for the second session in the year '45, he would invite not all those <term>Dissidents</term> <note>A legal term for non-Catholics in Poland who were granted religious liberty</note> from the Roman Church as he had before, but only the associates of the <term>Augsburg</term> <note>Lutheran</note> and <term>Reformed</term> <note>Calvinist</note> Confessions.

Indeed, the same King, in letters given to the people of Danzig <note>original: "Dantiscanos"; now Gdańsk, Poland</note> before the second session, explained his mind more openly: that he was inviting to that colloquy only those Dissidents in the Christian religion who profess the Holy Trinity. He was signaling publicly that we are indeed also Dissidents in the Christian religion, but that we were not invited to this colloquy—doubtless on the advice of the clergy <note>original: "spiritualium"</note>. They understand that we rely on no Councils and no Church Fathers for our articles of faith, but on the Holy Scriptures alone. From these Scriptures, they themselves believe that many articles of faith which they hold in common with the Lutherans and Reformed—and even this very article regarding the Holy Trinity, as it is believed by them—cannot be proven.

Since things stand this way, we owe no response to that impudent slanderer who deceived the credulous author of the *Theatrum* <note>likely referring to the *Theatrum Europaeum*, a famous contemporary chronicle of world events</note>, nor to that imprudent writer. *For a firebrand thrown into a river is extinguished of its own accord.* <note>original: "Titio enim in fluvium conjectus per se extinguitur"</note>

And therefore, anyone who wishes to render a fair judgment on these matters easily sees that, according to equity and reason, and the intent of our ancestors' covenant <note>The Warsaw Confederation of 1573, which established religious peace</note>, and the King's oath: the <term>Unitarians</term> are included in that public covenant. They ought to enjoy not only common rights, but also the benefits of honors and offices, if consideration is given to faith, equity, and merit, as well as to liberty, peace, and public safety. Furthermore, in this most recent upheaval of our fatherland <note>The "Swedish Deluge," the invasion of Poland by Sweden</note>, they conducted themselves in a decent and appropriate manner, and cannot be stained by any treachery or any mark of infamy.

Let the malevolent, then, no longer come forward with their objections and accusations. These are truly as futile in themselves as they are useless to those who make them, to the Kings (upon whose consciences the faith of this covenant rests and can never be violated with impunity), and to the fatherland. I would wish them to be warned by the saying of the secular poet:

> —do not break the treaties of peace,
> Nor value loyalty less than kingdoms <note>original: "neu rumpite fœdera pacis / Neu regnis postferte fidem"; a quote from the Roman poet Silius Italicus</note>

By the public violation of such loyalty, entire kingdoms are brought to extreme ruin and destruction.
